gitarre.title: Guitar
gitarre.lead: P4: E2 A2 D3 G3 C4 F4. Tone, pulse and repeatable phrases of your own. Right hand uses only a pick; hammer-ons, pull-offs and tapping use the left hand.

keys.title: Keyboard
keys.lead: Melody with a steady accompaniment. Playable on synthesizer and piano.

p0.title: Foundation
p0.goal: Check clean note changes, P4 orientation, notation and pulse. Recall familiar skills briefly; practise specific difficulties.

p1.title: Tonic and phrase
p1.goal: Hear E as a reference. Shape small motifs through repetition, rests and variation.

k0.title: Foundation
k0.goal: Check touch, reading and basic coordination. One sound is enough.

k1.title: Tonic and phrase
k1.goal: A steady reference in the left hand, repeatable melody in the right. Deliberately distinguish Aeolian and Phrygian.

u0-1.title: Entry check: tone and pulse
u0-1.goal: Play four steady bars with clear note endings. Control fretting pressure and unwanted sounds.
u0-1.text:
Tune E2 A2 D3 G3 C4 F4. Listen with low gain first, then repeat with your usual sound. Distortion changes sustain and makes undamped strings more audible.

Position the guitar so your wrists can move freely. Fret close behind the fret with just enough pressure. Thumb position and picking movement may change with the task. Use both hands to mute unused strings.

Entry check: play four bars with a note on each of the first three beats and silence on beat 4. If stable, use these exercises as checks. Explore unfamiliar movements without a click first; then test them in time.

e0-1-1.title: Open strings, whole notes
e0-1-1.instructions: Play the written open strings. Let each ring until the next bar; mute the previous string when changing. Read the names ahead, then repeat without names. Finish with four bars on E: three quarter notes and a quarter rest.
checklist: String changes without unwanted overlap?
Quarter rest silent; next entry on beat 1?
Two repetitions with a steady pulse?
e0-1-1.position: Position I through fret 4, with open strings.

e0-1-2.title: Chromatic fingers 1–2–3–4
e0-1-2.instructions: Use only the two written strings at frets 5–8. Place four fingers in sequence with minimal pressure. Mute the old string when crossing. Relax after two repetitions. Add the click once the movement is calm.
checklist: Notes equal in length and free of buzz?
Release fretting pressure between repetitions?
Unused strings silent?
e0-1-2.position: Position V, low E and A strings.

u0-2.title: P4: reference notes and intervals
u0-2.goal: Find E and C; hear and play minor thirds, fifths and octaves.
u0-2.text:
E A D G C F: adjacent strings are five semitones apart. A fifth needs seven: next higher string plus two frets gives 5 + 2 = 7. Minor third: 5 − 2 = 3. Major third: 5 − 1 = 4. Octave: two strings higher plus two frets gives 5 + 5 + 2 = 12.

These shifts work for fretted shapes wherever strings and frets are available. Open strings cannot move as open strings. Not every interval can be reached on the next string from every starting point.

Before each interval, imagine or hum the destination in a comfortable octave. Play it and compare.

e0-2-1.title: Find E
e0-2-1.instructions: Find E on the three lowest strings up to fret 12. Play and name the positions. Close the diagram and repeat in a different order. Then add the three highest strings.
checklist: E on the E, A and D strings recalled without searching?
Octaves recognised as the same note name at a different height?

e0-2-2.title: Find C
e0-2-2.instructions: Find C on the A, D and G strings up to fret 12. Play each C and the next E above it. Compare this major third with E–G in the following exercise.
checklist: Three C positions found without the diagram?
C–E and E–G sound different?

e0-2-3.title: Minor third and fifth
e0-2-3.instructions: Start with E on the A string, fret 7. Play G on the D string, fret 5, then B on the D string, fret 9. Play the minor third and fifth successively, then as two-note chords. Move both shapes down two frets: D–F and D–A. Sing each destination first.
checklist: E–G and E–B found without the diagram?
Shapes moved to D?
Target notes approximately sung before fretting?

u0-3.title: Reading I
u0-3.goal: Read short first-position phrases without stopping the pulse to search.
u0-3.text:
Guitar sounds an octave below its notation. The low open string sounds E2 but is written E3: in the space below the third ledger line below the treble staff.

Lines from bottom: E G B D F. Spaces: F A C E. B means German H; Bb means German B. Circled string numbers run from high to low: 1 = F, 6 = E. Finger 0 means an open string.

Read rhythm and starting pitch first, then the direction of neighbouring notes. Use aids for a first attempt, then hide them. Singing in a comfortable octave is enough.

Whole note: open head without a stem, four quarter-note beats. Half note: open head with a stem, two beats. Quarter note: filled head with a stem. Eighth note: one flag or beam, two per quarter. A dot adds half the original value. Rest symbols represent the same durations without sound. In 4/4, four quarter-note beats fit between barlines.

♯ raises a note by a semitone, ♭ lowers it; ♮ cancels the accidental. A key signature applies to the named notes in every octave. An individual accidental applies in its octave until the barline. Fretting fingers: 1 index, 2 middle, 3 ring, 4 little finger.

e0-3-1.title: Read the open strings
e0-3-1.instructions: Read the next note while the current one rings. Play once with aids and once without. If the open strings are already secure, proceed to the next exercise.
checklist: Read without note names or string numbers?
Changes on the first beat of the bar?
e0-3-1.position: Position I through fret 4, with open strings.

e0-3-2.title: C major, first position
e0-3-2.instructions: Ascend and descend in half notes. Here the finger number equals the fret; 0 means open. Read and play two bars first, then the full line. After a reading error, recover at the next bar rather than losing the pulse.
checklist: No searching pauses in either direction?
Continued in time after an error?
e0-3-2.position: Position I through fret 4, with open strings.

e0-3-3.title: New C-major reading phrase
e0-3-3.instructions: Find the starting pitch and clap the rhythm. Read without stopping. Correct the same phrase once, then generate another to check reading rather than memorisation.
checklist: Three new phrases read without searching pauses?
Repeated without aids on another practice day?
e0-3-3.position: Position I through fret 4, with open strings.

u0-4.title: Rhythm I
u0-4.goal: Hold note lengths and rests; re-enter accurately after silence.
u0-4.text:
Count quarters 1 2 3 4, eighths 1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and. Clap the written pattern before playing it on one note.

Count aloud on the first attempt, then count quietly and record the second. Rests remain part of the bar. In 3/4 the group starts again after three quarters; this does not automatically imply a waltz style.

e0-4-1.title: Quarters and halves
e0-4-1.instructions: Clap, then play the durations. Halves last two quarters; whole notes last four. Fully mute the quarter rest in the final bar.
checklist: Note endings as accurate as attacks?
Two repetitions without losing a beat?
e0-4-1.position: Position I through fret 4, with open strings.

e0-4-2.title: Eighths and rests
e0-4-2.instructions: Clap and count eighths, then play A. Mute rests deliberately. Repeat the unchanged phrase twice; do not add notes to catch up.
checklist: Even eighth notes?
Re-entry after the eighth rest on the correct subdivision?
e0-4-2.position: Position I through fret 4, with open strings.

e0-4-3.title: Three-four time
e0-4-3.instructions: Count 1 2 3. Play the phrase with a light emphasis on the first beat. A dotted half lasts two plus one quarters: a full 3/4 bar.
checklist: Secure return to beat 1 after the rest?
No extra fourth beat?
e0-4-3.position: Position I through fret 4, with open strings.

u0-5.title: Shape a sustained note
u0-5.goal: Distinguish straight tone from deliberately controlled vibrato.
u0-5.text:
Bending the string sideways raises its pitch; releasing the bend returns it to the original fretted pitch. This is not symmetrical movement below and above that pitch. Other vibrato techniques use different movements.

Start straight here and introduce small, slow vibrato later. This is an exercise constraint, not a universal rule: immediate vibrato can also work musically. Change width and speed separately, keeping hand and forearm mobile.

e0-5-1.title: Four bars, three tone variants
e0-5-1.instructions: G on the D string, fret 5, ring finger. Attack once per bar: bar 1 straight; bar 2 narrow vibrato from beat 3; bar 3 wider at the same speed; bar 4 straight again. Record and compare.
checklist: Vibrato returns to the original pitch each time?
Narrow and wide versions audibly different?
Other strings remain silent?
e0-5-1.position: Position III: G3 on D string, fret 5 with finger 3.

u0-6.title: Two voices: sustain and mute
u0-6.goal: Let an open bass string ring while the melody rests.
u0-6.text:
Two voices have independent durations. On the shared treble staff, melody stems point up and bass stems down. Whole notes have no stems. Read each voice separately, then combine them. Guitar still sounds an octave below the notation.

Use only a pick in the right hand. For a shared entry, place the bass on the pulse and pick the melody immediately afterwards: a deliberately brief spread attack. Mute unused strings when skipping or brushing across them. Never reattack a tied note. Then practise separate entries; tapping is not needed for these.

e0-6-1.title: Bass sustains, melody rests
e0-6-1.instructions: Pick bass and melody separately first. Together: E2 on beat 1, E3 immediately afterwards. Mute E3 after two quarters while E2 keeps ringing. Repeat the brief spread entry in the next bar. Stop both voices at the end.
checklist: Melody rest silent while the bass rings?
Both voices deliberately stopped at the end?
Two repetitions without unwanted string noise?
e0-6-1.position: Position II: melody on D string, bass on open E.

e0-6-2.title: Independent entries
e0-6-2.instructions: Start the melody on beat 2. Bass enters on beat 1 of each bar: E2, then A2. Mute E when changing to A. Release E3 exactly at the start of beat 4. No extra open string should ring.
checklist: Bass and melody enter separately?
Previous bass muted at the change?
Melody ends on the correct beat?
e0-6-2.position: Position II: E3 on D string; open E2 and A2.

u1-1.title: E as a reference, three notes as language
u1-1.goal: Hear a short idea, play it and repeat it exactly.
u1-1.text:
Begin each phrase on E and return to E. No looper is needed: the recurring tonic provides the reference. A drone of your own can be added later without changing the task.

Start with E, G and B. Hum, find them on the low E string and repeat. Then add the remaining E-Aeolian notes: E F# G A B C D. Steps to the octave: 2–1–2–2–1–2–2 semitones.

A scale run is orientation. Recognisable motifs, durations and rests turn this material into music.

e1-1-2.title: Three notes: idea and answer
e1-1-2.instructions: Use only E, G and B on the low E string. Sing an idea of at most three notes, play it in two bars, then rest for two bars. Repeat unchanged. On the next attempt, change only the last note. Record four cycles.
checklist: Sung contour matched on the guitar?
Motif recognisably identical twice?
Only the ending changed; rests retained?

e1-1-1.title: Ascending scale, half notes
e1-1-1.instructions: Low E string only, half notes, initially without vibrato. Hear F#–G and B–C as semitone steps. Return to your three-note motif and add exactly one new scale note.
checklist: Semitone steps found without the diagram?
New note added without losing the motif?
e1-1-1.position: Low E string, frets 0–12; move the hand with the pitch.

u1-2.title: Three strings, one phrase
u1-2.goal: Play E Aeolian on E, A and D; move the same idea into a compact position.
u1-2.text:
This window uses open strings through fret 5 on E, A and D. Fretted notes: fret 2 with finger 1, fret 3 with 2, fret 4 with 3, fret 5 with 4. Open strings need no finger.

The score specifies the string. In particular, G3 stays on the D string at fret 5. Automatically choosing open G would leave this window.

e1-2-1.title: Ascend and descend within the window
e1-2-1.instructions: Play two bars first, then the whole phrase. Follow the string indications; keep G3 on the D string. Transfer your earlier three-note motif into this window.
checklist: All notes on E, A and D strings?
Own motif recognisable in the new position?
e1-2-1.position: Open strings + position II through fret 5, E, A and D strings.

e1-2-2.title: Phrase, repeat, vary
e1-2-2.instructions: Two bars of melody, two bars of rest. Choose and sing the ending E, G or B first. Play the phrase, repeat it, then change only its rhythm. Four cycles with half-time drums.
checklist: Planned target reached?
Rhythm changed while pitches stayed the same?
Secure entry after two bars of rest?

e1-2-3.title: New E-Aeolian reading phrase
e1-2-3.instructions: Read in the three-string window. Establish contour and rhythm, then play without stopping. F# is in the key signature. Correct once before generating another phrase.
checklist: New phrase without searching pauses?
G3 remains on the D string?
e1-2-3.position: Open strings + position II through fret 5, E, A and D strings.

u1-pedal.title: Pedal note and melody
u1-pedal.goal: Provide a bass reference and independent melody on one guitar.
u1-pedal.text:
A pedal note is sustained or reiterated while other notes move above it. Here E is the fixed bass. This is a small form of polyphony: bass and melody keep their own durations.

Play each voice alone first. Then repeat the bass once per bar with melody above. Do not reattack a tied note. Open E limits transposition here: moving the melody leaves the bass on E.

Low distortion and a quieter bass make the melody easier to distinguish. Then test the same passage with your usual sound. Chords, arpeggios and moving bass lines build on this later.

e1-pedal-1.title: Open E beneath a singing voice
e1-pedal-1.instructions: Melody is on the D string, with picked open E bass. At shared bar openings pick E2 first and the melody immediately afterwards. Melody E3 is tied into bar two: reattack only the bass. In the last bar end the melody two quarters before the bass.
checklist: Bass quieter than melody?
Held E3 continues through the new bass attack?
Final melody rest silent while the bass rings?
e1-pedal-1.position: Position II, D string: E3 with 1, F#3 with 3, G3 with 4. Open E bass.

e1-pedal-2.title: Your own answer over E
e1-pedal-2.instructions: Use the written example as a question and play it unchanged once. Keep the bass and melody rhythms, but change melody pitches using E3, F#3 and G3. End the answer on E3. Notate your version and read it on another practice day.
checklist: Bass unchanged; melody deliberately varied?
Answer repeated without searching?
Own notation matches what you played?
e1-pedal-2.position: Position II on D string, open E bass.

u1-3.title: Long notes and rests
u1-3.goal: Shape a phrase through duration, a focal point and silence.
u1-3.text:
A tie joins notes of the same pitch: attack only the first and sustain their combined duration. A rest ends the note. Ties and phrasing slurs are different signs; this renderer shows ties only.

Emphasise a target through duration or attack. The highest pitch need not be the loudest. Compare two interpretations of the same motif.

e1-3-1.title: Ties
e1-3-1.instructions: Listen, count the durations and play. Do not reattack tied notes. Choose B or C as the focal point and make only that note more prominent.
checklist: No new attack under a tie?
Chosen focal point audible in the recording?
e1-3-1.position: Position I through fret 4, with open strings.

e1-3-2.title: Four bars of phrase, four of rest
e1-3-2.instructions: Use your familiar motif and lengthen one note as a focal point. Repeat the same phrase. Third attempt: a different focal point with the same pitches.
checklist: Motif recognisable despite longer notes?
Changed focal point changes the effect?
Secure entry after four bars of rest?

u1-4.title: Phrygian: F instead of F#
u1-4.goal: Hear and deliberately use the second scale degree as a colour.
u1-4.text:
E Aeolian uses F#, E Phrygian uses F; the other pitches are identical. This example retains a one-sharp key signature, so F receives a natural. An accidental applies to that pitch and octave until the barline.

F–E is our initial ending, not a universal requirement: F–G is a counterexample. The tension of F depends on bass, register, duration and accent among other things. No scale alone creates a band’s sound.

e1-4-1.title: F versus F#
e1-4-1.instructions: Compare the first two bars. Sing E–F#–G, then E–F–G. Play the full phrase. Repeat the pair without the diagram and describe the difference you hear in the log.
checklist: F and F# used in the correct version?
Difference audible without the diagram?
e1-4-1.position: Position I through fret 4, with open strings.

e1-4-2.title: Two paths through F
e1-4-2.instructions: Two bars of phrase, two of rest, using E, F, G and B. First end each phrase F–E. Then try F–G once and return to E later. Repeat the version that better matches your imagined sound.
checklist: Both endings deliberately tried?
Chosen version reproducible?
Pulse stays calm despite tension?

u1-5.title: Ear: from imagination to instrument
u1-5.goal: Find and notate a motif you have sung.
u1-5.text:
Record a short sung idea on your phone: three to five notes starting on E in a comfortable octave. Reproduce it without changing the recording in your mind while searching.

Clap its rhythm, find contour and pitches, then write them in staff notation. The recording remains the reference. Optionally use the same process on a short passage from your reference albums; a full transcription is unnecessary.

e1-5-1.title: Transcribe your own motif
e1-5-1.instructions: Sing a motif using E, G, A and B, record it and find it in the three-string window. Write rhythm and pitches on paper. On another practice day, read it and compare with the original recording.
checklist: Pitches match the sung recording?
Rhythm matches the recording?
Reproduced from your own score?

u1-6.title: Checkpoint: a small form
u1-6.goal: Develop and repeat a prepared musical idea.
u1-6.text:
Eight bars for one guitar alone: two motif, two answer, two variation, two ending. Open E bass on each bar’s first beat, melody on D and G strings. Second position up to fret 5: E3 F#3 G3 on D, A3 B3 on G. End the melody on E3.

Write two bars with both voices first. Read slowly, develop the form and record it. On another practice day, listen for independent note endings, steady bass and a recognisable melody. Then record without drums. If combining voices still stalls, return to the pedal-note unit.

e1-6-1.title: Eight bars of your own music
e1-6-1.instructions: Play the eight-bar miniature with your own bass voice. Bass once per bar; melody with long notes and a rest. Record with click or drums first, then alone. On another practice day, repeat from your notation.
checklist: Bass and melody remain independent?
Motif, answer and variation recognisable?
Rests and note endings controlled?
Repeated unaccompanied on another practice day?
e1-6-1.position: Position II on D and G strings through fret 5; open E bass.

ku0-1.title: Entry check: touch and pulse
ku0-1.goal: Play short phrases calmly and with control in each hand.
ku0-1.text:
Choose a sound with a clear attack. Sit with mobile forearms and wrists. Keep fingers loosely curved; arm and hand may support movement. Release keys at the end of their written duration, not automatically immediately.

Finger numbers apply to both hands: 1 = thumb, 5 = little finger. Play the two phrases separately. If secure without aids, move straight to coordination. Equal loudness is a control exercise, not an ideal for all music.

ke0-1-1.title: A-minor five-finger position, right hand
ke0-1-1.instructions: Right thumb on A4, little finger on E5. Start without a click, then add it. Read two bars ahead and play. Repeat without aids.
checklist: Pulse maintained without searching?
Notes roughly equal in loudness?
Hand stays mobile?

ke0-1-2.title: A-minor five-finger position, left hand
ke0-1-2.instructions: Left little finger on A2, thumb on E3. Read and play alone. Adjust the synthesizer octave if needed: C4 means MIDI note 60 here, regardless of the instrument display.
checklist: Bass clef read without names?
Written durations maintained?

ku0-2.title: One sound, one accompaniment
ku0-2.goal: Begin without having to program a sound.
ku0-2.text:
One sound across the keyboard is enough. Use a piano or electric piano on the MX49, or a clearly articulated polyphonic sound on the Nord Lead A1 or Blofeld. Split, layer, arpeggiator and long reverb tails are unnecessary for these exercises.

Check whether a stronger attack changes volume or timbre. If not, use rhythm, register and duration first. A sustained synthesizer tone behaves differently from a decaying piano tone.

Click and drums use the centrally selected MIDI output. When using the MX49 as both keyboard and drum sound source, put the drum kit on Part 10. The left hand supplies its own reference note.

ke0-2-1.title: Check sound and MIDI
ke0-2-1.instructions: Play a short note and a long note, then the same note gently and more firmly. Describe how the sound responds. Start the MIDI click and play four steady bars. Save the sound on the instrument if needed.
checklist: Short notes and rests clearly separated?
Response to attack checked?
Click audible from the intended device?

ku0-3.title: Keys and intervals
ku0-3.goal: Hear and play five adjacent scale notes as a shape.
ku0-3.text:
A semitone is one adjacent key, including black keys. A whole tone is two semitones. E–F and B–C are adjacent white keys only one semitone apart.

Start with five-note spaces: A B C D E, then E F# G A B and D E F G A. Right-hand fingers stay 1–2–3–4–5. Full minor scales extend further; each exercise covers only the first five degrees.

ke0-3-1.title: A minor: five notes
ke0-3-1.instructions: Right hand: A4 B4 C5 D5 E5, fingers 1–2–3–4–5. Ascend and descend. Sing a three-note idea from these notes and reproduce it. Repeat the idea, then change only the final note.
checklist: Ascended and descended without searching?
Three-note idea repeated twice?

ke0-3-2.title: E minor: five notes
ke0-3-2.instructions: Right hand: E4 F#4 G4 A4 B4, fingers 1–2–3–4–5. Ascend and descend. Sing a three-note idea from these notes and reproduce it. Repeat the idea, then change only the final note.
checklist: Ascended and descended without searching?
Three-note idea repeated twice?

ke0-3-3.title: D minor: five notes
ke0-3-3.instructions: Right hand: D4 E4 F4 G4 A4, fingers 1–2–3–4–5. Ascend and descend. Sing a three-note idea from these notes and reproduce it. Repeat the idea, then change only the final note.
checklist: Ascended and descended without searching?
Three-note idea repeated twice?

ke0-3-4.title: Fifths and thirds
ke0-3-4.instructions: Left A2–E3 with 5–1, first successive then together. Right A4–C5 with 1–3, then replace C5 with C#5. Compare minor and major thirds directly.
checklist: Fifth reached comfortably?
A–C and A–C# deliberately distinguished?

ku0-4.title: Reading I
ku0-4.goal: Read both clefs within a small pitch range.
ku0-4.text:
C4 lies on the ledger line below the treble staff or above the bass staff. Pitches here follow MIDI: C4 = 60. Instrument displays may use different octave numbers.

Treble lines: E G B D F; spaces: F A C E. Bass lines: G B D F A; spaces: A C E G. B = German H, Bb = German B.

Hands separately first, then together. Clap new rhythms before playing. Read direction and intervals rather than decoding every pitch in isolation.

Whole note: open head without a stem, four quarter-note beats. Half note: open head with a stem, two beats. Quarter note: filled head with a stem. Eighth note: one flag or beam, two per quarter. A dot adds half the value. Rests last as long as the corresponding notes. In 4/4, four quarter-note beats fit between barlines.

♯ raises by a semitone, ♭ lowers; ♮ cancels the accidental. A key signature applies in every octave; an individual accidental applies in its octave until the barline.

ke0-4-1.title: Contrary motion from C
ke0-4-1.instructions: Right hand ascends from middle C4; left hand descends from C3 one octave below. Play hands separately first, then together. The thumbs start on different keys. Combine the first two bars before extending the phrase.
checklist: Each hand secure without aids?
Note changes simultaneous?

ke0-4-2.title: New treble-clef phrase
ke0-4-2.instructions: Only C4–G4 with fingers 1–5. Clap the rhythm, find the starting pitch and read without stopping. Correct once before generating another phrase.
checklist: Three new phrases read in time?
Repeated without names on another day?

ke0-4-3.title: New bass-clef phrase
ke0-4-3.instructions: Only C3–G3, left fingers 5–1. Clap, read, correct and test a new phrase as with the right hand. Practise the hands separately initially.
checklist: Bass clef read without names?
Three new phrases without searching pauses?

ku0-5.title: Two hands, one pulse
ku0-5.goal: Sustain with the left hand; distinguish notes and rests with the right.
ku0-5.text:
Clap the right-hand rhythm first, then play the long left-hand notes alone. Combine one bar and extend only when each hand maintains its durations.

On piano the held bass decays; keep the key down for its written duration anyway. On synthesizer it may sustain. Both are appropriate for this task.

ke0-5-1.title: Whole notes against quarters
ke0-5-1.instructions: Left A2 with finger 5: reattack each bar and hold. Right A4 and E5 with 1 and 5. Keep the left key down through the right-hand rest. No pedal.
checklist: Left hand sustains through the right-hand rest?
Both hands begin together on beat 1?

ke0-5-2.title: Eighths and rests
ke0-5-2.instructions: Right hand alone without pedal. Clap the eighths first. Release the key when the rest begins. If the synth has a long release, choose a shorter sound.
checklist: Rest audible?
Entry after the eighth rest in time?

ke0-5-3.title: Three-four, both hands
ke0-5-3.instructions: Hold each left-hand dotted half for three quarters. Read the right hand alone, then combine. Lightly emphasise the first beat.
checklist: Three quarters per bar maintained?
Bass changes align with the first beat?

ku0-6.title: Dynamics and note endings
ku0-6.goal: Shape a phrase through touch and articulation.
ku0-6.text:
On piano, attack affects the beginning of a note. Pressing harder after the attack cannot make that note louder. A crescendo requires successive attacks. Synth response depends on the program.

Sustain extends notes after keys are released. Start without pedal. The optional pedal task applies to piano or a sound that responds appropriately. Connected finger playing is the regular alternative without a pedal.

ke0-6-1.title: An audible dynamic arc
ke0-6-1.instructions: E4: eight quarters gradually louder, then eight gradually softer. Shape an arc rather than forcing eight precisely different levels. If your synth does not respond to velocity, play the phrase detached, then connected instead.
checklist: Dynamic arc or articulation contrast audible?
Stronger attacks do not change the pulse?

ke0-6-2.title: Connect notes, optionally with pedal
ke0-6-2.instructions: Without pedal, connect A4–C5–E5–A4 using fingers 1–3–5–1. Optional sustain: attack the first note, then depress the pedal. At the next attack, briefly release and redepress it. This connects the new note while damping old ones.
checklist: Note changes controlled without pedal?
With pedal if available: old notes do not accumulate?

ku1-1.title: Tonic left, motif right
ku1-1.goal: Connect three notes into a repeatable melody.
ku1-1.text:
Start right hand E4, G4 and B4 with fingers 1, 3 and 5. Sing, play back and repeat a motif. Left hand initially E3 on each bar’s first beat; later E3–B3 together with 5–1. Hold without gripping.

Reattack every bar on piano and practise the same on synth. A separate pad is unnecessary. Add the full scale after the motif: right E4–E5 with 1–2–3–1–2–3–4–5. After G move the hand sideways and place the thumb on A rather than twisting it beneath a rigid hand.

ke1-1-2.title: Three notes over E
ke1-1-2.instructions: Sing and reproduce a three-note idea using E4, G4 and B4. Two bars melody, two bars left-hand reference only. Left E3 on every beat 1. Repeat the motif, then change only the ending. Four cycles.
checklist: Motif played identically twice?
Left hand steady during right-hand rests?
Change limited to the ending?

ke1-1-1.title: E Aeolian over a fifth
ke1-1-1.instructions: Right hand alone first, thumb change after G. Add left E3–B3 reattacked each bar. If coordination stalls, use only E3 left. Add exactly one scale note to your own motif afterwards.
checklist: Calm right-hand thumb change?
Left hand reattacks only on beat 1?
Motif extended by one note?

ku1-2.title: A melody breathes
ku1-2.goal: Long notes, clear rests and a shaped focal point.
ku1-2.text:
Ties join the same pitch: attack only at the start. The left-hand fifth is renewed each bar here, working equally on decaying piano and sustaining synth.

Shape a focal point through attack or duration; it need not be the highest pitch. Begin without pedal. Long reverb or release must not obscure the melody’s rests.

ke1-2-1.title: Ties over a steady bass
ke1-2-1.instructions: Hold right-hand ties without reattacking. Reattack left E3–B3 each bar. Read the right hand alone first. Choose B4 or C5 as the focal point and compare both versions.
checklist: Right-hand ties correct?
Left hand steady and quieter than the right?
Chosen focal point audible?

ke1-2-2.title: Four bars of melody, four of bass
ke1-2-2.instructions: Develop the three-note motif with a longer target note. Repeat the phrase; on the third attempt change only its focal point. During the four-bar melody rest, keep the left reference going.
checklist: Motif recognisable?
Right hand silent in its rest while left remains steady?
Next entry on beat 1?

ku1-3.title: Motif and answer
ku1-3.goal: Make a connection audible with a small amount of material.
ku1-3.text:
Repetition gives the ear a reference. Then change exactly one property: ending, rhythm or register. A contrast becomes meaningful when something recognisable precedes it.

Double-note thirds come later. Keep one melody voice in the right hand here. On synth or piano, a clear melody over a steady bass can already be a complete musical thought.

ke1-3-1.title: One motif, two endings
ke1-3-1.instructions: Play the written right-hand motif twice, with left tonic each bar. Replace the final B4 with E4. Sing and compare the more open and more closed endings.
checklist: Repetitions rhythmically identical?
Only the last pitch changed?
Both versions recalled without the diagram?

ke1-3-2.title: Answer rather than run scales
ke1-3-2.instructions: Two bars of your motif using E4, G4, A4 and B4, then two bars of answer. One right-hand voice, left E3 every beat 1. Answer with the same pitches but a longer ending. Two identical cycles, then one variation.
checklist: Answer relates to the motif?
Bass steady and melody clear?
Repeated without searching?

ku1-4.title: Phrygian: F instead of F#
ku1-4.goal: Compare two colours over the same tonic.
ku1-4.text:
E Aeolian contains F#, E Phrygian F. In this example a natural cancels the key-signature F# in that octave until the barline.

F–E is one possible ending. F–G is a counterexample to the claim that F must always descend. Test both with the same rhythm and bass.

ke1-4-1.title: F versus F#
ke1-4-1.instructions: Compare the first two bars right hand: E–F#–G versus E–F–G. Add left E3–B3 each bar. Play the full phrase without changing tempo at the white F key.
checklist: F and F# deliberately distinguished?
Left hand unchanged while right changes colour?

ke1-4-2.title: Phrygian with drums
ke1-4-2.instructions: Right E4, F4, G4 and B4; left E3 each bar. Two bars melody, two bass only. End F–E first, then try F–G and return to E later. Repeat your chosen version.
checklist: Both paths through F tried?
Chosen phrase reproducible?
Left hand in time?

ku1-5.title: From singing to playing
ku1-5.goal: Bring an imagined idea to the keys by ear.
ku1-5.text:
Sing a short idea from E, G, A and B in a comfortable octave and record it. Find the pitches on the keyboard afterwards. Keep the recording as the reference; do not unconsciously replace it with easier notes.

Write only the melody and rhythm in treble clef. Add left accompaniment after the melody matches. Optionally apply the same process to a short passage from your references later.

ke1-5-1.title: Transcribe your own motif
ke1-5-1.instructions: Record three to five sung notes. Clap the rhythm, find the melody with the right hand and notate it. Read it on another practice day and compare with the recording; then add left E3 each bar.
checklist: Pitches and rhythm match what you sang?
Recovered from your own score?
Melody unchanged when bass is added?

ku1-6.title: Checkpoint: a small form
ku1-6.goal: Play a repeatable miniature with melody and bass.
ku1-6.text:
Eight bars in E Aeolian: two motif, two answer, two variation, two ending. Left E3 or E3–B3 each bar. One right-hand melody with a deliberate rest; end on E.

Record with click or drums first. On another practice day, play unaccompanied and check a steady pulse: a bridge to any available piano. Use the same form on synth with suitable note endings. Check Phrygian separately with the same criteria later.

ke1-6-1.title: Eight bars for synth and piano
ke1-6-1.instructions: Play the eight-bar form twice. Right E Aeolian within E4–E5; left a steady reference. Listen on another practice day and change exactly one passage. Make the second recording without click or drums.
checklist: Motif and variation recognisable?
Melody clear above bass?
Rests audible?
Repeated without aids on two days, including once without accompaniment?

p2.title: Two-note shapes and arpeggios
p2.goal: Combine pedal bass, thirds and broken triads; read voices independently.

p3.title: Moving bass and lament
p3.goal: Move from a fixed pedal to a descending bass; keep the melody independent.

p4.title: Harmonic minor
p4.goal: Leading tone and dominant harmony; distinguish modal colour from tonal cadence.

p5.title: Sequence and figuration

p6.title: Contrasting colours

p8.title: An arrangement of your own
p8.goal: Combine pedal notes, moving bass, melody, arpeggios and chords into a complete solo piece.

e0-4-4.title: Muted eighths, open accents
e0-4-4.position: Open low E; fretting hand helps mute other strings.
e0-4-4.instructions: Alternate-pick the eighths. Rest the edge of the picking hand lightly near the bridge on low E: pitch audible, decay short. Second pass: play only the first eighth of each bar without palm muting, then return to short notes. Record both versions.
checklist: Pitch remains audible while muted?
Open accent only at the first beat?
Same pulse in both versions?

e2-1-1.title: Written study · Triads: minor and major
e2-1-1.instructions: Pick E bass first, then the upper three strings with a short controlled stroke. Keep unused strings muted. G3 and G#3 are on D frets 5 and 6; B3 and E4 remain fretted. Let the notes ring together after the spread attack.
checklist: Third change audible, other notes unchanged?
Two complete passes with clear releases?
e2-1-1.position: P4 · Frets 4–6; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

e2-1-2.title: Deliberate variation · Triads: minor and major
e2-1-2.instructions: Alternate minor and major without looking. Sing the new third before playing; keep bass and top-voice levels unchanged.
checklist: New third sung before playing?
Unchanged elements retained during comparison?
e2-1-2.position: P4 · Frets 4–6; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

e2-1-3.title: Original application · Triads: minor and major
e2-1-3.instructions: Write eight bars with one triad per bar. Keep E bass and use one major bar as contrast. Place it deliberately within the phrase and play the same form twice.
checklist: Major contrast reproduced in the same place?
Notated, recorded and read again on another practice day?
e2-1-3.position: P4 · Frets 4–6; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

ke2-1-1.title: Written study · Triads: minor and major
ke2-1-1.instructions: Read rhythm and each voice separately first, then play the complete texture. Left E3; right G4–B4–E5 or G#4–B4–E5. Use right 1–2–5; only the thumb moves a semitone.
checklist: Third change audible, other notes unchanged?
Two complete passes with clear releases?

ke2-1-2.title: Deliberate variation · Triads: minor and major
ke2-1-2.instructions: Alternate minor and major without looking. Sing the new third before playing; keep bass and top-voice levels unchanged.
checklist: New third sung before playing?
Unchanged elements retained during comparison?

ke2-1-3.title: Original application · Triads: minor and major
ke2-1-3.instructions: Write eight bars with one triad per bar. Keep E bass and use one major bar as contrast. Place it deliberately within the phrase and play the same form twice.
checklist: Major contrast reproduced in the same place?
Notated, recorded and read again on another practice day?

e2-2-1.title: Written study · Inversion and bass note
e2-2-1.instructions: Read rhythm and each voice separately first, then play the complete texture. Keep G3–B3–E4 above. Bass: open E2, G2 at E-string fret 3, B2 at A-string fret 2. Mute each previous bass at the change.
checklist: All three bass positions identified?
Two complete passes with clear releases?
e2-2-1.position: P4 · Frets 2–5; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

e2-2-2.title: Deliberate variation · Inversion and bass note
e2-2-2.instructions: Hold the top E across two bars while the other voices re-enter. Check that the bass still makes each inversion clear.
checklist: Long top voice independent of bass?
Unchanged elements retained during comparison?
e2-2-2.position: P4 · Frets 2–5; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

e2-2-3.title: Original application · Inversion and bass note
e2-2-3.instructions: Write eight bars using E–G–B–E bass twice. On the second pass change only the duration of the upper E. Play without drums and listen for a coherent form.
checklist: Bass path free of overlapping old notes?
Notated, recorded and read again on another practice day?
e2-2-3.position: P4 · Frets 2–5; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

ke2-2-1.title: Written study · Inversion and bass note
ke2-2-1.instructions: Read rhythm and each voice separately first, then play the complete texture. Retain the same right-hand chord; rehearse the written bass separately. Name the bass note and then the inversion at each change.
checklist: All three bass positions identified?
Two complete passes with clear releases?

ke2-2-2.title: Deliberate variation · Inversion and bass note
ke2-2-2.instructions: Hold the top E across two bars while the other voices re-enter. Check that the bass still makes each inversion clear.
checklist: Long top voice independent of bass?
Unchanged elements retained during comparison?

ke2-2-3.title: Original application · Inversion and bass note
ke2-2-3.instructions: Write eight bars using E–G–B–E bass twice. On the second pass change only the duration of the upper E. Play without drums and listen for a coherent form.
checklist: Bass path free of overlapping old notes?
Notated, recorded and read again on another practice day?

e2-3-1.title: Written study · Thirds with a melodic line
e2-3-1.instructions: Read rhythm and each voice separately first, then play the complete texture. For E3–G3 use A fret 7 and D fret 5. Then G3–B3 on D/G, A3–C4 on G/C. Move the hand with each change.
checklist: Major/minor thirds distinguished by ear?
Two complete passes with clear releases?
e2-3-1.position: P4 · Frets 2–7; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

e2-3-2.title: Deliberate variation · Thirds with a melodic line
e2-3-2.instructions: First balance both voices equally, then bring out the upper line with the same notes. Compare recordings at the same tempo.
checklist: Top line traceable in the recording?
Unchanged elements retained during comparison?
e2-3-2.position: P4 · Frets 2–7; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

e2-3-3.title: Original application · Thirds with a melodic line
e2-3-3.instructions: Invent a four-bar melody from G, B and C. Add a third below every second note only. Notate rests in the accompanying voice too.
checklist: Single notes and dyads alternate without hesitation?
Notated, recorded and read again on another practice day?
e2-3-3.position: P4 · Frets 2–7; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

ke2-3-1.title: Written study · Thirds with a melodic line
ke2-3-1.instructions: Read rhythm and each voice separately first, then play the complete texture. Right-hand thirds with 1–3 or 2–4; move the whole hand between positions. Quiet left E3 each bar. Also play the top line alone.
checklist: Major/minor thirds distinguished by ear?
Two complete passes with clear releases?

ke2-3-2.title: Deliberate variation · Thirds with a melodic line
ke2-3-2.instructions: First balance both voices equally, then bring out the upper line with the same notes. Compare recordings at the same tempo.
checklist: Top line traceable in the recording?
Unchanged elements retained during comparison?

ke2-3-3.title: Original application · Thirds with a melodic line
ke2-3-3.instructions: Invent a four-bar melody from G, B and C. Add a third below every second note only. Notate rests in the accompanying voice too.
checklist: Single notes and dyads alternate without hesitation?
Notated, recorded and read again on another practice day?

e2-4-1.title: Written study · Arpeggio above a bass
e2-4-1.instructions: The pick plays both bass and upper figure. At a shared entry, place bass on the pulse and the upper note immediately after it. Continue the written eighths with small string crossings while the bass rings. Bring out the top note without reattacking the bass.
checklist: Eighths even through chord changes?
Two complete passes with clear releases?
e2-4-1.position: P4 · Frets 2–5; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

e2-4-2.title: Deliberate variation · Arpeggio above a bass
e2-4-2.instructions: Play the same pattern accenting first its opening note, then its highest note. Keep bass quiet and eighths even.
checklist: Accent change without an extra bass attack?
Unchanged elements retained during comparison?
e2-4-2.position: P4 · Frets 2–5; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

e2-4-3.title: Original application · Arpeggio above a bass
e2-4-3.instructions: Write Em–C–G–Em twice as an eight-bar form. Use quarters first, then eighths, with the same chords. Finish together with the bass.
checklist: Denser second half at the same basic pulse?
Notated, recorded and read again on another practice day?
e2-4-3.position: P4 · Frets 2–5; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

ke2-4-1.title: Written study · Arpeggio above a bass
ke2-4-1.instructions: Read rhythm and each voice separately first, then play the complete texture. Prepare the right-hand triad, starting with 1–3–5–3. Left hand only at bar starts. Loop one bar before adding chord changes.
checklist: Eighths even through chord changes?
Two complete passes with clear releases?

ke2-4-2.title: Deliberate variation · Arpeggio above a bass
ke2-4-2.instructions: Play the same pattern accenting first its opening note, then its highest note. Keep bass quiet and eighths even.
checklist: Accent change without an extra bass attack?
Unchanged elements retained during comparison?

ke2-4-3.title: Original application · Arpeggio above a bass
ke2-4-3.instructions: Write Em–C–G–Em twice as an eight-bar form. Use quarters first, then eighths, with the same chords. Finish together with the bass.
checklist: Denser second half at the same basic pulse?
Notated, recorded and read again on another practice day?

e2-6-1.title: Written study · Power chords and muting
e2-6-1.instructions: Read rhythm and each voice separately first, then play the complete texture. E5: open E/A fret 2; A5: open A/D fret 2; B5: A fret 2/D fret 4. Strike only those strings. Use both hands to stop rests.
checklist: Only the intended two strings audible?
Two complete passes with clear releases?
e2-6-1.position: P4 · Frets 2–4; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

e2-6-2.title: Deliberate variation · Power chords and muting
e2-6-2.instructions: Repeat with palm muting, opening only beat 1 of each bar. Use low gain first, then your normal tone. Match comparison levels.
checklist: Open/muted changes tone rather than pulse?
Unchanged elements retained during comparison?
e2-6-2.position: P4 · Frets 2–4; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

e2-6-3.title: Original application · Power chords and muting
e2-6-3.instructions: Build eight bars from E5 and A5. Place one quarter rest in each bar, varying its position. Notate attacks and rests, then repeat from memory.
checklist: All written rests genuinely silent?
Notated, recorded and read again on another practice day?
e2-6-3.position: P4 · Frets 2–4; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

e2-rhythm-1.title: Written study · Short chords and offbeats
e2-rhythm-1.instructions: Use a short pick stroke across the upper three strings on the offbeat. Release fretting pressure at note-off and control open bass strings. Pick the bass separately on its written beat. Do not fill the eighth rest before the chord with an attack.
checklist: Chords precisely between clicks?
Two complete passes with clear releases?
e2-rhythm-1.position: P4 · Frets 2–5; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

e2-rhythm-2.title: Deliberate variation · Short chords and offbeats
e2-rhythm-2.instructions: Accent only the offbeat after beat 2. Clap first, then play the same chords. Keep bass and the other offbeats at their original levels.
checklist: Only the selected offbeat accented?
Unchanged elements retained during comparison?
e2-rhythm-2.position: P4 · Frets 2–5; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

e2-rhythm-3.title: Original application · Short chords and offbeats
e2-rhythm-3.instructions: Invent four bars with two offbeat chords and two omitted offbeats in each. Notate the rests and repeat the pattern over Em and C.
checklist: Omissions repeatable and bass stable?
Notated, recorded and read again on another practice day?
e2-rhythm-3.position: P4 · Frets 2–5; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

ke2-rhythm-1.title: Written study · Short chords and offbeats
ke2-rhythm-1.instructions: Read rhythm and each voice separately first, then play the complete texture. Right-hand chords are short while the left holds. No sustain pedal. Release with small movements rather than lifting the whole hand high.
checklist: Chords precisely between clicks?
Two complete passes with clear releases?

ke2-rhythm-2.title: Deliberate variation · Short chords and offbeats
ke2-rhythm-2.instructions: Accent only the offbeat after beat 2. Clap first, then play the same chords. Keep bass and the other offbeats at their original levels.
checklist: Only the selected offbeat accented?
Unchanged elements retained during comparison?

ke2-rhythm-3.title: Original application · Short chords and offbeats
ke2-rhythm-3.instructions: Invent four bars with two offbeat chords and two omitted offbeats in each. Notate the rests and repeat the pattern over Em and C.
checklist: Omissions repeatable and bass stable?
Notated, recorded and read again on another practice day?

e2-5-1.title: Written study · Hear a triad, build a phrase
e2-5-1.instructions: Read rhythm and each voice separately first, then play the complete texture. Play the upper line first on D/G/C strings. Add bass only at written bar starts. E can remain an audible reference through Em–C.

Two complete passes with clear releases?

ke2-5-1.title: Written study · Hear a triad, build a phrase

Two complete passes with clear releases?

ke2-5-2.title: Deliberate variation · Hear a triad, build a phrase

checklist: Closing notes written before checking?

ke2-5-3.title: Original application · Hear a triad, build a phrase

Notated, recorded and read again on another practice day?

ke3-1-2.title: Deliberate variation · Lamento: a descending bass

ke3-1-3.title: Original application · Lamento: a descending bass

e3-2-1.title: Written study · A circle-of-fifths path
e3-2-1.instructions: Read rhythm and each voice separately first, then play the complete texture. Connect upper triads without bass first. Retain common tones only when their fingering allows the next shape. Mute the old string at each bass change.

ke3-2-1.title: Written study · A circle-of-fifths path

e3-reading-1.title: Written study · Syncopation and tied entries
e3-reading-1.instructions: Melody is on D/G, with picked E bass. Pick each rhythm separately first while the foot keeps quarters. Briefly spread shared entries bass–melody. Sustain tied syncopated melody notes through the following bass attack.
checklist: No extra attacks under ties?
Two complete passes with clear releases?

e3-reading-2.title: Deliberate variation · Syncopation and tied entries
e3-reading-2.instructions: Deliberately reattack the tied notes once, then play them correctly without reattack. Describe the audible difference without changing the pulse.

checklist: Original piece notated, self-sufficient and reproduced on three days?
Notated, recorded and read again on another practice day?
e8-6-3.position: P4 · Frets 2–5; open strings as written. Show string cues when needed.

ke8-6-1.title: Written study · Final project: an original solo piece
ke8-6-1.instructions: Read rhythm and each voice separately first, then play the complete texture. Check balance, readable hand positions and deliberate releases. Left plays a broken bass figure in the triplet section; prepare hands separately. Make at least one recording with piano-like decay; another may use your synth tone.
checklist: All 32 model bars read with correct rhythms and voices?
Two complete passes with clear releases?

ke8-6-2.title: Deliberate variation · Final project: an original solo piece
ke8-6-2.instructions: Choose one section and change only texture, retaining harmony and motif. Replay the whole form and decide whether the change serves the overall arc.
checklist: Texture change preserves motif and overall form?
Unchanged elements retained during comparison?

ke8-6-3.title: Original application · Final project: an original solo piece
ke8-6-3.instructions: Compose and notate at least 32 bars with a returning motif, contrast, your own bass, one three-layer passage and a clear coda. Record on three separate practice days: with drums, unaccompanied, and with an improvised four-bar variation. Compare and revise deliberately.
checklist: Original piece notated, self-sufficient and reproduced on three days?
Notated, recorded and read again on another practice day?

u2-1.title: Triads: minor and major
u2-1.goal: Hear root, third and fifth as one harmony.
u2-1.text:
Em contains E–G–B; E major contains E–G#–B: only the third changes. Moving a chord tone to another octave preserves the chord. Play each tone separately and sing the third above the bass.

Pick E bass first, then the upper three strings with a short controlled stroke. Keep unused strings muted. G3 and G#3 are on D frets 5 and 6; B3 and E4 remain fretted. Let the notes ring together after the spread attack.

ku2-1.title: Triads: minor and major
ku2-1.goal: Hear root, third and fifth as one harmony.
ku2-1.text:
Em contains E–G–B; E major contains E–G#–B: only the third changes. Moving a chord tone to another octave preserves the chord. Play each tone separately and sing the third above the bass.

Left E3; right G4–B4–E5 or G#4–B4–E5. Use right 1–2–5; only the thumb moves a semitone.

u2-2.title: Inversion and bass note
u2-2.goal: Distinguish the lowest note from the upper voicing.
u2-2.text:
Em over E is root position, over G first inversion, over B second inversion. The lowest sounding note determines the inversion, not the shape above it. The melody can retain E as a common tone.

Keep G3–B3–E4 above. Bass: open E2, G2 at E-string fret 3, B2 at A-string fret 2. Mute each previous bass at the change.

ku2-2.title: Inversion and bass note
ku2-2.goal: Distinguish the lowest note from the upper voicing.
ku2-2.text:
Em over E is root position, over G first inversion, over B second inversion. The lowest sounding note determines the inversion, not the shape above it. The melody can retain E as a common tone.

Retain the same right-hand chord; rehearse the written bass separately. Name the bass note and then the inversion at each change.

u2-3.title: Thirds with a melodic line
u2-3.goal: Deliberately bring out the upper voice of a dyad.
u2-3.text:
E–G and A–C are minor thirds; G–B is major. Diatonic parallel thirds therefore change size. Read the upper line as the melody first, then add the lower line. Coordinate their releases.

For E3–G3 use A fret 7 and D fret 5. Then G3–B3 on D/G, A3–C4 on G/C. Move the hand with each change.

ku2-3.title: Thirds with a melodic line
ku2-3.goal: Deliberately bring out the upper voice of a dyad.
ku2-3.text:
E–G and A–C are minor thirds; G–B is major. Diatonic parallel thirds therefore change size. Read the upper line as the melody first, then add the lower line. Coordinate their releases.

Right-hand thirds with 1–3 or 2–4; move the whole hand between positions. Quiet left E3 each bar. Also play the top line alone.

u2-4.title: Arpeggio above a bass
u2-4.goal: Play broken triads with a clear upper voice.
u2-4.text:
An arpeggio distributes chord tones in time. Here each written eighth ends at the next melodic note; only the bass sustains. Longer overlap is a later artistic choice, not a substitute for controlled releases.

The pick plays both bass and upper figure. At a shared entry, place bass on the pulse and the upper note immediately after it. Continue the written eighths with small string crossings while the bass rings. Bring out the top note without reattacking the bass.

ku2-4.title: Arpeggio above a bass
ku2-4.goal: Play broken triads with a clear upper voice.
ku2-4.text:
An arpeggio distributes chord tones in time. Here each written eighth ends at the next melodic note; only the bass sustains. Longer overlap is a later artistic choice, not a substitute for controlled releases.

Prepare the right-hand triad, starting with 1–3–5–3. Left hand only at bar starts. Loop one bar before adding chord changes.

u2-6.title: Power chords and muting
u2-6.goal: Play fifths without thirds cleanly and in time.
u2-6.text:
E5 means E and B, not a five-note chord. Without a third it is not explicitly major or minor. In P4 the fifth is one string higher and two frets up. Muting determines clarity under gain.

E5: open E/A fret 2; A5: open A/D fret 2; B5: A fret 2/D fret 4. Strike only those strings. Use both hands to stop rests.

u2-rhythm.title: Short chords and offbeats
u2-rhythm.goal: Enter between clicks and release on time.
u2-rhythm.text:
Here the eighth rest falls on the beat and the chord on the offbeat. Keep counting while you play nothing on the click. A short chord needs a defined release; the next rest is not an extra attack.

Use a short pick stroke across the upper three strings on the offbeat. Release fretting pressure at note-off and control open bass strings. Pick the bass separately on its written beat. Do not fill the eighth rest before the chord with an attack.

ku2-rhythm.title: Short chords and offbeats
ku2-rhythm.goal: Enter between clicks and release on time.
ku2-rhythm.text:
Here the eighth rest falls on the beat and the chord on the offbeat. Keep counting while you play nothing on the click. A short chord needs a defined release; the next rest is not an extra attack.

Right-hand chords are short while the left holds. No sustain pedal. Release with small movements rather than lifting the whole hand high.

u2-5.title: Hear a triad, build a phrase
u2-5.goal: Find chord tones in an original melody.
u2-5.text:
A melody can imply a chord without playing all its notes together. Listen first to the upper closing notes. Sing them away from the instrument, then add bass. More notes do not automatically create more coherence.

Play the upper line first on D/G/C strings. Add bass only at written bar starts. E can remain an audible reference through Em–C.

ku2-5.title: Hear a triad, build a phrase
ku2-5.goal: Find chord tones in an original melody.
ku2-5.text:
A melody can imply a chord without playing all its notes together. Listen first to the upper closing notes. Sing them away from the instrument, then add bass. More notes do not automatically create more coherence.

Sing and play the right-hand melody alone first. Name left-hand bass notes before combining. Write down your fingering and keep it consistent.

u3-1.title: Lamento: a descending bass
u3-1.goal: Combine a slow descending bass with a singing upper voice.
u3-1.text:
E–D–C–B is a descending bass model. Its effect also depends on tempo, duration and upper voice; the notes alone do not guarantee sadness. Read bass and melody separately and compare their intervals at each bar start.

Play E3–D3–C3–B2 bass entirely on A at frets 7–5–3–2. Melody mainly on D. Move the hand down with the bass without shortening the upper line.

ku3-1.title: Lamento: a descending bass
ku3-1.goal: Combine a slow descending bass with a singing upper voice.
ku3-1.text:
E–D–C–B is a descending bass model. Its effect also depends on tempo, duration and upper voice; the notes alone do not guarantee sadness. Read bass and melody separately and compare their intervals at each bar start.

Try left 1–2–3–4 for the slow descending bass. Sing the right-hand line separately. Combine only when the left-hand motion no longer requires searching.

u3-2.title: A circle-of-fifths path
u3-2.goal: Follow common tones through several chords.
u3-2.text:
Em–Am–D–G–C–F#dim–B–Em links roots by descending fifths or ascending fourths, with a diminished fifth from C down to F# (an augmented fourth upward). B major contains D# and leads back to Em here. Hear chord tones rather than recalling shapes alone.

Connect upper triads without bass first. Retain common tones only when their fingering allows the next shape. Mute the old string at each bass change.

ku3-2.title: A circle-of-fifths path
ku3-2.goal: Follow common tones through several chords.
ku3-2.text:
Em–Am–D–G–C–F#dim–B–Em links roots by descending fifths or ascending fourths, with a diminished fifth from C down to F# (an augmented fourth upward). B major contains D# and leads back to Em here. Hear chord tones rather than recalling shapes alone.

Use compact right-hand voicings and left-hand roots. Look at a target before moving. The right hand should not copy every bass leap.

u3-reading.title: Syncopation and tied entries
u3-reading.goal: Sustain an accented subdivision across the next beat.
u3-reading.text:
A syncopation begins between beats and continues across a stronger beat. The tie does not create a second attack. Count eighths, mark quarters with your foot and count through rests.

Melody is on D/G, with picked E bass. Pick each rhythm separately first while the foot keeps quarters. Briefly spread shared entries bass–melody. Sustain tied syncopated melody notes through the following bass attack.

ku3-reading.title: Syncopation and tied entries
ku3-reading.goal: Sustain an accented subdivision across the next beat.
ku3-reading.text:
A syncopation begins between beats and continues across a stronger beat. The tie does not create a second attack. Count eighths, mark quarters with your foot and count through rests.

Hold long E3 notes on the left; rehearse the right-hand rhythm on one key. Check whether a new left-hand attack accidentally retriggers the right.

u3-4.title: Sixteenths and precise rests
u3-4.goal: Read four subdivisions per quarter without accelerating.
u3-4.text:
Sixteenths have two flags or beams. Four fill a quarter. Count “1 e and a” or four even syllables. A sixteenth rest occupies one of those slots; it does not shorten the bar.

Keep picking movements small and loose. Continue the motion internally through rests while muting the string. Start on one pitch, then add the written notes.

ku3-4.title: Sixteenths and precise rests
ku3-4.goal: Read four subdivisions per quarter without accelerating.
ku3-4.text:
Sixteenths have two flags or beams. Four fill a quarter. Count “1 e and a” or four even syllables. A sixteenth rest occupies one of those slots; it does not shorten the bar.

Begin on one right-hand key with alternating fingers, then use the written pitches. Release the key for rests. Keep the left hand independent of the fast subdivisions.

u3-3.title: Separate bass and melody by ear
u3-3.goal: Reduce a two-voice idea to its essential lines.
u3-3.text:
Transcribe the lowest entries first, then the highest. Write rhythm before pitch. The preview provides a fixed reference: do not silently alter what you heard to fit easier shapes.

Bass on E/A, melody on D/G. Listen away from the instrument, write the bass path and verify it alone before adding melody.

ku3-3.title: Separate bass and melody by ear
ku3-3.goal: Reduce a two-voice idea to its essential lines.
ku3-3.text:
Transcribe the lowest entries first, then the highest. Write rhythm before pitch. The preview provides a fixed reference: do not silently alter what you heard to fit easier shapes.

Reconstruct the heard bass with the left hand alone. Sing and find the right-hand melody. Combine only once both lines match.

u3-6.title: Chromatic bass, calm melody
u3-6.goal: Lead semitone bass steps without clipping the upper voice.
u3-6.text:
E–Eb–D–Db–C–B adds chromatic steps to the diatonic descent. Read repeated letter names with changing accidentals carefully. Let audible voice motion create tension rather than adding gain.

Bass entirely on A: frets 7–6–5–4–3–2. Melody on D. End each old bass while retaining the upper note for its written duration.

u3-5.title: Repeats and two endings
u3-5.goal: Play repeats and alternate endings without losing the form.
u3-5.text:
Play the section between repeat signs twice. Use ending 1 on the first pass and ending 2 on the second. The expanded order below the score is a checking aid; afterwards follow the signs alone.

Keep the repeated E bass steady. The first ending stays open on B, the second lands on E. Do not insert a fretting pause at the repeat.

ku3-5.title: Repeats and two endings
ku3-5.goal: Play repeats and alternate endings without losing the form.
ku3-5.text:
Play the section between repeat signs twice. Use ending 1 on the first pass and ending 2 on the second. The expanded order below the score is a checking aid; afterwards follow the signs alone.

Move both hands together at the repeat. Read the two endings separately first, then play the complete order.

u4-1.title: Leading tone and harmonic minor
u4-1.goal: Hear and read D# as a directed approach to E.
u4-1.text:
E harmonic minor is E F# G A B C D#. D#–E is a semitone; C–D# is an augmented second spanning three semitones. The leading tone has direction within a cadence, though other continuations are possible outside it.

Play the upper line on D/G/C. D#4 is C-string fret 3, E4 fret 4. Hear the semitone before moving the finger.

ku4-1.title: Leading tone and harmonic minor
ku4-1.goal: Hear and read D# as a directed approach to E.
ku4-1.text:
E harmonic minor is E F# G A B C D#. D#–E is a semitone; C–D# is an augmented second spanning three semitones. The leading tone has direction within a cadence, though other continuations are possible outside it.

Try right 1–2–3–1–2–3–4–5 for E4–E5. Sing C5–D#5 separately before inserting it in the line. Rehearse bass alone first.

u4-3.title: Cadence: tension and arrival
u4-3.goal: Shape Am–B7–Em as preparation, dominant and arrival.
u4-3.text:
In E minor, Am is iv, B7 is V7 and Em is i. B7 contains B–D#–F#–A. Here D# moves to E and A to G. Hear these motions individually; louder playing does not replace voice leading.

For B7 use F#3–A3–D#4 over B2. Slowly connect the semitone/whole-tone motions to Em. Avoid lifting every finger hurriedly at once.

ku4-3.title: Cadence: tension and arrival
ku4-3.goal: Shape Am–B7–Em as preparation, dominant and arrival.
ku4-3.text:
In E minor, Am is iv, B7 is V7 and Em is i. B7 contains B–D#–F#–A. Here D# moves to E and A to G. Hear these motions individually; louder playing does not replace voice leading.

Play the two resolutions as a right-hand dyad over left B–E first. Add the third right-hand chord tone and coordinate the timing.

u4-chords.title: Sixths, sevenths and chord symbols
u4-chords.goal: Distinguish Em, Em7, Em6, Cmaj7 and B7 by ear.
u4-chords.text:
Em7 adds D, Em6 adds C#. Cmaj7 contains C–E–G–B; B7 contains B–D#–F#–A. “maj7” means a major seventh; “7” uses a minor seventh. A symbol specifies tones, not register or duration.

Check the P4 voicings one note at a time. In Em7 use D4 at G fret 7 and E4 at C fret 4. Keep bass and top voice audible through the change.

ku4-chords.title: Sixths, sevenths and chord symbols
ku4-chords.goal: Distinguish Em, Em7, Em6, Cmaj7 and B7 by ear.
ku4-chords.text:
Em7 adds D, Em6 adds C#. Cmaj7 contains C–E–G–B; B7 contains B–D#–F#–A. “maj7” means a major seventh; “7” uses a minor seventh. A symbol specifies tones, not register or duration.

Left plays the root, right the other three tones. Name each right-hand pitch before playing. Fingering may change between chords; keep the top line connected.

u4-2.title: A diminished seventh in motion
u4-2.goal: Lead D#–F#–A–C as four voices into Em.
u4-2.text:
D#dim7 stacks minor thirds: D#–F#–A–C. Steps of three semitones give 3+3+3 to the diminished seventh C. The symmetry allows different interpretations; here resolution to Em establishes the role. Play each voice’s destination separately.

Bass D#3 is on A fret 6, with F#3 on D4, C4 on G5 and A4 on F4. Spread the chord low to high with the pick. Deliberately mute the C string and skip it or brush it silently; it is not part of this chord. Check every sounding string slowly first.

ku4-2.title: A diminished seventh in motion
ku4-2.goal: Lead D#–F#–A–C as four voices into Em.
ku4-2.text:
D#dim7 stacks minor thirds: D#–F#–A–C. Steps of three semitones give 3+3+3 to the diminished seventh C. The symmetry allows different interpretations; here resolution to Em establishes the role. Play each voice’s destination separately.

Left D#3, right F#4–A4–C5; then left E3 with right G4–B4–E5. Play individual resolutions before the complete four-voice sonorities.

u4-4.title: Lead the inner voices
u4-4.goal: Combine a retained top note with moving inner voices.
u4-4.text:
Across D7–G, D can remain on top while F# moves to G and C to B. Not every voice must move at each chord change. Hear the inner line alone, then within the full sonority.

Hold D4 at C fret 2 as a common top note. For D7–G move F#3/G3 on D and C4/B3 on G. Mute the D3 bass when moving to G2.

ku4-4.title: Lead the inner voices
ku4-4.goal: Combine a retained top note with moving inner voices.
ku4-4.text:
Across D7–G, D can remain on top while F# moves to G and C to B. Not every voice must move at each chord change. Hear the inner line alone, then within the full sonority.

Retain the upper right-hand finger on D5 while the lower fingers move. Prepare left D–G separately; do not hide unclear transitions with sustain pedal.

u4-6.title: Fifth/sixth changes in a riff
u4-6.goal: Play a bass riff with precise upper-interval changes.
u4-6.text:
E–B is a fifth and E–C# a major sixth: seven and nine semitones. These dyads are not complete E6 chords because the third is absent. Use straight eighths first; shuffle follows in phase 5.

Open E plus A frets 2/4; then open A plus D frets 2/4. Change the upper finger while retaining the root reference. Mute unused strings consistently.

u4-5.title: Make a cadence your own
u4-5.goal: Combine modal colour and a functional ending in one form.
u4-5.text:
A long E-pedal passage can remain open; Am–B7–Em then focuses the direction. Decide where the ending starts. Reserving D# for that point makes its contrast with D easier to hear.

First half: open E and single melody. Then use the familiar compact chords. Do not add a fretting pause at the transition.

ku4-5.title: Make a cadence your own
ku4-5.goal: Combine modal colour and a functional ending in one form.
ku4-5.text:
A long E-pedal passage can remain open; Am–B7–Em then focuses the direction. Decide where the ending starts. Reserving D# for that point makes its contrast with D easier to hear.

Left starts with E3, then the cadence roots. Right changes from a single melody to triads without a sudden jump in level.

u5-1.title: Sequence: move a motif
u5-1.goal: Move a motif by scale steps while preserving its identity.
u5-1.text:
A diatonic sequence preserves directions and scale-step distances, not necessarily semitone sizes. This example moves the same four-note motif within E Aeolian. Sing each new starting note first.

Read in the D/G window first. Use the C string for C4; open E bass remains. Do not mask the position change with a louder bass attack.

ku5-1.title: Sequence: move a motif
ku5-1.goal: Move a motif by scale steps while preserving its identity.
ku5-1.text:
A diatonic sequence preserves directions and scale-step distances, not necessarily semitone sizes. This example moves the same four-note motif within E Aeolian. Sing each new starting note first.

Check the new right-hand five-note space before each move. Adapt fingering to the motif instead of forcing the same fingers regardless of black keys.

u5-2.title: Three layers: bass, figure, melody
u5-2.goal: Hold a melody while the inner voice continues.
u5-2.text:
Three layers have separate roles: bass anchors harmony, inner quarters provide motion, long top notes form the melody. Practise each pair before combining all three. Do not reattack melody with every inner note.

Briefly spread the shared entry bass–inner voice–melody with the pick. Hold the top string while picking the inner quarters. Reattack only voices due to enter. Later, a prepared left-hand hammer-on from silence can start an inner voice together with a picked attack; first secure the technique in the phase 5 legato unit.

ku5-2.title: Three layers: bass, figure, melody
ku5-2.goal: Hold a melody while the inner voice continues.
ku5-2.text:
Three layers have separate roles: bass anchors harmony, inner quarters provide motion, long top notes form the melody. Practise each pair before combining all three. Do not reattack melody with every inner note.

Left plays bass. Right holds the top with 5 while 1/2/3 move inside. Practise upper and inner voices with the right hand alone before adding left.

u5-groove.title: Triplets against straight eighths
u5-groove.goal: Alternate two and three subdivisions at a fixed quarter pulse.
u5-groove.text:
A bracketed 3 means three written eighths in the time of two ordinary eighths. Both groups fill one quarter. Count two, then three even syllables per quarter without changing the quarter-note tempo.

Start triplets on E3 with small alternate-picking movements. Continuous alternate picking reverses the starting stroke on the next quarter; that is intentional.

ku5-groove.title: Triplets against straight eighths
ku5-groove.goal: Alternate two and three subdivisions at a fixed quarter pulse.
ku5-groove.text:
A bracketed 3 means three written eighths in the time of two ordinary eighths. Both groups fill one quarter. Count two, then three even syllables per quarter without changing the quarter-note tempo.

Start with right 1–2–3 for each quarter while left plays steady bar starts. Relax after groups without inserting a pause.

u5-4.title: 12/8: four large pulses
u5-4.goal: Read and accompany twelve eighths as four groups of three.
u5-4.text:
12/8 contains twelve eighths, grouped here as 3+3+3+3. Tempo refers to the dotted quarter: four pulses per bar. These eighths are ordinary notes in the meter, not separately marked triplets.

Pick the bass on pulses 1 and 3 and play the upper eighth-note figure between them. Briefly spread shared entries low to high. Preserve the regular eighth spacing afterwards and accent group starts only lightly.

ku5-4.title: 12/8: four large pulses
ku5-4.goal: Read and accompany twelve eighths as four groups of three.
ku5-4.text:
12/8 contains twelve eighths, grouped here as 3+3+3+3. Tempo refers to the dotted quarter: four pulses per bar. These eighths are ordinary notes in the meter, not separately marked triplets.

Hold each left dotted half for two large pulses. Read right-hand groups of three. Play only each group’s first note before filling in the others.

u5-6.title: Legato: hammer-on and pull-off
u5-6.goal: Reduce picked attacks without losing rhythm or level.
u5-6.text:
A slur connects different pitches; unlike a tie, it does not merge repeated pitches. Pick the first note, then create the next with a hammer-on or pull-off. Preview demonstrates pitches and rhythm, not the physical technique’s timbre.

D string: E3 fret 2 with 1, F#3 fret 4 with 3, G3 fret 5 with 4. Prepare the target finger before a pull-off and release the string with control rather than pulling far away.

Only after ordinary hammer-ons and pull-offs are even at low gain: introduce left-hand tapping as a hammer-on from silence. Do not pick the D string first. Tap E3 at fret 2 with finger 1 using a short precise movement, then mute it cleanly. Avoid excess force; aim for a clear note and silent neighbouring strings. Then align the left-hand attack with a picked E2. The right hand keeps the pick.

u5-3.title: Sequence over changing bass
u5-3.goal: Control motif contour and harmonic rhythm together.
u5-3.text:
The figure repeats its rhythm while bass changes every bar: one chord per bar is the harmonic rhythm. Check strong-beat notes first; they should clarify each harmony.

Read the melody ahead of each bass change. Pick the new bass first, immediately followed by the upper note written at the same onset. Continue the figure without accidentally muting the bass. End the old bass at the next change.

ku5-3.title: Sequence over changing bass
ku5-3.goal: Control motif contour and harmonic rhythm together.
ku5-3.text:
The figure repeats its rhythm while bass changes every bar: one chord per bar is the harmonic rhythm. Check strong-beat notes first; they should clarify each harmony.

Left plays root, fifth, octave, fifth in quarters; the diminished chord uses a diminished fifth. Start with 5–2–1–2, allowing the hand to move. Read the right-hand figure separately before combining both moving lines.

u5-5.title: Compare shuffle and swing deliberately
u5-5.goal: Hear ternary phrasing and read it in ordinary eighth notation.
u5-5.text:
Shuffle can be practised as long and short triplet portions. Swing often uses ordinary eighths plus a performance indication. Preview uses 2:1 as a study model; real swing ratios vary with tempo and style. There is no universal swing percentage.

Play long–short on the right while retaining bass once per bar. Use smaller movements at faster tempos; do not swallow short notes. Check the rhythm without gain too.

ku5-5.title: Compare shuffle and swing deliberately
ku5-5.goal: Hear ternary phrasing and read it in ordinary eighth notation.
ku5-5.text:
Shuffle can be practised as long and short triplet portions. Swing often uses ordinary eighths plus a performance indication. Preview uses 2:1 as a study model; real swing ratios vary with tempo and style. There is no universal swing percentage.

Right plays long–short while left stays unchanged. Start with alternating E4–G4 before the full phrase. Avoid locking the hand and arm on every long note.

u6-1.title: Fourth-based sonorities
u6-1.goal: Balance fourth-based sonorities above a clear bass reference.
u6-1.text:
E–A–D stacks two perfect fourths, five semitones each. Without a third, major/minor identity is ambiguous. Bass changes the interpretation. Compare the same upper sonority over E and A before assigning a fixed chord label.

E3–A3–D4 lie on D/G/C at fret 2. A small barre is possible; check each string separately. Briefly spread the bass and upper quartal voicing with the pick. Mute A when using E bass, then let the intended bass sustain.

ku6-1.title: Fourth-based sonorities
ku6-1.goal: Balance fourth-based sonorities above a clear bass reference.
ku6-1.text:
E–A–D stacks two perfect fourths, five semitones each. Without a third, major/minor identity is ambiguous. Bass changes the interpretation. Compare the same upper sonority over E and A before assigning a fixed chord label.

Try right 1–2–5 for E4–A4–D5. With a smaller hand prepare notes consecutively, then sound together only in a comfortably reachable voicing.

u6-2.title: C Lydian: the raised fourth
u6-2.goal: Deliberately compare F# and F above C.
u6-2.text:
C Lydian is C D E F# G A B. Only F changes to F# compared with C major. Make C audible as reference; the same notes over E produce another modal effect. The raised fourth is a colour, not a compulsory resolution rule.

C3 bass at A fret 3. Melody on D/G/C; F#3 at D fret 4. Keep C bass deliberately quieter than the upper phrase.

ku6-2.title: C Lydian: the raised fourth
ku6-2.goal: Deliberately compare F# and F above C.
ku6-2.text:
C Lydian is C D E F# G A B. Only F changes to F# compared with C major. Make C audible as reference; the same notes over E produce another modal effect. The raised fourth is a colour, not a compulsory resolution rule.

Left C3; right reads within C4–B4. Prepare a finger for F# and avoid lifting the hand high when returning to white keys.

u6-3.title: Register changes without a new idea
u6-3.goal: Play a recognisable motif in two octaves.
u6-3.text:
Octave transposition changes register, not note names or rhythm. It still changes presence and density. First check that the higher motif retains its durations and accents.

First phrase on D/G, second on C/F. Look at the target before attacking; bass remains open E. Decide the return fingering too.

ku6-3.title: Register changes without a new idea
ku6-3.goal: Play a recognisable motif in two octaves.
ku6-3.text:
Octave transposition changes register, not note names or rhythm. It still changes presence and density. First check that the higher motif retains its durations and accents.

Move the right hand an octave while retaining left bass. Release the old shape and prepare at the target. The higher version stays below C6.

u6-4.title: Density and release as musical controls
u6-4.goal: Shape two distinct textures from the same pitches.
u6-4.text:
Density comes from simultaneous voices and their decay. More reverb or gain can conceal lines. Shape it first through playing: long bass, short middle, clear melody. Only then compare sounds at similar levels.

Pick only: briefly spread the shared bar opening from bass through inner voice to melody. Let bass and melody ring afterwards; pick only the subsequent inner quarters.
