Mute the inner voice with the fretting hand at its written release without stopping the melody string. Keep the inner voice completely silent in bar two. Start with low gain, then use your usual amp sound. This version does not require tapping.

ku6-4.title: Density and release as musical controls
ku6-4.goal: Shape two distinct textures from the same pitches.
ku6-4.text:
Density comes from simultaneous voices and their decay. More reverb or gain can conceal lines. Shape it first through playing: long bass, short middle, clear melody. Only then compare sounds at similar levels.

Begin without sustain. On synth choose release short enough to reveal rests; on piano control the same endings with fingers.

u6-5.title: Chromatic approaches
u6-5.goal: Reach a chord tone deliberately from a neighbouring pitch.
u6-5.text:
A chromatic neighbour lies a semitone from its target and need not belong to the home scale. Its role depends on destination and accent. Play the target alone first, then approach it briefly from below.

A#3–B3 on G frets 3–4; G#3–A3 on G 1–2. Prepare the target finger close to the fret. Avoid large searching motions.

ku6-5.title: Chromatic approaches
ku6-5.goal: Reach a chord tone deliberately from a neighbouring pitch.
ku6-5.text:
A chromatic neighbour lies a semitone from its target and need not belong to the home scale. Its role depends on destination and accent. Play the target alone first, then approach it briefly from below.

Prepare black neighbour and white target as a small movement. Hear the right-hand destination while holding the chord root on the left.

u6-7.title: Natural harmonics
u6-7.goal: Produce clear octave harmonics and use them as a texture change.
u6-7.text:
A light touch above fret twelve suppresses parts of the string’s vibration; the harmonic sounds one octave above the open string. Diamond heads here show sounding harmonic pitches. Preview plays their pitches without imitating the timbre.

Touch directly above fret twelve rather than pressing between frets. Pick, release the touching finger and mute other strings. E/A/D/G/C/F produce E3/A3/D4/G4/C5/F5.

u6-6.title: Dark reference, bright contrast
u6-6.goal: Distinguish E Aeolian and C Lydian through bass and phrasing.
u6-6.text:
The modes share pitch classes but have different centres, E or C. Changing bass alone may not suffice; give the new centre time and a suitable phrase ending. Make the return audible as a return.

Use open E bass and C at A fret 3. In the contrast hold F#3 deliberately over C. Prepare returning bass and first melody note separately.

ku6-6.title: Dark reference, bright contrast
ku6-6.goal: Distinguish E Aeolian and C Lydian through bass and phrasing.
ku6-6.text:
The modes share pitch classes but have different centres, E or C. Changing bass alone may not suffice; give the new centre time and a suitable phrase ending. Make the return audible as a return.

Left E3 and C3; right retains the same pitch collection. Rest on C or E in the C section, then confirm E as centre for longer on the return.

u7-1.title: Three against two
u7-1.goal: Distribute three upper entries evenly against two bass pulses.
u7-1.text:
Three quarter-note triplets occupy two ordinary quarters. Subdivide their shared span into six: upper entries on 1,3,5 and lower on 1,4. Eventually remove the counting aid while preserving the shared start.

Pick each voice separately first. Then pick bass quarters while the left hand produces upper notes using prepared hammer-ons from silence and suitable pull-offs. A note on a new string needs a fresh left-hand attack on that string; a pull-off on the previous string cannot create it. Both hands meet at shared entries. This is an advanced application of the legato unit; slow down rather than altering the 3:2 rhythm.

ku7-1.title: Three against two
ku7-1.goal: Distribute three upper entries evenly against two bass pulses.
ku7-1.text:
Three quarter-note triplets occupy two ordinary quarters. Subdivide their shared span into six: upper entries on 1,3,5 and lower on 1,4. Eventually remove the counting aid while preserving the shared start.

Left plays quarters, right quarter-note triplets. Tap on your thighs first, then use one key each. Hands share the start, not every attack.

u7-2.title: 3+3+2 within 4/4
u7-2.goal: Displace accents without restarting the measure.
u7-2.text:
Eight eighths can be accented 3+3+2 while remaining one 4/4 bar. Accents fall on beat 1, the offbeat after 2, and beat 4. Bass and drums retain the regular meter against the melodic grouping.

Create accents with attack, not extra duration. E bass on beats 1 and 3. Do not rush the last group of two.

ku7-2.title: 3+3+2 within 4/4
ku7-2.goal: Displace accents without restarting the measure.
ku7-2.text:
Eight eighths can be accented 3+3+2 while remaining one 4/4 bar. Accents fall on beat 1, the offbeat after 2, and beat 4. Bass and drums retain the regular meter against the melodic grouping.

Left plays halves, right even eighths with three accents. If the patch ignores velocity, clarify accents by slightly shortening unaccented notes.

u7-3.title: Grouped 7/8 and 5/8
u7-3.goal: Hear odd meters as recurring groups.
u7-3.text:
Here 7/8 is grouped 2+2+3: count “1-2, 1-2, 1-2-3”. Follow with 5/8 grouped 2+3. Tempo counts eighths, not quarters: at 120 eighths per minute each eighth lasts half a second.

Pick the bass at group starts and the upper eighth-note line. Briefly spread shared entries bass–melody, then keep following eighths on their grid. Later the left hand can attack the shared melody entry while the pick plays bass. Combine rhythm first, then pitches.

ku7-3.title: Grouped 7/8 and 5/8
ku7-3.goal: Hear odd meters as recurring groups.
ku7-3.text:
Here 7/8 is grouped 2+2+3: count “1-2, 1-2, 1-2-3”. Follow with 5/8 grouped 2+3. Tempo counts eighths, not quarters: at 120 eighths per minute each eighth lasts half a second.

Left holds quarter, quarter, dotted quarter group durations. Right plays eighths. Count the complete final group of three before the next beat 1.

u7-4.title: Minor pentatonic with target notes
u7-4.goal: Shape a phrase with a clear destination from five pitches.
u7-4.text:
E minor pentatonic: E G A B D, degrees 1 b3 4 5 b7. F# and C are omitted from E Aeolian. Fewer notes do not replace phrasing: repetition, silence and a target make the statement.

D string E3/G3, G string A3/B3, C string D4/E4. Do not import a standard-tuning box. Sing the target before crossing to the higher string.

ku7-4.title: Minor pentatonic with target notes
ku7-4.goal: Shape a phrase with a clear destination from five pitches.
ku7-4.text:
E minor pentatonic: E G A B D, degrees 1 b3 4 5 b7. F# and C are omitted from E Aeolian. Fewer notes do not replace phrasing: repetition, silence and a target make the statement.

Organise E4–E5 in two small groups. Try 1–2–3–1–2–3 for E–G–A–B–D–E ascending. Left plays E3, then the written changes.

u7-solo.title: Solo, segno and coda
u7-solo.goal: Leave a solo section and land its return reliably.
u7-solo.text:
D.S. means return to the segno. Ignore “to coda” on the first pass; after returning, jump from that point to the coda sign. This example follows 1–2–3–4–2–3–5–6. Count the form before playing. The first bar is written as a count-in: melody enters on beat 4 as a pickup to bar 2. Abbreviated pickup notation omits the preceding rests; the following full measure still begins on beat 1.

Read the melody on the first visit; replace it with an equally long original motif on the second. Retain the bass rhythm and ending.

ku7-solo.title: Solo, segno and coda
ku7-solo.goal: Leave a solo section and land its return reliably.
ku7-solo.text:
D.S. means return to the segno. Ignore “to coda” on the first pass; after returning, jump from that point to the coda sign. This example follows 1–2–3–4–2–3–5–6. Count the form before playing. The first bar is written as a count-in: melody enters on beat 4 as a pickup to bar 2. Abbreviated pickup notation omits the preceding rests; the following full measure still begins on beat 1.

Vary the right-hand solo while retaining the left. Prepare the right-hand coda position without stopping the left.

u7-6.title: Bending towards a heard target
u7-6.goal: Bend a whole tone, hold the target and stop cleanly.
u7-6.text:
A whole tone is two semitones. Hear normally fretted B4 first, then bend A4 to exactly that pitch. The arrow shows the destination. Check intonation before adding vibrato at the target.

High F string: B4 at fret 6, A4 at fret 4. Bend A with the ring finger supported by other fingers. Mute before releasing to avoid an unintended descending note.

u7-5.title: Tempo and longer performances
u7-5.goal: Play the same musical passage reliably at slow and faster tempos.
u7-5.text:
Tempo is a separate skill. A clean slow pass does not guarantee a fast one. Start at a secure tempo, increase in small steps and note the first specific unstable spot. Practise it briefly, then restore the context.

Use small attacks, fixed string choices and prepared changes. Reduce movement at higher tempos rather than increasing fretting pressure.

ku7-5.title: Tempo and longer performances
ku7-5.goal: Play the same musical passage reliably at slow and faster tempos.
ku7-5.text:
Tempo is a separate skill. A clean slow pass does not guarantee a fast one. Start at a secure tempo, increase in small steps and note the first specific unstable spot. Practise it briefly, then restore the context.

Set fingering before the tempo series. Begin arm movements for jumps while the last note still sounds. Playing louder is not a tempo aid.

u8-1.title: Form: return and contrast
u8-1.goal: Organise a longer statement from familiar motifs.
u8-1.text:
The model has four four-bar sections: A, varied A, contrasting B, returning A. Retained rhythm and motif opening make the return recognisable. Plan section boundaries before adding more notes.

Mark string changes at section boundaries. Play bass and melody separately through all sixteen bars before combining.

ku8-1.title: Form: return and contrast
ku8-1.goal: Organise a longer statement from familiar motifs.
ku8-1.text:
The model has four four-bar sections: A, varied A, contrasting B, returning A. Retained rhythm and motif opening make the return recognisable. Plan section boundaries before adding more notes.

Learn the left-hand bass as its own form. Know each section’s right-hand opening from memory; this supports recovery without replacing reading.

u8-2.title: Solo arrangement in three layers
u8-2.goal: Combine melody, figuration and bass into a playable arrangement.
u8-2.text:
Begin with a singable melody. Add bass, then inner voices only where hands and ears have room. A written rest is a musical choice. The example moves from two to three layers.

For each held note check which string remains free for the next. If two voices need the same string, change position or notate a deliberate release.

ku8-2.title: Solo arrangement in three layers
ku8-2.goal: Combine melody, figuration and bass into a playable arrangement.
ku8-2.text:
Begin with a singable melody. Add bass, then inner voices only where hands and ears have room. A written rest is a musical choice. The example moves from two to three layers.

Where practical, right 4/5 retain the top while 1/2/3 handle the middle. Do not force an octave stretch: revoice or omit an inner note and notate that decision.

u8-3.title: Carry a motif into another key
u8-3.goal: Transpose an idea by pitch relationships rather than shape memory.
u8-3.text:
E to A is a perfect fourth, five semitones upward. E–G–B becomes A–C–E while intervals and durations stay the same. Open strings and fingering still require a fresh check.

Open E bass becomes open A. Redistribute melody over G/C; do not treat an open note as a movable fret.

ku8-3.title: Carry a motif into another key
ku8-3.goal: Transpose an idea by pitch relationships rather than shape memory.
ku8-3.text:
E to A is a perfect fourth, five semitones upward. E–G–B becomes A–C–E while intervals and durations stay the same. Open strings and fingering still require a fresh check.

Right E4–G4–B4 becomes A4–C5–E5. Transpose left bass accordingly. Name pitches before placing the hands.

u8-4.title: Score, silence and D.C. al Fine
u8-4.goal: Create a readable score including a return and silence.
u8-4.text:
D.C. al Fine means return to the beginning and stop on reaching Fine again. Ignore Fine on the first visit. Here four sounding bars lead to two silent bars and the return: 1–2–3–4–5–6–1–2–3–4. In a multi-measure rest, the number above the rest bar gives the number of silent measures. Both bars remain written out here to check the counting.

Mute all strings through the silent bars while counting internally. Prepare the restart in time. Avoid creating an accidental count-in with string noise.

ku8-4.title: Score, silence and D.C. al Fine
ku8-4.goal: Create a readable score including a return and silence.
ku8-4.text:
D.C. al Fine means return to the beginning and stop on reaching Fine again. Ignore Fine on the first visit. Here four sounding bars lead to two silent bars and the return: 1–2–3–4–5–6–1–2–3–4. In a multi-measure rest, the number above the rest bar gives the number of silent measures. Both bars remain written out here to check the counting.

Release keys and pedal completely during silent bars. Prepare the next position quietly; long synth release must not obscure the written silence.

u8-5.title: A performance starts before the first note
u8-5.goal: Present a short form without trial starts.
u8-5.text:
Before starting, hear the tonic internally, choose tempo and know the first entry and ending. After an error keep pulse and aim for the next secure landmark. Practise starting mid-piece so every error does not force a restart.

Check tuning, set the intended level and prepare the opening shape. Play clean first, then with your tone at a comparable level.

ku8-5.title: A performance starts before the first note
ku8-5.goal: Present a short form without trial starts.
ku8-5.text:
Before starting, hear the tonic internally, choose tempo and know the first entry and ending. After an error keep pulse and aim for the next secure landmark. Practise starting mid-piece so every error does not force a restart.

At an unfamiliar piano briefly check register and pedal response. Choose a secure key and start with a simple bass-and-melody form without hunting for sounds.

u8-7.title: Self-sufficient guitar transitions
u8-7.goal: Connect harmonic, pedal, figure and chord without breaking flow.
u8-7.text:
A solo arrangement does not need every voice continuously. Transitions matter: a decaying note can prepare movement, a rest can articulate a texture change. Put every deliberate interruption in the score.

Play the E-string harmonic above fret twelve, then move to the low position. Use the written rest for travel. In the three-layer section hold the top string and mute inner voices selectively.

u8-6.title: Final project: an original solo piece
u8-6.goal: Read, shape and develop a complete notated form.
u8-6.text:
The 32-bar model combines motif, contrast, three layers, triplets and cadence. It is a working example, not a substitute for your own piece. Check four bars, then eight, then the whole form. Completion requires audible shaping and repeatable decisions.

Check bass muting, held melody, free strings for inner voices and position changes. Note essential finger/position cues; do not replace rhythm reading with tablature.

ku8-6.title: Final project: an original solo piece
ku8-6.goal: Read, shape and develop a complete notated form.
ku8-6.text:
The 32-bar model combines motif, contrast, three layers, triplets and cadence. It is a working example, not a substitute for your own piece. Check four bars, then eight, then the whole form. Completion requires audible shaping and repeatable decisions.

Check balance, readable hand positions and deliberate releases. Left plays a broken bass figure in the triplet section; prepare hands separately. Make at least one recording with piano-like decay; another may use your synth tone.

theorie.title: Theory
theorie.lead: What the references do, why it works and what they share. Notation, harmony, rhythm, sound and form built on E–A–D. Listen, model, apply.

t0.title: Tone and notation
t0.goal: Frequency, overtones, tuning, complete pitch and rhythm notation, a listening method. Map the references and understand distortion physically.

tu0-1.title: Frequency, overtones, interval as ratio
tu0-1.goal: Hear and calculate intervals as frequency ratios; know the overtone series on E.
tu0-1.text:
A tone is a periodic vibration. The low E string vibrates at about 82.4 Hz (E2). A string does not only vibrate as a whole but simultaneously in halves, thirds, quarters. These partial vibrations are overtones. Their frequencies are integer multiples: 2f, 3f, 4f. For E2 = 82.4 Hz: 164.8 (E3), 247.2 (B3), 329.6 (E4), 412 (≈G#4), 494.4 (B4), 576.8 (≈D5), 659.2 (E5).

The series therefore contains the octave, the fifth, the major third and a low minor seventh. The seventh partial sits 31 cents below the tempered D, the fifth partial 14 cents below G#. A power chord E–B reinforces partials that are already in the string. That is why it stays stable under distortion.

Intervals are ratios: octave 2:1, fifth 3:2, fourth 4:3, major third 5:4, minor third 6:5. Small numbers sound fused, large numbers rough. Equal temperament replaces these ratios with powers of 2^(1/12); the fifth becomes 2 cents too small, the major third 14 cents too wide. On guitar you hear this as beating thirds under gain.

An instrument's timbre depends on which partials are present and how strong. A piano has slightly stretched overtones (inharmonicity), a synthesizer sawtooth has all partials at amplitude 1/n, a square wave only the odd ones. This is the starting point for phase 6.

te0-1-1.title: Listen · Frequency, overtones, interval as ratio
te0-1-1.instructions: Type O Negative, *October Rust*, "Love You to Death": listen to the first distorted guitar entry after the piano intro. Decide whether the guitar plays fifths or thirds, without an instrument. Then check with the guitar: which partials do you hear above the root? Claim: fifths and octaves, no thirds in the low register (verify).
checklist: Fifth or third decided without an instrument, then checked?
Timestamp and impression logged?

te0-1-2.title: Model · Frequency, overtones, interval as ratio
te0-1-2.instructions: The overtone series on E2, partials 1–8. Play each tone on guitar or keyboard and sing it. Compute each partial from 82.4 Hz and compare with the tempered pitch: where is the largest deviation? Harmonics over frets 12, 7 and 5 of the E string give partials 2, 3 and 4 directly.
checklist: All eight frequencies calculated and the two largest deviations named?
Partials 2, 3, 4 found as harmonics?

te0-1-3.title: Application · Frequency, overtones, interval as ratio
te0-1-3.instructions: Record E2 and B2 together, once clean, once with gain. Describe in the log which additional pitches appear with gain. Repeat with E2 and G2. State in one sentence why doom riffs put fifths low and thirds high.
checklist: Four recordings, clean/gain difference described?
Sentence about register choice logged?

tu0-2.title: Why E A D: fourths, fifths and their complements
tu0-2.goal: Understand the logic of guitar tuning and read E–A–D as a chain of fourths with three centres.
tu0-2.text:
The fourth (5 semitones) and the fifth (7 semitones) complete each other to the octave: 5 + 7 = 12. Going up a fourth lands on the same letter as going down a fifth. E up to A, A up to D: this is the same motion as E down to A down to D in the circle of fifths. The low guitar strings follow this chain. The bass has it complete: E A D G.

Standard tuning breaks the chain between G and B (a major third) so that six strings fit two octaves E2–E4 and major/minor shapes are reachable with four fingers. Pure fourths (P4: E A D G C F) keep the geometry identical on all strings: every interval has one shape that works everywhere. The price is a range up to F4 and unfamiliar chord shapes. Type O Negative tune the same standard chain a fourth lower: B E A D F# B (verify). The relationships stay, the register drops.

E–A–D as a pitch set are three possible centres. In A: E is V, D is IV, the classic cadence axis. In E: A is IV, D is bVII, the modal axis of E Aeolian or E Mixolydian. In D: A is V, E is II. The same three tones therefore carry a functional and a modal reading. The course builds both.

Open strings are pedal tones without a fretting hand. On E, A and D you can hold a pedal over any of the three centres and move above it. That is the practical reason this music works so well on guitar: the foundation costs no finger.

te0-2-1.title: Listen · Why E A D: fourths, fifths and their complements
te0-2-1.instructions: Anathema, *Eternity*, "Sentient" and the opening of "Angelica": determine the bass foundation of the first minute of each. Does it stay on one tone or alternate between two centres? Claim: long pedal tones, changes by a fourth or fifth (verify). Write the root you hear as a letter, not as a shape.
checklist: Root of both passages written as a letter?
Interval between the centres determined?

te0-2-2.title: Model · Why E A D: fourths, fifths and their complements
te0-2-2.instructions: Bar 1: standard tuning, bar 2: P4. The first four strings are identical. Count the semitones between all neighbouring strings in both tunings. Under each string write its tone as a degree in E, A and D (e.g. D = bVII in E, IV in A, I in D).
checklist: Semitone gaps of both tunings fully counted?
Degree table for E, A and D written?

te0-2-3.title: Application · Why E A D: fourths, fifths and their complements
te0-2-3.instructions: Play eight bars using only the open strings E, A, D as bass, two bars per centre and back to E. Listen for where the change sounds like a cadence (V–I) and where like a modal colour change (I–bVII). Note order and effect.
checklist: Cadential and modal effect named at specific changes?
Eight bars recorded?

tu0-3.title: Pitch notation complete
tu0-3.goal: Master clefs, octave registers, key signatures, accidentals and enharmonics without gaps.
tu0-3.text:
Five lines, one clef fixes one pitch. Treble clef: G4 on the second line. Bass clef: F3 on the fourth line. C4 sits between both staves on a ledger line. Guitar sounds an octave lower than written; in this course the sounding E2 appears as E3 in the treble staff. Bass is likewise written an octave up in the bass clef. Keyboard is written at pitch.

Octave numbers: C4 = MIDI 60 = 261.6 Hz. Each octave doubles the frequency and raises the number by one. E2 is the low guitar string, E1 the low bass string, B0 the low string of a guitar tuned to B (verify: Type O Negative).

Key signatures: sharps in the order F C G D A E B, flats in the order B E A D G C F. The last sharp plus a semitone is the major key; the second-to-last flat is the major key. Minor sits a minor third below. Em has one sharp (F#), Am none, Dm one flat (Bb). The three centres of this course sit next to each other in the circle of fifths.

Accidentals last until the barline in the same octave. Enharmonics: G# and Ab are the same key but not the same function. In E major G# is the third, in E minor Ab would be a foreign tone. Write a tone the way it moves: leading tones upward as sharps, descending passing tones as flats. That is why the chromatic bass E–Eb–D–Db–C–B in phase 3 is written with flats.

te0-3-1.title: Listen · Pitch notation complete
te0-3-1.instructions: My Dying Bride, *Turn Loose the Swans*, "Sear Me MCMXCIII": piano and violin without guitar. Determine the key by ear from the phrase endings and write its signature. Check at the keyboard whether the third is major or minor. Claim: minor, violin in the register above C5 (verify).
checklist: Key and signature written, third checked?
Violin register named as an octave number?

te0-3-2.title: Model · Pitch notation complete
te0-3-2.instructions: E Aeolian ascending with key signature, E harmonic minor descending with the accidental D#. Name every note with octave number. Write the same line in the bass clef two octaves lower on paper. Write D#5 once as Eb5 and explain why that would be wrong here.
checklist: All 16 tones named with octave, bass-clef version written?
Reason for D# instead of Eb logged?

te0-3-3.title: Application · Pitch notation complete
te0-3-3.instructions: Write the open strings of guitar (P4), bass (E A D G) and the lowest key of your 49-key keyboard, each at sounding pitch and, where customary, in transposed notation. Next to it write the key signatures of Em, Am, Dm, E, A, D. Check at the instrument.
checklist: Sounding and written registers correct for all strings?
Six key signatures without looking up?

tu0-4.title: Rhythm notation complete
tu0-4.goal: Read and write all note values, dots, ties, rests, time signatures and beaming reliably.
tu0-4.text:
Whole, half, quarter, eighth, sixteenth: each step halves. A dot adds half, a second dot adds another quarter. A tie joins equal pitches into one duration; a slur joins different pitches and says nothing about duration. Rests have the same values as notes; a whole rest hangs below the fourth line, a half rest sits on the third.

The time signature gives the number of beats on top and the note value of one beat below. 4/4: four quarters. 3/4: three quarters. 6/8, 9/8, 12/8: compound, eighths group in threes, the felt pulse is the dotted quarter. 5/8 and 7/8: eighths group unequally, here 2+3 and 2+2+3. The tempo mark always states which value is counted: ♩ = 60, ♩. = 60 or ♪ = 120 mean three different things.

Beams show grouping: per quarter in 4/4, per group of three in 12/8. A syncopation sits between beats and sounds across the next beat; it is written with a tie, not as a hidden value across the beat. Rule: every beat in the bar stays visible.

Doom lives on tempi between 50 and 80 quarters. At ♩ = 60 a whole note lasts four seconds. A riff of four whole notes is a sixteen-second thought. The references stretch time this way, and notation has to show it: whole and half notes are normal values, not exceptions.

te0-4-1.title: Listen · Rhythm notation complete
te0-4-1.instructions: My Dying Bride, "The Crown of Sympathy": count the tempo of the first guitar phrase in quarters per minute (stopwatch, 8 beats). Decide whether the guitar thinks in whole, half or quarter notes. Compare with Vivaldi, *Winter*, movement 1, opening: tempo and smallest value. Claim: the doom phrase in halves and wholes, Vivaldi in eighths at a similar pulse (verify).
checklist: Both tempi measured and logged?
Smallest note value of both passages determined?

te0-4-2.title: Model · Rhythm notation complete
te0-4-2.instructions: Seven bars on one tone: quarters, eighth pairs, dotting, eighth rests, sixteenths, a tie across the barline. Clap each bar alone, then all with the click. Write the counting syllables (1 and 2 e and a) under every bar. Explain why bars 6–7 use a tie instead of a note crossing the barline.
checklist: All seven bars labelled with counting syllables?
Tie rule explained in one sentence?

te0-4-3.title: Application · Rhythm notation complete
te0-4-3.instructions: Write one bar each in 4/4, 3/4, 6/8, 12/8, 7/8 (2+2+3) and 5/8 (2+3) with correct beaming, each with at least one rest and one dotted value. Add the matching tempo unit (♩, ♩. or ♪). Play every bar four times on one tone.
checklist: Six bars with correct beaming and tempo unit?
Every bar four times without losing the pulse?

tu0-5.title: Listening method: rhythm before pitch, bass before melody
tu0-5.goal: Have a fixed order for transcribing that holds up on dense recordings.
tu0-5.text:
Transcribing rarely fails at the ear, mostly at the order. The method: 1. Form: count sections, bars per section. 2. Pulse and meter: tap along, find the accent, measure tempo. 3. Bass: lowest voice, note changes per bar, letters only at first. 4. Clap the melody's rhythm on one tone. 5. Melody pitches, starting from the first and last note of each phrase. 6. Inner voices and chord types last.

The bass is the key because in this music it determines the chord. The guitar often plays only fifths; whether the chord is major or minor is told by the vocals, the keyboards or by nothing at all. A chord symbol without a third is more honest than a guessed third.

Tools: half speed without pitch change, a two-bar loop, singing along in a comfortable octave. Not: guessing shapes and hearing the recording to fit. When two tones seem possible, play both and let the recording decide.

For Baroque, reverse it: the bass moves, the upper voice is often a sequence. Recognise the sequence formula first (which interval is transposed how many times), then write it out. In Type O Negative voices are doubled in octaves; only the lowest voice counts for the notation.

te0-5-1.title: Listen · Listening method: rhythm before pitch, bass before melody
te0-5-1.instructions: Type O Negative, "Red Water (Christmas Mourning)": first vocal section. Run the six steps of the method and stop after each. Write the bass tones as letters per bar, then the rhythm of the vocal melody. Melody pitches only in the third pass. Claim: the bass changes less than once per bar (verify).
checklist: Six steps logged individually?
Bass letters written before melody pitches?

te0-5-2.title: Model · Listening method: rhythm before pitch, bass before melody
te0-5-2.instructions: Listen to the preview three times without looking at the notes. Pass 1: bass letters. Pass 2: clap the upper voice rhythm. Pass 3: upper voice pitches, first and last note first. Only then compare. Mark which step needed the most attempts.
checklist: Three passes in the given order?
Weakest step named in the log?

te0-5-3.title: Application · Listening method: rhythm before pitch, bass before melody
te0-5-3.instructions: Choose a two-bar excerpt from Vivaldi, *Summer*, movement 3 (Presto). Identify the sequence formula of the upper voice first, then the bass, then notate. Write out the two bars and play them slowly on the keyboard. Compare with the recording.
checklist: Sequence formula named before writing out?
Two bars notated and compared at the keyboard?

tu0-6.title: Mapping the references: instruments, registers, roles
tu0-6.goal: For each reference album know who occupies which register and carries which role.
tu0-6.text:
Four roles carry almost every piece: foundation (bass, low guitar, organ pedal), pulse (drums, continuo rhythm, riff attack), pad (keyboards, strings, sustained chords) and line (vocals, violin, lead guitar). Registers sort roughly: foundation E1–E3, riffs E2–E4, pads C3–C6, line C4–C6.

My Dying Bride, *Turn Loose the Swans*: two guitars, often in thirds or octaves; violin and keyboards (Martin Powell) as line and pad; bass mostly follows the riff; drums in half-time. Vocals alternate between growl in the riff register and spoken voice.

Type O Negative, *October Rust*: guitar tuned to B, bass with chorus and octaver as a second pad, keyboards (Josh Silver) as organ/choir/bells, vocals low and doubled in octaves. Very few instruments, a great deal of register: everything is wide.

Anathema, *Eternity*: clean arpeggio guitar and distorted rhythm guitar at the same time, keyboards as a string pad, clear vocals in the middle register. The bass carries long tones, the drums hold quarters.

Vivaldi, *Le quattro stagioni*: solo violin (line), ripieno strings (pad and pulse), continuo (foundation: cello, harpsichord/organ). Biber, *Harmonia artificioso-ariosa*: two violins (or violas d'amore) over continuo; the line is doubled, the pad emerges from the two-part writing itself.

Shared: a foundation that changes more slowly than the line. That is the structure this course rebuilds on guitar alone or keyboard alone.

te0-6-1.title: Listen · Mapping the references: instruments, registers, roles
te0-6-1.instructions: Listen to one minute each from five pieces, one per reference: "Your River" (MDB), "Green Man" (Type O), "Eternity Part I" (Anathema), *Spring* movement 1 (Vivaldi), Partita I, first movement (Biber). For each fill a table: foundation, pulse, pad, line, each with instrument and estimated register. Claim: in all five the foundation changes less often than the line (verify).
checklist: Five tables with four roles filled in?
Claim about rate of change checked for each piece?

te0-6-2.title: Model · Mapping the references: instruments, registers, roles
te0-6-2.instructions: Four registers in turn: foundation (E2–B2), riff (E3–B3), pad (G4–E5), line (G5–B5). Play the four bars on the keyboard and hear how each layer feels. Then all four together as one sound: describe which layer is missed least when you drop it.
checklist: Four layers played alone and together?
Most dispensable layer named with a reason?

te0-6-3.title: Application · Mapping the references: instruments, registers, roles
te0-6-3.instructions: Write a register map for your own setup: P4 guitar, bass (if available), 49-key keyboard, synths. For each source enter which of the four roles it can take in solo playing and which role is inevitably missing when playing alone. This map is the basis for phase 8.
checklist: All own sources entered with register and roles?
Missing role in solo playing named?

tu0-7.title: Distortion as a nonlinear system
tu0-7.goal: Understand why fifths carry under gain and thirds turn muddy; calculate difference tones.
tu0-7.text:
A linear amplifier outputs only the frequencies that go in. Distortion cuts the waveform (clipping). This creates extra overtones for every tone and combination tones for every pair: the sum and difference of the frequencies and their multiples. For two tones f1 and f2 you get f2 − f1, f1 + f2, 2f1 − f2 and more.

Fifth 3:2 (E3 = 165 Hz, B3 = 247 Hz): difference 82 Hz = E2. The combination tone is the root an octave lower. The power chord reinforces itself. Sum 412 Hz ≈ G#4: a slight major colouring that you really hear under heavy distortion.

Major third 5:4 (E4 = 330, G#4 = 415): difference 85 Hz ≈ E2. Again the root, two octaves down. The major third is therefore tolerable under gain when it sits high.

Minor third 6:5 (E4 = 330, G4 = 392): difference 62 Hz ≈ B1/C2. A foreign tone that does not belong to the Em chord. The lower the third sits, the louder and lower this foreign tone becomes. That is the physical reason low minor thirds turn to mud under distortion and why doom guitars omit the third, place it high or leave it to the keyboard.

Consequences: power chords low, thirds high or clean. Two guitars in thirds (My Dying Bride) therefore sit in the register above E3 with moderate gain. Type O Negative often let vocals and organ carry the thirds. More gain means more combination tones, hence fewer tolerable intervals.

te0-7-1.title: Listen · Distortion as a nonlinear system
te0-7-1.instructions: My Dying Bride, "The Songless Bird": find a passage where both guitars play in thirds and one where they play fifths or octaves. Compare register and perceived gain. Claim: the thirds sit higher and sound less distorted than the fifth riffs (verify).
checklist: Third and fifth passages found, registers estimated?
Perceived gain of both passages compared?

te0-7-2.title: Model · Distortion as a nonlinear system
te0-7-2.instructions: Top: the interval; bottom: the calculated difference tone. Recompute all three: frequencies from the acoustics appendix, take the difference, find the nearest tone. Then play each interval on the guitar with heavy gain and check whether the difference tone matches the bass. Bar 3 yields a tone outside Em.
checklist: Three difference tones calculated yourself?
Foreign tone in bar 3 heard at the instrument or logged as inaudible?

te0-7-3.title: Application · Distortion as a nonlinear system
te0-7-3.instructions: Build a four-bar riff using the same pitch classes E, G, B: bars 1–2 only fifths and octaves low, bars 3–4 the third G in the register above E4. Record with your usual gain. Formulate a rule for your own rig: from which register does the minor third stay clean?
checklist: Riff recorded with varied third register?
Own register rule logged?

t1.title: Centre and mode
t1.goal: Root, pedal and the seven modes. Aeolian, Phrygian, Dorian, Lydian as colours over E, A and D. Distinguish modal from tonal.

tu1-1.title: Root, drone, pedal
tu1-1.goal: Know what makes a tone the centre, and why a pedal tone is what makes modality audible in the first place.
tu1-1.text:
A centre is created not by a scale but by weight: duration, recurrence, low register, accent and final position. A tone that lies long, returns often, sits in the bass and ends phrases is heard as the root, whatever runs above it. That is the pedal tone. A drone is the same idea without interruption.

Over an E pedal the melody determines the mode: F# or F, C or C#, D or D#. Without the pedal the same melody would be ambiguous. E F G A B C D over E is Phrygian, the same tones over C are C major, over A they are A minor. The bass decides, not the pitch set.

The references work with pedals almost throughout. Anathema hold whole sections on one bass tone and change only the guitar colour above it. Type O Negative let bass and organ lie while the vocal shifts the third back and forth. Vivaldi builds pedal points into the ritornelli (organ point on the dominant before the return). Biber sets a repeated bass model in the ciaccone, a rhythmicised pedal.

For you: the open E, A or D bass is the pedal. Everything this course teaches about modes is at first just "which tones over which pedal". Cadences come later and need bass changes.

te1-1-1.title: Listen · Root, drone, pedal
te1-1-1.instructions: Anathema, "The Beloved": listen to the opening and count how many bars the bass stays on one tone before changing. Then decide whether the guitar above changes the third or the second. Claim: at least eight bars on one bass tone, colour change only in the upper voice (verify).
checklist: Number of pedal bars counted?
Changed scale degree named?

te1-1-2.title: Model · Root, drone, pedal
te1-1-2.instructions: One pedal, four colours: Phrygian (F), Aeolian (F#), Dorian (C#), major (G#). Only one tone changes each time. Listen to each bar twice and name the changed tone before looking at the notes. Then play the four bars over your own E pedal on guitar or keyboard.
checklist: Four changed tones named without the score?
Four bars played over your own pedal?

te1-1-3.title: Application · Root, drone, pedal
te1-1-3.instructions: Play eight bars of E pedal and sing over it. Every two bars change exactly one tone (F/F#, C/C#, D/D#, G/G#). Record. Write which change has the strongest effect and which hardly registers. Repeat over an A pedal with the matching tones (Bb/B, F/F#, G/G#, C/C#).
checklist: Four changes over E and over A recorded?
Strongest and weakest change named?

tu1-2.title: The seven modes from one pitch set
tu1-2.goal: Know all modes as a reordering of the same seven tones and build them over each of the three centres.
tu1-2.text:
The white keys C D E F G A B contain seven modes, depending on which tone is the centre: C Ionian (major), D Dorian, E Phrygian, F Lydian, G Mixolydian, A Aeolian (minor), B Locrian. The semitones always lie between E–F and B–C; their position relative to the centre makes the character.

Semitone pattern (steps in semitones): Ionian 2-2-1-2-2-2-1, Dorian 2-1-2-2-2-1-2, Phrygian 1-2-2-2-1-2-2, Lydian 2-2-2-1-2-2-1, Mixolydian 2-2-1-2-2-1-2, Aeolian 2-1-2-2-1-2-2, Locrian 1-2-2-1-2-2-2.

Order by brightness: Lydian, Ionian, Mixolydian, Dorian, Aeolian, Phrygian, Locrian. Each step to the right lowers exactly one tone: #4 → 4, 7 → b7, 3 → b3, 6 → b6, 2 → b2, 5 → b5. That is the order of the circle of fifths. Knowing this, you can build any mode over any centre in seconds.

Over E: E Lydian (E F# G# A# B C# D#), E major, E Mixolydian (D), E Dorian (G, C#), E Aeolian (G, C), E Phrygian (F), E Locrian (F, Bb). Over A and D likewise. The references use Aeolian (base colour), Phrygian (darkening), Dorian (brightening within minor), Lydian and Ionian (contrast). Locrian has no perfect fifth and does not work as a centre; it appears only in passing.

te1-2-1.title: Listen · The seven modes from one pitch set
te1-2-1.instructions: Type O Negative, "Green Man": determine the mode of the main section over the bass. Is the third major? Is the seventh minor? Claim: major third with minor seventh, i.e. Mixolydian, or plain major (verify, both are plausible; decide on the seventh degree).
checklist: Third and seventh determined separately?
Mode with reasoning logged?

te1-2-2.title: Model · The seven modes from one pitch set
te1-2-2.instructions: Seven modes over E from bright to dark; each bar lowers exactly one tone. Mark the new tone in every bar. Play the series on the keyboard and sing along. Then, without the score, build the same series over A and over D and write the tones down.
checklist: Seven changed tones marked?
Series over A and D written without a model?

te1-2-3.title: Application · The seven modes from one pitch set
te1-2-3.instructions: Take a four-bar motif of five tones and play it over an E pedal in Aeolian, Dorian, Phrygian and Lydian, without changing rhythm or contour. Record all four. Order them by ear from bright to dark and check the order against the table.
checklist: Four versions recorded with identical rhythm?
Impression matches the brightness order, deviation noted?

tu1-3.title: Aeolian and Phrygian: the base colours of doom
tu1-3.goal: Recognise b6 and b2 as the two tones that carry the dark sound of the references.
tu1-3.text:
Aeolian is natural minor: 1 2 b3 4 5 b6 b7. Its characteristic tone is b6, in E the C. The step b6 → 5 (C → B) is a semitone down and the most common closing move in this music. The chord on b6 is major (C), the one on b7 as well (D). The progression Em–C–D–Em is therefore the base model of modal minor: three chords, no leading tone, no dominant.

Phrygian lowers the 2 as well: 1 b2 b3 4 5 b6 b7, in E the F. The semitone above the root pushes the melody downward; F–E is the Phrygian close. The chord on b2 is major (F), on 5 diminished (Bdim). Phrygian therefore has no usable dominant chord; it lives from the melodic motion b2–1.

My Dying Bride use Aeolian as the default state and slip into Phrygian to darken, often in the violin. Type O Negative mostly stay Aeolian, but the bass emphasises b6 as its own chord (C over E minor). Anathema use b6 as a pad (C chord under an E melody), and the effect is not grief but width.

The trap: b6 and b2 are both semitone neighbours of a chord tone (5 and 1). Both create downward tension. Difference: b6 resolves into the fifth, b2 into the root. The second case feels more final.

te1-3-1.title: Listen · Aeolian and Phrygian: the base colours of doom
te1-3-1.instructions: My Dying Bride, "Turn Loose the Swans" (title track): find the spot where the violin first plays a b2 (semitone above the root). Compare with a passage that uses only b6. Claim: the piece begins Aeolian and darkens to Phrygian in the violin (verify).
checklist: b2 spot and b6 spot found?
Difference in effect in one sentence?

te1-3-2.title: Model · Aeolian and Phrygian: the base colours of doom
te1-3-2.instructions: Bars 1–4 Aeolian: Em–C–D–Em, close via C–B in the melody. Bars 5–8 Phrygian: Em–F–Em, close F–E. The bass plays fifths like a low guitar. Play both halves and name which semitone step makes each close. Then swap: end bar 4 with F–E and bar 8 with C–B.
checklist: Both closing moves named?
Swapped version played and difference described?

te1-3-3.title: Application · Aeolian and Phrygian: the base colours of doom
te1-3-3.instructions: Write eight bars over an E pedal: four Aeolian, four Phrygian. Use exactly one of the two closes in each half. Transpose the same eight bars to A (b6 = F, b2 = Bb) and play both versions. Note which key has the darker effect on your instrument and why (register).
checklist: Eight bars notated in E and in A?
Register reasoning logged?

tu1-4.title: Dorian and Lydian as contrast colours
tu1-4.goal: Know the brightened modes as a means of contrast within one piece.
tu1-4.text:
Dorian is minor with a major sixth: 1 2 b3 4 5 6 b7, in E the C#. The chord on IV becomes major (A instead of Am). Em–A is the basic Dorian motion; it sounds minor but not mournful. Anathema use it in brighter sections, and many doom bands reach for it when a riff should "float" without turning major.

Lydian is major with a raised fourth: 1 2 3 #4 5 6 7, in C the F#. Same pitch classes as E Aeolian, different centre. The #4 does not pull down like an ordinary 4; it hovers. The chord on II is major (D over C). In this music Lydian usually does not arise from new tones but from bass changes: an E minor piece whose bass stays on C sounds Lydian as long as F# appears in the melody.

That is the core of this course: E Aeolian, C Lydian, G Ionian, D Mixolydian, A Dorian, B Phrygian are one pitch set. The bass chooses the colour. A piece can begin dark on E, widen on C, float Dorian on A and close on E without a single foreign tone.

Vivaldi does not know this modal thinking as a system, but the effect occurs: the long pedal point at the end of the first Spring movement holds the harmony still. In the partitas Biber writes movements over a sustained bass that sound Dorian or Mixolydian before the cadence sorts them tonally.

te1-4-1.title: Listen · Dorian and Lydian as contrast colours
te1-4-1.instructions: Anathema, "Eternity Part II" or "Radiance": find a section in which the bass sits on C or A while the guitar keeps the E minor pitch set. Determine the mode that results. Claim: at least one passage sounds Lydian (major with #4) through the bass alone (verify).
checklist: Bass tone and resulting mode determined?
#4 actually heard in the melody?

te1-4-2.title: Model · Dorian and Lydian as contrast colours
te1-4-2.instructions: Bars 1–2: Em–A, Dorian brightening via C#. Bars 3–4: C bass under E minor tones, the F# makes it Lydian. Bars 5–6: A minor as the way back, close on E. Play the eight bars and name centre and mode per bar. Then replace C# in bar 2 with C and hear the difference.
checklist: Centre and mode named per bar?
C#/C comparison described?

te1-4-3.title: Application · Dorian and Lydian as contrast colours
te1-4-3.instructions: Compose twelve bars without any tone foreign to the E minor set: four on E, four on C, four on A, then close on E. The melody may repeat; only the bass changes. Record and write the mode name above each section.
checklist: Three centres with the same pitch set?
Mode names above each section correct?

tu1-5.title: E–A–D: I–IV–V, chain of fourths, three centres
tu1-5.goal: Read the same three roots functionally, modally and as equal centres.
tu1-5.text:
Three tones, three readings.

Functional in A: D is IV (subdominant), E is V (dominant). A–D–E–A is the cadence that has defined tonality since the Baroque. E as dominant needs the major third G# so that a leading tone into A exists. Without G#, E minor is not a dominant but a modal neighbour.

Modal in E: A is IV, D is bVII. Em–A–D–Em has no leading tone; D major contains F#, which does not pull to E but stays. This is the motion of almost all reference riffs: the bass moves in fourths and fifths, but the harmony stays inside one mode. A sense of travel without a sense of arrival.

As three centres: any of the three can be the root for a section. E dark (Aeolian/Phrygian), A Dorian or Aeolian, D Mixolydian or major. A piece that shifts between them does not modulate in the tonal sense; it shifts weight within one pitch set.

The chain of fourths E–A–D is also the direction in which cadences fall: V → I is a descending fifth, the same path. The Baroque uses it as the circle-of-fifths sequence (phases 3 and 4). Doom uses it as a bass riff without resolution. The tones are the same, the expectation differs, and expectation comes from thirds and sevenths, not from roots.

te1-5-1.title: Listen · E–A–D: I–IV–V, chain of fourths, three centres
te1-5-1.instructions: Type O Negative, "Be My Druidess": write the roots of the main riff as letters. Determine whether they lie a fourth or fifth apart. Then listen to Vivaldi, *Autumn*, movement 1, opening: write the first bass roots. Claim: both move in fourths/fifths, but only Vivaldi has leading tones (verify).
checklist: Root sequences of both passages written?
Leading tone named in Vivaldi, ruled out in Type O?

te1-5-2.title: Model · E–A–D: I–IV–V, chain of fourths, three centres
te1-5-2.instructions: Bars 1–4: A–D–E–A, functional, with G# as leading tone in bar 3. Bars 5–8: Em–A–D–Em, modal, with G instead of G#. The bass is nearly identical in both halves. Play both and describe what bar 3 does differently from bar 8. Then replace G# in bar 3 with G and hear the cadence disappear.
checklist: Difference between bar 3 and bar 8 in one sentence?
G#/G swap played and effect described?

te1-5-3.title: Application · E–A–D: I–IV–V, chain of fourths, three centres
te1-5-3.instructions: Write two versions of the same eight-bar bass riff on E, A, D: one with a leading tone (G# before A or C# before D) in exactly one place, one with none. Record both. Decide which you would use for a doom piece and which for a Baroque model, and justify with the third.
checklist: Two versions with identical bass notated?
Assignment with third-based reasoning logged?

tu1-6.title: Modal or tonal: when a chord has function
tu1-6.goal: Have a criterion for saying at any point whether harmony pushes or rests.
tu1-6.text:
Tonal means: chords have roles (tonic, subdominant, dominant), and the dominant creates an expectation the tonic fulfils. The expectation comes from two tones: the leading tone (7 → 1, semitone up) and the seventh of the dominant (4 → 3, semitone or whole tone down). Together they form a tritone, the most unstable interval. B7 to Em: D# → E, A → G.

Modal means: chords are colours over a centre. They follow each other but do not resolve. There is no tritone forcing anything. Em–C–D–Em can run forever. That is not more primitive but a different form of time: state instead of path.

Criterion: does the chord before the root contain the leading tone (in E: D#)? Then tonal. Does it contain b7 (D) or no third at all? Then modal. Doom and gothic are almost entirely modal; the few tonal moments therefore hit hard. Type O Negative occasionally place a real dominant at chorus ends, and exactly there it sounds like the Beatles (verify). Vivaldi is entirely tonal; the sequences are chains of dominants. Biber sits in between: dance movements tonal, ciaccone modally coloured.

Consequence for your pieces: decide per section. A modal section may be long because it does not push. A tonal close may be short because it resolves. Do not mix casually; an accidental D# in a modal riff sounds like a mistake, a planned one like arrival.

te1-6-1.title: Listen · Modal or tonal: when a chord has function
te1-6-1.instructions: Type O Negative, "Haunted" and "Die with Me": find one section ending in each. Determine whether the chord before the root contains a leading tone. Then listen to Vivaldi, *Spring*, movement 1, end of the first ritornello: leading tone audible? Claim: Type O mostly without leading tone, Vivaldi always with (verify).
checklist: Three closes classified as modal/tonal?
Leading tone named as a pitch each time?

te1-6-2.title: Model · Modal or tonal: when a chord has function
te1-6-2.instructions: Bars 1–4 modal (D before Em), bars 5–8 tonal (B7 before Em). Only bars 3 and 7 differ. Play both halves and describe the expectation before the last bar. Name the two tones in B7 that create the tension and where they go.
checklist: Expectation before bar 4 and bar 8 compared?
D# → E and A → G named?

te1-6-3.title: Application · Modal or tonal: when a chord has function
te1-6-3.instructions: Take your phase-1 motif from the instrument course. Write a sixteen-bar form: twelve bars modal on E without D#, four bars of close with exactly one B7. Play the form twice, once with and once without the B7. Note whether the modal part feels complete without the close.
checklist: Sixteen bars with exactly one leading-tone chord notated?
Completeness without the close assessed?

tu1-7.title: Anathema, Eternity: pad, bass and time
tu1-7.goal: Read a whole album as an application of modality and derive rules for long sections from it.
tu1-7.text:
*Eternity* (1996) is the transition from doom-death to atmospheric rock. What remains: slow harmony, pedal tones, long forms. What is new: clean guitar arpeggios as pad, keyboards as strings, clear vocals. The album shows how modality carries without distortion.

Observations to verify: sections are long, often 16 or 32 bars on two or three chords. The bass changes rarely and mostly by a fourth or a third (E → C, E → A). The arpeggios keep their figure across the change; only one or two tones adapt. The melody sits in the middle (C4–C5), the pad above, the bass far below. Between them is air. That air is the sound.

The model behind it is Pink Floyd, the model before that is Baroque: Vivaldi's Largo movements (*Winter*, movement 2) are exactly this: a pad (pizzicato strings), a bass (long), a line (solo violin). The difference is harmony: Vivaldi changes tonally every bar, Anathema modally every four to eight bars.

Rules for long modal sections: 1. The bass changes at most every four bars. 2. The figure (arpeggio) stays, the tones adapt. 3. The melody has rests longer than its phrases. 4. One tone of the pad stays across the whole section (common tone). 5. Density rises only once, at the end.

te1-7-1.title: Listen · Anathema, Eternity: pad, bass and time
te1-7-1.instructions: Anathema, "Eternity Part I" complete. Draw a timeline: section boundaries, bass tone per section, bars per section, density (1–4 roles active). Check the five rules from the text one by one. Claim: rules 1 and 2 hold throughout, rule 5 holds once per piece (verify).
checklist: Timeline with bass tones and bar counts drawn?
Five rules individually confirmed or refuted?

te1-7-2.title: Model · Anathema, Eternity: pad, bass and time
te1-7-2.instructions: Eight bars after the five rules: bass every two bars, figure stays, E and E5 lie over everything as common tones, one tone adapts per change. Play the figure on the keyboard, sing a melody with long rests over it. Mark which tone changed at every bass change.
checklist: Changed tone marked per bass change?
Melody sung with rests longer than phrases?

te1-7-3.title: Application · Anathema, Eternity: pad, bass and time
te1-7-3.instructions: Write a 32-bar section after the five rules over E, C, A, E (eight bars each). Notate figure, bass and a melody with at least 50 % rests. Density rises only in the last four bars. Record and judge whether 32 bars carry without changing the figure.
checklist: 32 bars with unchanged figure notated?
Density rise only at the end, verdict logged?

t2.title: Dyads and triads
t2.goal: Triad, inversion, power chord, thirds and sixths, voice leading, voicing in low tunings, two-part writing and the complete chord symbol system.

tu2-1.title: Triad, inversion, spacing
tu2-1.goal: Know the four triad types, their inversions and the difference between inversion and spacing.
tu2-1.text:
A triad is root, third, fifth. Four types by third and fifth: major (major third, perfect fifth), minor (minor third, perfect fifth), diminished (minor third, diminished fifth), augmented (major third, augmented fifth). In semitones: major 4+3, minor 3+4, diminished 3+3, augmented 4+4.

Within a scale a triad arises on every degree. E Aeolian: Em, F#dim, G, Am, Bm, C, D. E harmonic minor replaces Bm with B and D with D#dim. The major chords on b6 and b7 (C, D) are the modal sound; the major chord on 5 (B) is the tonal one.

Inversion means which chord tone is in the bass: root position (1), first inversion (3 in the bass), second inversion (5 in the bass). Spacing means how far apart the tones above are distributed: close position (all within an octave), open position (with gaps). Em in open position E2–B3–G4 sounds entirely different from E4–G4–B4 but is the same chord in the same inversion.

On guitar and in this music open spacing is the rule: bass low, third high. Reason: the difference tones from phase 0. On keyboard close spacing in the right hand is comfortable but turns muddy below E3. Rule for both: no thirds below C3.

te2-1-1.title: Listen · Triad, inversion, spacing
te2-1-1.instructions: Type O Negative, "Love You to Death", piano intro: for the first four chords determine type (major/minor) and spacing (close/open). Where is the third: left or right hand? Claim: open spacing, third on top, root low (verify).
checklist: Four chords with type and spacing written?
Position of the third determined?

te2-1-2.title: Model · Triad, inversion, spacing
te2-1-2.instructions: Bars 1–2: the same Em close and open. Bars 3–4: first and second inversion (G and B in the bass). Bars 5–7: major, diminished, augmented over the same E. Bar 8: back to Em. Play each bar, say type, inversion and spacing aloud. Listen especially to how close (bar 1) and open (bar 2) differ.
checklist: Eight bars named with type, inversion, spacing?
Close/open effect described?

te2-1-3.title: Application · Triad, inversion, spacing
te2-1-3.instructions: Write all seven triads of E Aeolian in open spacing (bass below C3, third above C4). Play them on the keyboard as a sequence and mark which are major, minor, diminished. Repeat for A Aeolian and D Aeolian without looking up.
checklist: 21 triads notated with type?
Diminished chord found on degree 2 in every key?

tu2-2.title: The power chord: voicings and sub-octave
tu2-2.goal: Know the three power chord shapes and the role of the octave below; understand Type O Negative's bass sound.
tu2-2.text:
A power chord is root and fifth, often with the octave: 1–5 or 1–5–8. Without a third it is neither major nor minor; the third is supplied by the context (vocals, keyboard, melody) or by no one. The third shape is the inverted fifth: 5–1 (a fourth), e.g. B2–E3. It sounds heavier because the root is on top and the difference tone (E2, an octave below the root) replaces the bass. Doom bands use this fourth shape when the bass is absent or when the riff should sound lower than the tuning allows.

The octave below: Type O Negative produce it electronically. Peter Steele played bass with an octaver and chorus; the result is a foundation an octave below the played tone that at the same time hovers wide (verify). The octaver produces exactly the difference tone from phase 0, only under control. Guitar in B, bass with sub-octave, organ above: three registers that never collide.

On P4 the fifth lies one string up, two frets over; the octave two strings up, two frets over. The fourth shape lies on two neighbouring strings at the same fret. Every shape moves anywhere.

Power chords carry riffs, not harmony. A sequence of power chords is a bass line with reinforcement. Adding their thirds is the job of the other instruments or of the next unit.

te2-2-1.title: Listen · The power chord: voicings and sub-octave
te2-2-1.instructions: Type O Negative, "Wolf Moon": isolate the bass in the main riff. Do you hear two octaves at once (octaver)? Do you hear beating (chorus)? Compare with My Dying Bride, "Your River": bass follows the guitar without effects? Claim: Type O wide and octaved, MDB dry and in unison (verify).
checklist: Octaver and chorus in Type O confirmed or rejected?
Bass role in MDB described?

te2-2-2.title: Model · The power chord: voicings and sub-octave
te2-2-2.instructions: Three power chord shapes over E, then A5 and D5 (chain of fourths), back to E5. Bar 3 shows the fourth shape B–E: the bass E2 here is the difference tone a distorted amp produces by itself. Play all shapes on P4 and find the fret geometry for each. Play bar 3 with and without the written bass and check whether the amp supplies the E2.
checklist: Three shapes found on P4?
Difference tone in bar 3 checked without the written bass?

te2-2-3.title: Application · The power chord: voicings and sub-octave
te2-2-3.instructions: Write an eight-bar riff of power chords only on E, A, D that uses each of the three shapes at least twice. Notate bass (roots) and guitar separately. Play it and decide where a third is missing and which instrument would have to supply it.
checklist: All three shapes in the riff, bass notated separately?
Missing third with instrument assignment logged?

tu2-3.title: Thirds, sixths, parallel motion
tu2-3.goal: Build diatonic thirds and sixths, hear their size and understand My Dying Bride's two-guitar sound.
tu2-3.text:
Two voices a third apart moving through a scale alternate between major and minor thirds. In E Aeolian: E–G minor, F#–A minor, G–B major, A–C minor, B–D minor, C–E major, D–F# major. The sixth is the inversion of the third: G–E (major sixth) is E–G inverted. Minor third ↔ major sixth, major third ↔ minor sixth. Thirds sound dense, sixths open; both are "sweet" intervals, the standard parallels of the Baroque.

My Dying Bride often lead two guitars in parallel thirds or sixths above the riff, and the violin adds a third voice on top (verify). The trick: thirds in the register above E4 and with less gain than the riff. Below that it turns to mud (phase 0). Sixths tolerate gain better than thirds because their difference tone is usually a chord tone: for G3–E4 (major sixth, 5:3) the difference of 196 and 330 Hz is 134 Hz ≈ C3, a foreign tone that fits a C major context, a b6 in Em. Do the arithmetic yourself; the rule is: major sixths work lower than minor thirds.

Vivaldi writes parallel thirds in almost every ritornello, often between first and second violin; the motion comes from the bass. Biber sets two violins in thirds and sixths and then switches to contrary motion so it does not turn saccharine. This alternation is the rule: parallels are a colour, not a state.

For you: notating thirds means writing two voices, not one chord. Both have their own note endings.

te2-3-1.title: Listen · Thirds, sixths, parallel motion
te2-3-1.instructions: My Dying Bride, "The Snow in My Hand": find the first passage with two guitars a third or sixth apart. Determine the interval (sing both voices) and the register. Compare with Biber, Partita II, a slow movement: where do the violins run parallel, where in contrary motion? Claim: MDB stay parallel, Biber switches within a few bars (verify).
checklist: Interval and register in MDB determined?
Parallel and contrary motion located in Biber?

te2-3-2.title: Model · Thirds, sixths, parallel motion
te2-3-2.instructions: Bars 1–2 thirds, bars 3–4 sixths, both through E Aeolian over an E pedal. Under each interval write "major" or "minor". Sing the lower voice while the preview plays, then the upper. Play the thirds an octave lower with gain and hear where they become unclean.
checklist: All 14 intervals labelled major/minor?
Lower limit of clean thirds on your rig noted?

te2-3-3.title: Application · Thirds, sixths, parallel motion
te2-3-3.instructions: Take a four-bar power chord riff (E, C, D, E). Above it write a melody and a second voice in thirds. In bar 3 replace the thirds with sixths, in bar 4 with contrary motion (one voice up, one down). Record all three layers.
checklist: Three layers notated, bars 3 and 4 changed?
Recording with an audible second voice?

tu2-4.title: Voice leading: common tone, shortest path
tu2-4.goal: Think of chord changes as motion of individual voices; apply the two basic rules.
tu2-4.text:
A chord change is not a change of shape but three or four voices that each move or stay individually. Rule 1: common tones stay. Rule 2: the other voices take the shortest path, usually a semitone or whole tone. Rule 3 (Baroque): avoid two voices moving in parallel octaves or fifths when they are meant to be heard as independent. In a riff rule 3 does not apply: power chords are deliberate parallel fifths.

Em → C: E and G stay, B moves to C. Em → Am: E stays, G → A, B → C. Em → D: no common tone, everything shifts a step: E → D or F#, G → F#, B → A. Em → B7: B stays, E → D#, G → F# or A. This produces voicings in which the top voice almost stands still while the bass leaps. That is exactly what you hear in Type O Negative's organ and in Anathema's pad: the bass makes the motion, on top one tone changes (verify).

Vivaldi and Biber are the teachers: in the continuo the harpsichordist voices by these rules, and the string parts are set so that every voice remains singable. Singable is the criterion: can you sing every voice of your voicing on its own? Then the voice leading is good.

On guitar voice leading often means leaving one finger down and moving two. On keyboard it means not shifting the right hand but individual fingers.

te2-4-1.title: Listen · Voice leading: common tone, shortest path
te2-4-1.instructions: Type O Negative, "Red Water (Christmas Mourning)", organ part in the chorus: follow only the top organ voice through four chord changes. How often does it move? How far? Claim: at most one step per change, often none (verify).
checklist: Top voice traced through four changes and written?
Moves counted in semitones/whole tones?

te2-4-2.title: Model · Voice leading: common tone, shortest path
te2-4-2.instructions: Eight chords with minimal voice leading in three upper voices. Draw a line for each voice through all eight bars and count the semitones of every move. Find the largest leap and explain why it is necessary (D has no common tone with Em). Play on the keyboard keeping fingers down where possible.
checklist: Three voice lines drawn with semitone counts?
Largest leap found and justified?

te2-4-3.title: Application · Voice leading: common tone, shortest path
te2-4-3.instructions: Write the progression Em–Am–D–G–C–B7–Em in three upper voices by the rules. Every voice must be singable alone. Then transfer it to guitar: which fingers stay down? Where does P4 force a different voicing? Notate both versions.
checklist: Seven chords with singable voices notated?
Guitar version with held fingers marked?

tu2-5.title: Voicing in low tunings: Type O Negative
tu2-5.goal: Know how a low tuning changes register, voicing and arrangement.
tu2-5.text:
Type O Negative tune the guitar to B (B E A D F# B), a fourth below standard (verify). The lowest string sits at B1 ≈ 61.7 Hz. All shapes stay the same, all tones sound a fourth lower. An E shape sounds as B, an A shape as E. This matters to you because P4 is the same idea in the other direction: same geometry, different pitch space.

What a low tuning forces: 1. Thirds move upward or disappear because the difference tones fall below 40 Hz and become mere pressure. 2. Chords widen: root on the lowest string, next tone at the earliest an octave above. 3. The bass can no longer sit below the guitar; it doubles it or goes lower still with an octaver. 4. The keyboards take over the register C4–C6 entirely because the guitar no longer reaches it.

*October Rust* shows the result: the guitar is a low, wide carpet, often only root and fifth, widened with chorus. The organ has the thirds. The vocal sits low and is doubled an octave higher. The arrangement is a layer cake without overlap.

For P4 the reverse applies: your highest string is F4, you have more room on top than standard and the same below. Thirds are clean from the C string up. You do not need a low tuning; if you want one, the rule is: everything down by the same number of semitones, thirds up by the same number of strings.

te2-5-1.title: Listen · Voicing in low tunings: Type O Negative
te2-5-1.instructions: Type O Negative, "Haunted": sort the registers: where is the guitar, the bass, the organ, the two vocal voices? Estimate the octave for each. Claim: guitar B1–B3, bass with sub-octave below, organ from C4, vocals around E2–E3 and E3–E4 (verify).
checklist: Five registers estimated with octave numbers?
Overlaps found or ruled out?

te2-5-2.title: Model · Voicing in low tunings: Type O Negative
te2-5-2.instructions: The layer cake in four bars: guitar only the fifth, low; organ with the third from G4; vocal line between (E4–D4). Nothing overlaps. Play the layers one after another on the keyboard. Then move the organ an octave lower (G3) and hear what happens to the third.
checklist: Three layers played separately and together?
Effect of the lower organ third described?

te2-5-3.title: Application · Voicing in low tunings: Type O Negative
te2-5-3.instructions: Plan an arrangement for your means: P4 guitar (state register), keyboard, optional bass. Assign every source a register that overlaps with no other, and decide who carries the third. Write four bars in which every source uses only its register, and record them layer by layer.
checklist: Register plan without overlap written?
Third carrier decided and four bars recorded?

tu2-6.title: Two-part writing: types of motion
tu2-6.goal: Recognise and deliberately use parallel, oblique and contrary motion, as violin and guitar do in My Dying Bride.
tu2-6.text:
Two voices can move in four ways. Parallel: same direction, same interval (thirds, sixths). Similar: same direction, different interval. Oblique: one voice holds, the other moves (the pedal with melody from phase 1). Contrary: opposite directions. The mixture keeps two-part writing alive; pure parallels sound like one voice with an effect.

Consonances between two voices: octave, fifth, third, sixth. Dissonances: second, seventh, tritone, and the fourth when formed against the bass. In the Baroque a dissonance is prepared (the tone was previously a consonance) and resolved stepwise downward. That is the suspension: 4–3 or 7–6 over a held bass. Vivaldi's Largo movements consist of chains of such suspensions. Doom bands do this intuitively: the violin in My Dying Bride holds a tone while the guitar changes beneath, and the held tone becomes dissonant for a bar before moving on (verify).

Biber is the school for this: the two violins of *Harmonia artificioso-ariosa* constantly swap roles. The canons (one voice follows the other at a distance) show that the same melody can be consonant against itself when the types of motion are right.

For guitar alone: bass and melody are already two-part writing. Oblique motion (pedal) is the default, contrary motion (bass falls, melody rises) the climax.

te2-6-1.title: Listen · Two-part writing: types of motion
te2-6-1.instructions: My Dying Bride, "Black God": piano and violin. In the first minute determine the type of motion between the violin and the piano top voice at four points. Find at least one held violin tone that becomes dissonant across a change. Claim: mostly oblique motion with one suspension per phrase (verify).
checklist: Four points noted with type of motion?
One suspension (preparation, dissonance, resolution) located?

te2-6-2.title: Model · Two-part writing: types of motion
te2-6-2.instructions: Four bars, four types of motion: bar 1 oblique over E, bar 2 parallel thirds, bar 3 contrary motion, bar 4 suspension: A held over E (fourth, dissonant) resolving to G (third). Name the interval for every pair of tones. Play bar 4 several times and hold the A longer until the dissonance is clear.
checklist: All intervals of the four bars named?
Suspension played with prolonged dissonance?

te2-6-3.title: Application · Two-part writing: types of motion
te2-6-3.instructions: Write eight bars for bass and melody (guitar alone or two hands): at least two bars of each type of motion and exactly one prepared suspension. Mark every bar with its type of motion. Play and check whether the contrary motion works as the climax.
checklist: Four types of motion and one suspension marked?
Climax effect of contrary motion assessed?

tu2-7.title: Chord symbols complete
tu2-7.goal: Translate every common symbol into tones and back, including extensions, sus, add and slash chords.
tu2-7.text:
A symbol names root, third, fifth and additions. Reading order: root (C), type (nothing = major, m = minor, dim/° = diminished, aug/+ = augmented), seventh (7 = minor, maj7/Δ = major), extensions (9, 11, 13), alterations (b5, #5, b9, #9, #11, b13), additions (add9, add11), omissions (no3, no5), bass (/E).

Seventh chords: C7 = C E G Bb (dominant seventh). Cmaj7 = C E G B. Cm7 = C Eb G Bb. Cm(maj7) = C Eb G B. Cdim7 = C Eb Gb Bbb (A). Cm7b5 = C Eb Gb Bb (half-diminished, ø). C6 = C E G A. Cm6 = C Eb G A.

Extensions build on the seventh: C9 = C7 + D. C11 = C9 + F (the third is usually omitted because E rubs against F). C13 = C9 + A. Cmaj9 = Cmaj7 + D. Cm9, Cm11 likewise. Without a seventh the addition is called add: Cadd9 = C E G D. Cmadd9 = C Eb G D, a favourite sound of Anathema and many post-doom bands.

sus replaces the third: Csus4 = C F G, Csus2 = C D G. Without a third the chord is neither major nor minor, like the power chord, but with tension. C5 = C G. Slash: C/E is C major with E in the bass (first inversion), C/G second inversion; Em/C is something else: an Em sound over C, in fact a Cmaj7 without root doubling. The bass decides.

The symbol fixes tones, not spacing, doubling or duration. Two players with the same symbol play different voicings. For your notation: symbols above the notes are commentary, the notes are the truth.

te2-7-1.title: Listen · Chord symbols complete
te2-7-1.instructions: Anathema, "Angelica": the chord that opens the chorus. Does it contain a ninth (add9)? A sus tone? Sing all the tones you hear and write the symbol. Compare with Type O Negative, "Be My Druidess", organ chord in the chorus: seventh audible? Claim: Anathema madd9, Type O plain triads (verify).
checklist: Symbol written for both chords?
All heard tones sung individually?

te2-7-2.title: Model · Chord symbols complete
te2-7-2.instructions: Eight symbols, eight voicings. Cover the symbols, listen to each bar and write all tones. Derive the symbol. Bars 5 and 7 have the same upper voices over C: why is one called Cmaj7 and the other Em/C? Bar 8: B7b9 contains C, the b9; name where C and D# want to go.
checklist: Eight symbols derived from the tones?
Cmaj7/Em/C question and b9 resolution answered?

te2-7-3.title: Application · Chord symbols complete
te2-7-3.instructions: Write a table of all symbol types from the text with tones over E, A and D (one column per root). Play every chord over A on the keyboard in open spacing. Choose four that suit your sound and write an eight-bar progression with symbols above the notes.
checklist: Table complete for three roots?
Eight-bar progression with symbols and written-out notes?

t3.title: Bass and motion
t3.goal: Lamento, circle of fifths, ostinato and ritornello. The bass as foundation or countervoice, its register, and the language of drums.

tu3-1.title: The lamento bass: from Baroque to doom
tu3-1.goal: Know the descending tetrachord as the model shared by all five references.
tu3-1.text:
The lamento bass is a descending path from the root to the fifth: diatonic E–D–C–B or chromatic E–Eb–D–Db–C–B. In the 17th century it was the fixed formula for lament (Monteverdi, Purcell's "Dido's Lament"). Vivaldi uses it in slow movements, Biber in ciaccone as a repeated bass model.

Why it works: every step is small, the direction is unambiguous, and the goal (the fifth B) is the dominant, the point of greatest expectation. A different chord can be built over each bass tone: Em, D (or Bm/D), C, B. The melody can hold (E over all four) or rise in contrary motion. The bass does the work; the upper voice may be simple.

Doom did not quote the lamento bass; it rediscovered it: Em–D–C–B is the progression of countless slow riffs, mostly as power chords. My Dying Bride use it diatonically, often with the violin as a held voice (verify). Type O Negative prefer the chromatic version in the organ (verify). Anathema take the first step (E–D) and linger.

The reverse, the ascending tetrachord B–C–D–E, is the arrival after the descent. Together they form an eight-bar model: four bars down, four up. That is already a complete form.

te3-1-1.title: Listen · The lamento bass: from Baroque to doom
te3-1-1.instructions: My Dying Bride, "The Crown of Sympathy": find a section in which the bass descends in four steps. Write the four tones and decide whether it is diatonic or chromatic. Do you hear a held voice above? Claim: diatonic lamento with sustained violin (verify). Then Vivaldi, *Winter*, movement 2: the bass of the Largo in its first four bars.
checklist: Four bass tones in MDB written, diatonic/chromatic decided?
Bass of the Vivaldi Largo written and compared?

te3-1-2.title: Model · The lamento bass: from Baroque to doom
te3-1-2.instructions: Bars 1–4 diatonic lamento with thirds above. Bars 5–10 chromatic version; the upper voices fall in parallel sixths, one semitone per step. Bars 11–12 arrival on Em. Play both versions and name above each bar the chord the bass forms with the two upper voices. Which version creates more expectation before bar 11?
checklist: Chords of both versions named?
Expectation comparison logged?

te3-1-3.title: Application · The lamento bass: from Baroque to doom
te3-1-3.instructions: Write eight bars: four bars of lamento descending (diatonic or chromatic, your choice), four bars of the ascending tetrachord B–C–D–E. Above it a melody that holds (E) during the descent and falls in contrary motion during the ascent. Play with half-time drums and record.
checklist: Descent and ascent notated with matching melodic motion?
Recording with drums?

tu3-2.title: Circle of fifths and sequence models
tu3-2.goal: Understand the circle-of-fifths sequence and its variants as the engine of Baroque harmony and use it as riff material.
tu3-2.text:
The circle-of-fifths sequence strings roots in falling fifths (or rising fourths): E–A–D–G–C–F#–B–E. In E Aeolian this yields Em–Am–D–G–C–F#dim–B(m)–Em. Each chord is the "dominant" of the next in terms of bass motion, even when it is minor. That is why the sequence creates pull without needing a leading tone. With a leading tone (B instead of Bm at the end) the tonal arrival is added.

Vivaldi builds whole ritornelli from falling fifths, often with seventh chords: each chord has a seventh that falls into the third of the next. That is the chain of sevenths (phase 4). In Summer, movement 3, and Winter, movement 1, you hear it as the engine of the storms (verify). In Biber falling fifths appear in the dance movements, often with sequences of the upper voice above.

Other sequence models: falling thirds (E–C–A–F#: each chord shares two tones with the next, very soft), falling seconds (the lamento), rising fifths (the reverse, builds instead of releasing). A sequence also transposes a motif of the upper voice stepwise; bass and upper voice move as a pattern.

In doom the circle of fifths is rarely complete; two links suffice: Em–Am, Am–D, D–G. Type O Negative do have passages that run through four links, mostly in choruses, and there it immediately sounds "classical" (verify). Rule: the more links, the stronger the pull, the less modal.

te3-2-1.title: Listen · Circle of fifths and sequence models
te3-2-1.instructions: Vivaldi, *Summer*, movement 3 (Presto): find a spot where the bass roots fall in fifths and write at least four links. Then Type O Negative, "My Girlfriend's Girlfriend", chorus: write the roots. Claim: Vivaldi runs through six or more links, Type O at most three (verify).
checklist: At least four falling-fifth links in Vivaldi written?
Roots of the Type O chorus classified as sequence or non-sequence?
