te3-2-2.title: Model · Circle of fifths and sequence models
te3-2-2.instructions: Complete circle of fifths through E Aeolian with a leading tone at the end (B instead of Bm). The upper voice is a sequence: the same three-tone motif (5–3–1 of each chord) falls with the bass. Mark where the motif changes its semitone spacing because of the scale. Play only the bass and sing the sequence. Replace D# in bar 7 with D and hear the arrival vanish.
checklist: Semitone changes of the motif marked?
Bass played, sequence sung, D#/D compared?

te3-2-3.title: Application · Circle of fifths and sequence models
te3-2-3.instructions: Write three four-bar riffs with the same motif: one over falling fifths (Em–Am–D–G), one over falling thirds (Em–C–Am–F#dim), one over rising fifths (Em–Bm–F#dim–C). Play all three and describe the direction of tension (building, releasing, floating). Choose one for a doom riff and justify.
checklist: Three sequence models notated with the same motif?
Tension direction described per model, choice justified?

tu3-3.title: Ostinato and ritornello
tu3-3.goal: Understand repetition as a form principle: the repeated bass model (Biber) and the returning tutti (Vivaldi) versus the riff.
tu3-3.text:
An ostinato is a pattern that repeats unchanged while something above it changes. The ciacona in Biber is the purest form: a four- or eight-bar bass model with endless variations above. Listeners know the bass after the second pass and only hear what is new. The riff is the same principle: a doom riff repeats and vocals, violin or lead guitar vary above it.

The ritornello (Vivaldi) is the other repetition: a tutti section that returns between solo episodes, often shortened or in another key. The form of a Vivaldi movement: R – solo – R′ – solo – R″ – solo – R. The return is recognition; the episodes are the journey. Transferred to rock: chorus and verse, except that Vivaldi's chorus is a little different every time.

Both principles answer the same question: how long may something stay the same? Ostinato: very long, if something moves above it. Ritornello: only briefly, but often. My Dying Bride combine both: a riff runs eight to sixteen times (ostinato), and a section returns after a long absence (ritornello). The effect of return after ten minutes is the strongest weapon of long forms.

Rules: an ostinato needs a layer of variation above it, otherwise it becomes stasis. A ritornello needs contrast between its appearances, otherwise it is mere repetition. Both need a plan for when they end.

te3-3-1.title: Listen · Ostinato and ritornello
te3-3-1.instructions: Biber, Partita III (or another with a ciacona): count the bars of the bass model and how often it repeats. Write the bass tones. Then Vivaldi, *Spring*, movement 1: count the ritornello entries and note which are shortened. Claim: Biber's bass repeats over 20 times, Vivaldi's ritornello appears five times (verify).
checklist: Bass model written and repetitions counted?
Ritornello entries noted with lengths?

te3-3-2.title: Model · Ostinato and ritornello
te3-3-2.instructions: A ciacona model in 3/4: four-bar bass E–B–C–B in quarters, chords as middle voice, a variation above on the second pass. Play bass and chords in a loop and invent a new upper voice on every pass without changing the bass. Count how many passes you can fill before you run out of ideas.
checklist: At least four passes played with different upper voices?
Bass unchanged in all passes?

te3-3-3.title: Application · Ostinato and ritornello
te3-3-3.instructions: Write a form with a ritornello: four bars R (riff with chords), eight bars episode (bass and melody only, different centre), R shortened to two bars, eight bars episode, R complete. Write the bar counts as a plan, then the notes. Play the form and check whether the shortened R is recognisable as a return.
checklist: Form plan with bar counts and complete notes?
Recognisability of the shortened ritornello assessed?

tu3-4.title: Bass: foundation or countervoice
tu3-4.goal: Distinguish the three bass roles and know when the bass doubles the riff, carries the chord or is itself a melody.
tu3-4.text:
The bass has three possible roles. 1. Doubling: it plays the guitar riff an octave lower. Result: pressure, unity, no extra information. Standard in doom (My Dying Bride, mostly). 2. Foundation: it plays roots in long values while the guitar plays chords or figures. Result: calm, room for motion above. Standard in Anathema and in every Baroque continuo. 3. Countervoice: it has its own line moving independently, with passing tones, leaps and rhythm. Result: two-part writing, density. Peter Steele in Type O Negative alternates between 2 and 3, often in the same piece, and there his bass is the actual melody (verify).

The Baroque continuo is the source of all three: the cellist plays the bass line, which is at once foundation (roots on the strong beats) and countervoice (passing tones between). The figures tell the harpsichordist which chords belong above. The bass is the score; everything else is execution.

For you without a bassist: the guitar alone has to choose the role. Open strings give foundation (role 2). A moving bass on the low string with melody above is role 3 and the hardest thing the instrument course demands. Role 1 is impossible in solo playing and is hinted at by the octave in the power chord.

Rule: the bass changes less often than the melody (role 2) or as often (role 3), never more often. When the bass is busier than the upper voice, the register tips over.

te3-4-1.title: Listen · Bass: foundation or countervoice
te3-4-1.instructions: Type O Negative, "Love You to Death" and "In Praise of Bacchus": for two sections each determine the bass role (1, 2 or 3). Sing the bass line at a role-3 spot. Compare with Anathema, "Suicide Veil": one role throughout? Claim: Steele switches within a piece, Anathema stay in role 2 (verify).
checklist: Four sections classified by bass role?
One role-3 line sung back?

te3-4-2.title: Model · Bass: foundation or countervoice
te3-4-2.instructions: Bars 1–2: bass doubles the melody (role 1). Bars 3–4: bass holds roots under chords (role 2). Bars 5–8: bass moves as its own line with passing tones against a calm upper voice (role 3). Play all three and describe which role leaves the most room for the melody and which gives the most pressure.
checklist: Three roles played and distinguished?
Room and pressure effects named?

te3-4-3.title: Application · Bass: foundation or countervoice
te3-4-3.instructions: Write twelve bars for guitar alone: four bars role 2 (open bass, melody above), four bars role 3 (moving bass on the low string, melody holds), four bars return to role 2. Notate both voices. The bass line in role 3 must be singable on its own.
checklist: Twelve bars with role change notated?
Bass line in role 3 sung on its own?

tu3-5.title: Bass register and frequency space
tu3-5.goal: Know where bass, kick, guitar and keyboard sit in frequency space and recognise overlap as the cause of mud.
tu3-5.text:
Frequency ranges for orientation: sub-bass 20–60 Hz (kick fundamental, octaver, B0–B1). Bass 60–250 Hz (E1 to B3, the foundation). Low mids 250–500 Hz (the area where guitar chords and bass overtones collide). Mids 500–2000 Hz (vocals, guitar presence, violin). Highs from 2 kHz (attack, hi-hat, air).

A tone is not only its fundamental. E2 (82 Hz) has overtones at 165, 247, 330, 412 Hz and beyond. A distorted E5 power chord fills the range 80–2000 Hz almost completely. When the bass plays the same, the same overtones are added, only louder. That is doubling (role 1) and sounds like a wall. When guitar and bass sit in different registers instead, there is room for keyboards and vocals.

The doom sound lives on one decision: who owns 80–250 Hz? In My Dying Bride the guitar, the bass doubles. In Type O Negative the bass with sub-octave; the guitar is tuned low but with chorus and fewer lows. In Anathema the guitar, the bass sits beneath and is slim. All three work; none lets two instruments be equally strong in that range.

For you: guitar alone owns everything. With keyboard added: keyboard not below C3 unless the guitar is silent. With drums: kick around 50–80 Hz, i.e. below the low E; snare around 200 Hz and 2–4 kHz. The kick shares space with the bass, not with the guitar.

te3-5-1.title: Listen · Bass register and frequency space
te3-5-1.instructions: Listen to 30 seconds of riff each from "Your River" (MDB), "Wolf Moon" (Type O), "Sentient" (Anathema) on the same headphones. Answer for each: who owns 80–250 Hz? Is the kick below or above the bass? Claim: three different answers to the first question (verify).
checklist: Owner of the bass range named for all three?
Kick position relative to the bass determined?

te3-5-2.title: Model · Bass register and frequency space
te3-5-2.instructions: Frequency spaces as a score: bass/kick around E2 (60–90 Hz), guitar fifth E3–B3 (165–250 Hz), keyboard from G4 (392 Hz). Play the layers one after another on the keyboard, then together. Move the guitar fifth to E2–B2 and hear the collision with the bass. Compute the fundamental of every tone.
checklist: Fundamentals of all tones computed?
Collision with the shifted guitar fifth heard?

te3-5-3.title: Application · Bass register and frequency space
te3-5-3.instructions: Record a four-bar riff three times: guitar alone, guitar plus keyboard pad from C3, guitar plus keyboard pad from C4. At equal loudness judge which version is clearest. Formulate your register rule for keyboard over guitar.
checklist: Three versions compared at equal loudness?
Register rule logged?

tu3-6.title: Drums I: pulse, backbeat, half-time, hi-hat
tu3-6.goal: Read the grammar of a drum pattern: what kick, snare and hi-hat each say.
tu3-6.text:
A drum pattern has three levels. The hi-hat (or ride) gives the subdivision: quarters, eighths or sixteenths. It is the grid everything else hangs on. The snare gives the backbeat: in 4/4 on 2 and 4 (straight) or only on 3 (half-time). The kick gives the foundation and links to the bass: on 1 and 3 or on 1 alone, plus syncopations doubling the bass rhythm.

Half-time is the doom standard: at ♩ = 60 with snare on 3 the bar feels like ♩ = 30 in half notes. The same riff with snare on 2 and 4 sounds twice as fast although the tempo is the same. The snare defines the felt speed; the tempo only defines the hi-hat.

Hi-hat language: closed = dry, grid; open = accent, sustain; half open = noise, pad. A pattern with the hi-hat in quarters lets the riff breathe; one in eighths drives; sixteenths fill. Doom needs air: quarters or eighths, open only on the last beat before the 1.

Dynamics: the kick on 1 is louder than the one on 3. The hi-hat on the beats is louder than in between (accent structure). Without this weighting every pattern sounds like a machine. In Type O Negative many drums are programmed and deliberately weighted for exactly that reason (verify). In My Dying Bride a human plays, and the half-time snare often lands minimally late, which increases the weight (verify).

Device-neutral: every pattern is a grid of steps (16 per bar at sixteenths), one instrument with velocity per step. Whether SR-18, Digitakt or SP-404: grid, instrument, velocity, swing.

te3-6-1.title: Listen · Drums I: pulse, backbeat, half-time, hi-hat
te3-6-1.instructions: My Dying Bride, "Your River", first riff with drums: determine hi-hat subdivision, snare position (2+4 or 3) and kick pattern. Write the pattern as a 16-step grid. Then Type O Negative, "Green Man": the same. Claim: MDB half-time with quarter hi-hat, Type O straight with eighth hi-hat (verify).
checklist: Two patterns written as 16-step grids?
Snare position of both pieces determined?

te3-6-2.title: Model · Drums I: pulse, backbeat, half-time, hi-hat
te3-6-2.instructions: Drums as notes: top hi-hat (B4), middle snare (E4), bottom kick (E2). Bars 1–2 half-time: hi-hat in quarters, snare on 3, kick on 1 with a syncopation. Bars 3–4 straight: hi-hat in eighths, snare on 2 and 4, kick on 1 and 3. Tap both with two hands and one foot. Switch between the half-time accompaniment (preset) and your own counting and hear the felt halving of tempo.
checklist: Both patterns tapped with hands and foot?
Felt halving of tempo at the same click confirmed?

te3-6-3.title: Application · Drums I: pulse, backbeat, half-time, hi-hat
te3-6-3.instructions: Write three 16-step grids for your phase-1 riff: half-time with quarter hi-hat, half-time with eighth hi-hat, straight with eighth hi-hat. Enter velocities (three levels). Program them on an available device or tap them on your thighs to the riff and decide which grid carries the riff best.
checklist: Three grids with velocities written?
Choice with reason logged?

tu3-7.title: Drums II: doom drumming, fills as form, building patterns
tu3-7.goal: Understand fills, crashes and pattern changes as form signals and build a pattern device-neutrally.
tu3-7.text:
In slow music the drums are less an engine than an architect. They mark form boundaries: a fill in the last bar before a section, a crash on the 1 of the new section, a pattern change (half-time → straight) at the transition from verse to chorus. Without these signals the listener does not hear the form; with them the harmony has less to do.

Doom drumming: tempo 50–80, half-time, kick tied to the bass rhythm, toms instead of snare for transitions, crash with long decay, ride instead of hi-hat in open sections. The rests are long; one hit every two seconds is normal. So every hit has to sit. In My Dying Bride the fills are often only two or three tom hits; at this tempo that suffices (verify). Type O Negative work with machine-like identical patterns and set form boundaries by dropping out: one bar without drums before the chorus (verify).

The Baroque has no drum kit but the same function: the continuo marks cadences by thickening (more chord strokes) and the ritornelli by tutti entry. Vivaldi's storms are drum music without drums: sixteenth-note tremolo in the bass is the double kick of the 18th century.

Building a pattern, device-neutral: 1. Choose the grid (16 steps per bar, twelve in 12/8). 2. Put the hi-hat on the grid (every second or fourth step). 3. Snare on step 9 (half-time) or 5 and 13 (straight). 4. Kick on 1 and on the steps where the bass attacks. 5. Velocity: hits on 1 and 9 strong, others medium, in-between hits soft. 6. Fill: last bar before a form boundary, drop the hi-hat, toms on steps 13–16. 7. Swing only if the riff is ternary (phase 5).

te3-7-1.title: Listen · Drums II: doom drumming, fills as form, building patterns
te3-7-1.instructions: My Dying Bride, "The Songless Bird": mark every form boundary and note which drum signal announces it (fill, crash, pattern change, dropout). Then Type O Negative, "Be My Druidess": the same. Claim: MDB signal with tom fills, Type O with dropouts and crashes (verify).
checklist: All form boundaries of both pieces noted with drum signal?
Signal types counted and compared?

te3-7-2.title: Model · Drums II: doom drumming, fills as form, building patterns
te3-7-2.instructions: Six bars: three bars of half-time pattern, one fill bar (hi-hat off, toms as G4/E4 eighths on 3 and 4), then a change to the straight pattern with eighth hi-hat as a new section. Tap the form along. Write the fill as a 16-step grid with velocities. Then build the same on a device or with your voice and check whether the change after the fill reads as a new section.
checklist: Fill written as a grid with velocities?
Section change after the fill audible?

te3-7-3.title: Application · Drums II: doom drumming, fills as form, building patterns
te3-7-3.instructions: Take the 16-bar form from your instrument course (phase 8, A–A′–B–A). Write a drum plan: pattern per section, signal at every boundary, velocity contour. As grids, device-neutral. Program it on a device of your choice or tap it to the recording. Check whether a listener could recognise the four sections without harmony.
checklist: Drum plan with pattern, signals and velocities per section?
Form recognisability without harmony assessed?

t4.title: Functional harmony
t4.goal: Harmonic and melodic minor, cadence types, seventh chords, dim7, secondary dominants, modulation, Baroque formulas and the question of when doom avoids function.

tu4-1.title: Harmonic and melodic minor
tu4-1.goal: Know the three minor forms as tools for dominant and melodic motion, not as scales to memorise.
tu4-1.text:
Natural minor (Aeolian) has no leading tone; the chord on 5 is minor (Bm in E minor). To get a dominant you raise the 7: D → D#. That yields harmonic minor: E F# G A B C D#. The step C–D# is an augmented second (three semitones), melodically awkward, harmonically useful. The chord on 5 becomes major (B), on 7 diminished (D#dim), on 3 augmented (G+).

Melodic minor also raises the 6 to avoid the augmented second: E F# G A B C# D#, ascending. Descending you traditionally fall back to natural minor because the leading-tone tension is only needed upward. In practice: before a cadence ascend with C# and D#, afterwards descend with D and C.

Vivaldi works in minor almost always this way: melodies rise melodic, fall natural, and the cadence always has the leading tone. Winter (F minor) is a textbook: hear the alternation between Eb and E in the solo violin depending on direction (verify).

Doom uses harmonic minor almost only in one place: the ending. The leading tone appears when a section is really meant to end, and otherwise not. Type O Negative occasionally have the dominant with leading tone in choruses (verify); My Dying Bride occasionally use the augmented second in the violin as an "oriental" colour (verify). Rule: harmonic minor for chords, melodic minor for melody, natural minor for everything else.

te4-1-1.title: Listen · Harmonic and melodic minor
te4-1-1.instructions: Vivaldi, *Winter*, movement 1: follow the solo violin in one ascending and one descending passage. Do you hear the difference between raised and natural 6 and 7? Then My Dying Bride, "Turn Loose the Swans": can you find an augmented second in the violin? Claim: Vivaldi switches by direction, MDB use the augmented second as colour (verify).
checklist: Direction-dependent 6/7 heard in Vivaldi?
Augmented second in MDB found or ruled out?

te4-1-2.title: Model · Harmonic and melodic minor
te4-1-2.instructions: Three minor forms up and down, then an application: bars 7–8 rise melodic (C#, D#) into the cadence and fall natural (D, C) afterwards. Sing every form. Play bar 3 (harmonic) and hear the augmented second C–D#. Replace the D in bar 8 with D# and hear why the descent with D sounds more natural.
checklist: Three forms sung, augmented second located?
D/D# in the descent compared?

te4-1-3.title: Application · Harmonic and melodic minor
te4-1-3.instructions: Write eight bars of melody over Em–Am–B7–Em (two bars each) applying the rule: ascend before B7 with C# and D#, descend after Em with D and C. Mark every raised tone. Play the melody over the chords on the keyboard, then the melody alone on guitar.
checklist: Raised tones only ascending before the dominant?
Melody played on both instruments?

tu4-2.title: Dominant, leading tone, cadence types
tu4-2.goal: Hear and write the four cadence types; know which appears in which reference.
tu4-2.text:
A cadence is a harmonic close. Four types: authentic: V → I (B7 → Em). Perfect when both are in root position and the melody ends on the root; otherwise imperfect. Plagal: IV → I (Am → Em), the "amen" close, without leading tone, soft. Half cadence: ends on V (… → B7), open, demands continuation. Deceptive: V → VI (B7 → C), the dominant resolves to the wrong chord, surprise and extension.

The dominant works through two tones: leading tone (D#) up to E, seventh (A) down to G. Together a tritone. Without the seventh B major is a weaker dominant; without the leading tone (Bm) none at all. The subdominant (Am) prepares: it contains C, which falls to B, and A, which stays and becomes the seventh of B7. Am–B7–Em is therefore the complete formula: preparation, tension, release.

Vivaldi: almost every phrase ends authentically, section boundaries often with a deceptive cadence in order to continue (verify). Biber: dance movements authentic, half cadence in the middle of each part. Type O Negative: plagal and authentic in choruses, the Beatles share (verify). My Dying Bride: almost only plagal or no cadence at all; sections end by stopping, not by resolving (verify). Anathema: half cadences never resolved, as a state of suspension.

The choice of cadence type is the most important decision at a section ending. Authentic closes, plagal calms, half cadence opens, deceptive extends.

te4-2-1.title: Listen · Dominant, leading tone, cadence types
te4-2-1.instructions: Find one section ending each in: Vivaldi, *Autumn*, movement 1; Type O Negative, "Love You to Death"; My Dying Bride, "Your River"; Anathema, "Far Away". Determine the cadence type or "no cadence". Claim: four different answers (verify).
checklist: Four endings classified?
Leading tone and seventh heard or marked as absent each time?

te4-2-2.title: Model · Dominant, leading tone, cadence types
te4-2-2.instructions: Four cadences: bars 1–3 authentic (Am–B7–Em), bars 4–5 plagal (Am–Em), bars 6–7 half cadence (Am–B7, open), bars 8–10 deceptive and afterthought (B7–C–Em). Play each and pause after the last chord: is the close complete? Trace D# and A in bar 2 and bar 8: where does each go?
checklist: Four cadence types played and completeness assessed?
Path of D# and A in the deceptive cadence named?

te4-2-3.title: Application · Dominant, leading tone, cadence types
te4-2-3.instructions: Write a sixteen-bar form with four groups of four whose endings are, in order, half cadence, deceptive, plagal, authentic. Write out melody and bass. Play and judge whether the order forms an arc (open → extended → calmed → closed).
checklist: Four cadence types notated in the given order?
Arc effect assessed in the log?

tu4-3.title: Seventh chords and the chain of sevenths
tu4-3.goal: Build all seventh chord types of the minor key and play the Baroque chain of sevenths over the circle of fifths.
tu4-3.text:
The seventh turns a triad into a direction. It is a dissonance against the root and wants to fall stepwise. Types in E Aeolian on every degree: Em7 (i), F#m7b5 (iiø), Gmaj7 (III), Am7 (iv), Bm7 (v), Cmaj7 (VI), D7 (VII). With harmonic minor: B7 (V7) and D#dim7 (vii°7). With melodic minor also C#m7b5 and Gmaj7#5.

Five types by construction: dominant seventh (major + minor seventh: B7, D7), major seventh (major + major seventh: Cmaj7, Gmaj7), minor seventh (minor + minor seventh: Em7, Am7), half-diminished (diminished + minor seventh: F#m7b5), fully diminished (diminished + diminished seventh: D#dim7). The character runs from striving (dominant seventh) via soft (maj7, m7) to unstable (ø, °7).

The chain of sevenths: in the circle of fifths the seventh of each chord falls into the third of the next. Em7 (D) → Am7 (C is the third, D falls to C), Am7 (G) → D7 (F#), D7 (C) → Gmaj7 (B), Gmaj7 (F#) → Cmaj7 (E), Cmaj7 (B) → F#m7b5 (A), F#m7b5 (E) → B7 (D#), B7 (A) → Em (G). Two voices alternate: one holds, one falls. That is Vivaldi's sequence engine and the basis of every Baroque modulation.

In doom sevenths are rare because they create direction. Where they occur they are mostly m7 and maj7 as colour without resolution: Anathema set Em7 and Cmaj7 as pads (verify), Type O Negative use dominant sevenths only at closes (verify). The chain of sevenths itself belongs to the Baroque; as a riff it would be too tonal.

te4-3-1.title: Listen · Seventh chords and the chain of sevenths
te4-3-1.instructions: Vivaldi, *Summer*, movement 1: find a sequence in which you hear a falling voice bar by bar (chain of sevenths). Write the falling tones. Then Anathema, "Eternity Part III": do you hear sevenths in the pads, and do they resolve? Claim: Vivaldi resolves every seventh, Anathema none (verify).
checklist: Falling voice in Vivaldi written over at least four chords?
Resolution behaviour in Anathema described?

te4-3-2.title: Model · Seventh chords and the chain of sevenths
te4-3-2.instructions: Chain of sevenths through E minor. In the two main voices (stems up) one holds while the other falls a step: the seventh becomes the third of the next chord. Trace both lines and mark every seventh. Play only bass and the two main voices, then with the third voice. Name the type of every seventh chord.
checklist: All sevenths marked and their fall traced?
Seven chord types named?

te4-3-3.title: Application · Seventh chords and the chain of sevenths
te4-3-3.instructions: Write two four-bar examples: one with sevenths that resolve (chain of sevenths over Am–D7–Gmaj7–Cmaj7), one with sevenths as colour without resolution (Em7–Cmaj7 as pads, seventh stays). Play both. Decide which belongs in a doom context and which sounds Baroque, and justify with the voice leading.
checklist: Both examples notated, sevenths marked?
Assignment with voice-leading reasoning logged?

tu4-4.title: The diminished seventh chord and its ambiguity
tu4-4.goal: Understand dim7 as a symmetrical chord with four resolutions and use it as a switch between keys.
tu4-4.text:
D#dim7 = D# F# A C: three minor thirds. The chord divides the octave into four equal parts. Therefore every inversion is again a dim7 in root position: F#dim7, Adim7, Cdim7 contain the same tones. There are only three different dim7 chords in total.

Each of the four tones can be a leading tone and resolve a semitone upward: D# → E (Em), F# → G (Gm), A → Bb (Bbm), C → Db (Dbm). One dim7 can therefore land in four keys, each a minor third apart. That is the classic modulation switch: enter as vii°7 of the old key, exit as vii°7 of the new.

As dominant substitute: D#dim7 → Em corresponds to B7b9 without root (B D# F# A C). The sound is sharper than B7 because the tritone is present twice (D#–A and F#–C). In the Baroque the dim7 is the chord for terror and storm: Vivaldi sets it in the thunderstorms, often as tremolo (verify). In doom it appears as a bass passing tone (E–D#–D, phase 3) and in Type O Negative's organ pads as "church sound" (verify). My Dying Bride use it in the violin over a held bass as a tension tone (verify).

Practical: a dim7 over its own root (Edim7 = E G Bb Db) is something different from the leading-tone dim7 (D#dim7). The first is a colour over E, the second a dominant into E. Confusing them leads to wrong symbols.

te4-4-1.title: Listen · The diminished seventh chord and its ambiguity
te4-4-1.instructions: Vivaldi, *Summer*, movement 3 (storm): find a chord that sounds "stacked" and directionless before it resolves. Sing its tones: are they all minor thirds? Then Type O Negative, "Red Water (Christmas Mourning)", organ: is there such a chord? Claim: Vivaldi yes, as tremolo; Type O yes, in passing (verify).
checklist: dim7 in Vivaldi confirmed by singing the thirds?
dim7 in Type O found or ruled out?

te4-4-2.title: Model · The diminished seventh chord and its ambiguity
te4-4-2.instructions: The same dim7 (D# F# A C) resolves four times into four keys: Em, Gm, Bbm, Dbm. Each time the bass takes a different chord tone as the leading tone. Play the four resolutions and name for each which tone is the leading tone and where the other three go. Count the semitones between the four target keys.
checklist: Four resolutions named with leading tone and voice paths?
Distance between target keys recognised as a minor third?

te4-4-3.title: Application · The diminished seventh chord and its ambiguity
te4-4-3.instructions: Write eight bars that move from E minor to G minor via a dim7 and return via a second dim7. Notate every dim7 with both symbols (vii°7 of the old and the new key). Play the passage and judge whether the change reads as modulation or as a colour shift.
checklist: Two dim7 chords notated with double naming?
Effect as modulation or colour assessed?

tu4-5.title: Secondary dominants
tu4-5.goal: Be able to make any chord of the key briefly the tonic without leaving the key.
tu4-5.text:
A secondary dominant is the dominant of a chord other than the tonic. In E minor: E7 → Am (V7/iv), A7 → D (V7/VII), D7 → G (V7/III), G7 → C (V7/VI), F#7 → B (V7/V). Each introduces a foreign tone (G# in E7, C# in A7; in G7 = G B D F the F is foreign; in F#7 = F# A# C# E the A# and C# are foreign). The foreign tone is the leading tone into the target chord.

Effect: the target chord becomes the tonic for a moment without the key changing. Em–E7–Am: the G# in E7 turns the tonic into the dominant of the subdominant. That is a standard route in the Baroque and in the Beatles-adjacent side of Type O Negative (verify). Vivaldi strings secondary dominants in the circle of fifths: E7–A7–D7–G7–C, each chord the dominant of the next, the chain from phase 3 with dominant sevenths throughout.

In doom secondary dominants almost never occur because they bring major thirds and direction. The exception is V7/iv (E7 → Am): the change from Em to E major (phase 2 of the instrument course) is exactly that when Am follows. My Dying Bride occasionally use the major third as a surprise without the resolution to Am, i.e. as pure colour (verify).

Notation: V7/iv reads "five-seven of four". The slash here means reference, not bass tone. Context decides whether Em/G (bass tone) or V/iv (reference) is meant; when in doubt write it out.

te4-5-1.title: Listen · Secondary dominants
te4-5-1.instructions: Type O Negative, "Love You to Death", chorus: is there a major chord with a foreign tone that "pulls" into the next chord? Write it and its target. Then Vivaldi, *Autumn*, movement 3: find a run of three chords each the dominant of the next. Claim: Type O one secondary dominant per chorus, Vivaldi chains (verify).
checklist: Secondary dominant in Type O written with target or ruled out?
Chain of three in Vivaldi written?

te4-5-2.title: Model · Secondary dominants
te4-5-2.instructions: Three secondary dominants in one progression: E7 → Am (G#), D7 → G (F#, no foreign tone here, but seventh C), G7 → C (F). Then B7 → Em as the real dominant. Mark every foreign tone and its leading-tone path. Play the progression once with and once without the seventh chords (Em–Am–G–C–Em) and describe what the secondary dominants add.
checklist: Foreign tones and leading-tone paths marked?
Version with and without secondary dominants compared?

te4-5-3.title: Application · Secondary dominants
te4-5-3.instructions: Write an eight-bar riff in E minor containing exactly one secondary dominant (V7/iv or V7/VI) at a form boundary. The rest stays modal. Play it with power chords (roots only, the major third missing) and with full voicing. Judge whether the secondary dominant exists at all without the third.
checklist: Exactly one secondary dominant at a form boundary?
Power-chord and voiced versions compared?

tu4-6.title: Modulation: fifth-related and third-related
tu4-6.goal: Know two routes into a new key and which is Baroque and which is doom-typical.
tu4-6.text:
Modulation means: a new centre is confirmed, usually by its own cadence. Two main routes.

Fifth-related (Baroque): the new key lies a fifth higher or lower and shares six of seven tones. E minor → B minor (one sharp more) or A minor (one less). Route: a shared chord (pivot), then the dominant of the new key. Am is iv in E minor and i in A minor; Am–E7–Am confirms A minor. Vivaldi modulates in every fast movement from the tonic to the dominant or to the relative key (minor → relative major: e → G) and back (verify). Biber likewise in every dance movement: the first part ends in the dominant, the second returns.

Third-related (doom, Romanticism): the new key lies a minor or major third away and shares fewer tones; the change is a jolt. E → C (major third down, "shift into width"), E → G (minor third up, relative, soft), E → C# or Eb (foreign, hard). Type O Negative often change sections third-related without a pivot, simply through the bass: chorus a third higher than the verse (verify). My Dying Bride shift whole riffs by a minor third (verify), the metal variant of the sequence.

Chromatic mediant: E major → C major or E minor → C minor, same type, a third apart, two foreign tones. The sound is cinematic. Anathema use it rarely, Type O Negative occasionally in the organ (verify).

Rule: fifth-related for routes that are meant to lead back. Third-related for contrast that may be heard as a break.

te4-6-1.title: Listen · Modulation: fifth-related and third-related
te4-6-1.instructions: Biber, Partita V, a two-part dance movement: determine the key at the end of the first part relative to the beginning (a fifth up? relative?). Then My Dying Bride, "The Snow in My Hand": is there a riff change where the same riff returns shifted by a third? Claim: Biber fifth-related, MDB third-related (verify).
checklist: Target key of the first Biber part determined?
Third shift in MDB found or ruled out?

te4-6-2.title: Model · Modulation: fifth-related and third-related
te4-6-2.instructions: Bars 1–4 fifth-related: Am as pivot, E7 as the new dominant, arrival in A minor. Bars 5–8 third-related: Em → C → G → Em without dominant, bass and common tones only. Play both halves and name where expectation arises (bar 3) and where the jolt is (bar 6). Which half could continue endlessly?
checklist: Pivot and new dominant in bars 1–4 named?
Jolt point and endless-loop capability assessed?

te4-6-3.title: Application · Modulation: fifth-related and third-related
te4-6-3.instructions: Write sixteen bars: eight in E minor, then a change to G minor (minor third, two foreign tones Bb and Eb) for four bars, then a return via a pivot or a dominant. Notate both changes and name their type. Play the form and judge which change reads as a break and which as a route.
checklist: Both changes notated and typed?
Break/route effect logged?

tu4-7.title: Baroque formulas and their path into metal
tu4-7.goal: Know five fixed formulas from Vivaldi and Biber that live on in doom and gothic.
tu4-7.text:
Baroque is formula music: a small stock of turns, endlessly recombined. Five of them migrated straight into metal.

1. Phrygian cadence: iv6 → V in minor, a semitone down in the bass (C → B), a whole tone up in the top voice (A → B). Ends on the dominant, open. Vivaldi closes slow movements with it (verify). In doom it is the riff ending C5 → B5 with an open continuation.

2. Neapolitan: the major chord on b2 (F major in E minor), usually in first inversion (F/A), before the dominant. F → B7 → Em. The semitone step F → E in the top voice is the same as in the Phrygian of phase 1, but here as a cadence. Biber sets it in the sarabandes (verify), My Dying Bride as an F5 power chord before the root (verify).

3. Lamento: phase 3. 4. Circle of fifths with chain of sevenths: phase 4. 5. Pedal point on the dominant: the bass holds B while Em, Am, C, B7 change above before Em arrives. Creates maximum expectation; Vivaldi before every return of the ritornello (verify). Anathema hold dominant pedals without resolution; that is their state of suspension.

What metal leaves out: the thirds. All five formulas work with power chords because they are defined in the bass. What metal adds: repetition. A Baroque formula appears once per phrase; a riff repeats it eight times. The difference between Vivaldi and doom is not the material but the rate of repetition.

te4-7-1.title: Listen · Baroque formulas and their path into metal
te4-7-1.instructions: In Vivaldi, *Winter*, movements 2 and 3, and in My Dying Bride, "Your River", find one example each of two of the five formulas. Write bass and top voice of the moment. Claim: Phrygian cadence and dominant pedal in Vivaldi, Neapolitan and lamento in MDB (verify).
checklist: Four formula examples written with bass and top voice?
Repetition rate of the formula counted in both sources?

te4-7-2.title: Model · Baroque formulas and their path into metal
te4-7-2.instructions: Bars 1–2 Phrygian cadence (C → B in the bass, A → B on top), open on B. Bars 3–5 Neapolitan F/A → B7 → Em; hear F → E in the top voice across three bars. Bars 6–9 dominant pedal: B held, Em, Am, B7 above, arrival. Play each formula alone, then all. Write each as a power-chord version (bass plus fifth only) and check whether it stays recognisable.
checklist: Three formulas played individually and named?
Power-chord versions written, recognisability assessed?

te4-7-3.title: Application · Baroque formulas and their path into metal
te4-7-3.instructions: Build a sixteen-bar riff from two formulas: eight bars lamento (twice), four bars Neapolitan cadence, four bars dominant pedal with arrival. All as power chords plus one melody voice. Play it with half-time drums at 60 and at 120 and note from which tempo it sounds Baroque instead of doom.
checklist: Sixteen bars with three formulas notated as power chords?
Tempo tipping point logged?

tu4-8.title: When doom avoids function and why
tu4-8.goal: Understand the refusal of the cadence as a deliberate device and choose intentionally between rest and resolution.
tu4-8.text:
Tonal music is music of expectation: every dominant promises, every tonic delivers. Doom refuses the promise. That is not inability but a form of time. A section that does not cadence promises nothing, so it does not disappoint, so it can last long. Ten minutes of Vivaldi without a cadence would be unbearable; ten minutes of My Dying Bride without a cadence is the piece.

Three refusals: 1. No major dominant: Bm or D instead of B7 before Em; the leading tone is missing, the root returns like a repetition, not like an arrival. 2. No close on the tonic: the section ends on C or D and the next begins on E; the change is a form boundary without resolution. 3. Ending by stopping: the riff breaks off, silence or a single tone. Type O Negative often do this with one bar of rest; My Dying Bride with a ringing chord (verify).

Why it works: expectation arises from leading tone and seventh (phase 1). Without them the chord change is a colour change, and colour changes are not urgent. The listener is moved from wanting to hearing. That is the kinship with modal music before 1600 and with the drone.

When function nonetheless: once per piece, at the end or at the climax. There a real cadence lands with the force of ten minutes of abstention. Type O Negative occasionally end pieces with a major tonic (Picardy third), a Baroque trick (verify). Vivaldi does not have this effect because he resolves constantly.

Decision per section: refuse or resolve. And per piece: where the one resolution sits.

te4-8-1.title: Listen · When doom avoids function and why
te4-8-1.instructions: My Dying Bride, "The Crown of Sympathy" complete: count the sections and mark which end with refusal 1, 2 or 3. Is there a single real cadence? Where? Claim: at most one, at the end or the climax (verify). Then Type O Negative, "Haunted", ending: major tonic?
checklist: All section endings classified by refusal type?
Position of the one cadence (or its absence) noted?

te4-8-2.title: Model · When doom avoids function and why
te4-8-2.instructions: The same riff three times with three endings: bars 1–4 return without leading tone (refusal 1). Bars 5–8 end on D and silence (refusals 2 and 3). Bars 9–12 real cadence with B7 and major tonic (Picardy). Play all three and describe the effect of each ending in one word. Then extend bars 1–4 to 16 bars by playing them four times and check whether they still carry.
checklist: Three endings played and each described in one word?
Sixteen-bar repetition without cadence assessed?

te4-8-3.title: Application · When doom avoids function and why
te4-8-3.instructions: Take your longest own piece from the instrument course. Mark every section ending as refusal 1, 2, 3 or cadence. If more than one cadence occurs, remove all but one and decide where it sits. Play the revised version and compare the recording with the old one.
checklist: All section endings classified?
Reduced to one cadence and comparison logged?

t5.title: Time
t5.goal: Subdivision, triplets, 12/8, swing, polyrhythm, odd meters, tempo and decay, rubato and agogics: how slow music shapes time.

tu5-1.title: Subdivision: binary, ternary, 12/8
tu5-1.goal: Grasp duple and triple subdivision as the two basic kinds of time and read 12/8 as notated triple.
tu5-1.text:
A pulse can be divided in two or in three. Two: eighths in 4/4, the straight feel. Three: triplets in 4/4 or eighths in 12/8, the rocking feel. All further subdivisions are combinations: sixteenths = 2×2, sextuplets = 2×3 or 3×2, 6/8 = 2 pulses × 3.

12/8 is the honest way to notate triple: four dotted quarters per bar, each in three eighths. The tempo mark names the dotted quarter. Triplets in 4/4 are the same sound with different writing; you use them when the triple occurs only occasionally. Rule: more than half the piece ternary → 12/8 (or 6/8), otherwise triplets.

Doom is mostly binary and slow, but the rocking variant occurs: Type O Negative have 6/8 and 12/8 pieces, and the waltz tone (3/4, one pulse in three) is their Beatles and Sabbath heritage (verify). My Dying Bride switch between binary and ternary within a piece, often at section boundaries (verify). Vivaldi writes gigues and pastorales in 12/8 or 6/8: the Danza pastorale of Spring is 12/8 (verify). Biber likewise in gigues.

The difference is physical: binary is walking, ternary is rocking. A riff conceived binary becomes softer and longer in 12/8. Playing the same tone sequence in both subdivisions is the best exercise for hearing the difference, not just counting it.

te5-1-1.title: Listen · Subdivision: binary, ternary, 12/8
te5-1-1.instructions: Vivaldi, *Spring*, movement 3 (Danza pastorale): count the pulse and the subdivision. Then Type O Negative, "Be My Druidess" and "Green Man": which is binary, which ternary? Claim: Vivaldi 12/8, one of the Type O pieces ternary (verify). Tap the pulse with one hand and the subdivision with the other for each.
checklist: Subdivision of all three pieces determined?
Pulse and subdivision tapped simultaneously?

te5-1-2.title: Model · Subdivision: binary, ternary, 12/8
te5-1-2.instructions: Four bars of 12/8: arpeggio in groups of three, bass in dotted halves (two big pulses). Count "1-2-3 2-2-3 3-2-3 4-2-3". Then play the same tone sequence in 4/4 as straight eighths (E G B E G B E G) and hear how the riff "walks" instead of "rocks". In 12/8 the tempo mark names the dotted quarter.
checklist: Four big pulses counted instead of twelve equal ones?
Binary version of the same tones played and compared?

te5-1-3.title: Application · Subdivision: binary, ternary, 12/8
te5-1-3.instructions: Write one riff twice: as 4/4 with straight eighths and as 12/8. Same tone sequence, same chords, same basic pulse (♩ = ♩.). Record both with matching accompaniment. Decide which version feels heavier and state why (number of attacks per pulse, accent spacing).
checklist: Both versions notated and recorded?
Heaviness verdict with reason logged?

tu5-2.title: Swing and shuffle
tu5-2.goal: Read ternary phrasing in binary notation, understand the ratio as a parameter and know where the references swing.
tu5-2.text:
Swing shifts the second eighth of every quarter backward. Notation shows straight eighths with the indication "swing" or "shuffle"; performance is long–short. The ratio varies: 2:1 (triplet shuffle, 67 %), 3:2 (60 %), 3:1 (dotted, 75 %). At slow tempo the ratio becomes more extreme, at fast tempo straighter. There is no correct value, only a fitting one.

Shuffle is the blues term, swing the jazz term; musically the same principle, culturally different ratios and accents. In metal it is usually called shuffle and comes from blues via Black Sabbath. Type O Negative have shuffle sections; "Cinnamon Girl" as a cover carries the rock shuffle into the doom context (verify). My Dying Bride rarely swing, but their triplet riffs are related.

The Baroque swings in a sense as well: the French practice of "notes inégales" plays notated equal eighths unequally, long–short. Whether Vivaldi (Italian) was played this way is disputed; historically informed recordings sometimes do (verify on your recording). The point for you: unequal eighths have been a performance decision, not a notation question, for 300 years.

Device-neutral: swing on drum machines is a percentage that shifts the even sixteenths or eighths. 50 % = straight, 67 % = triplet, 75 % = dotted. The riff has to play the same ratio, otherwise it rubs. Rule: fix the swing value before practising the riff.

te5-2-1.title: Listen · Swing and shuffle
te5-2-1.instructions: Type O Negative, "Cinnamon Girl": determine the swing ratio of the eighths by ear (2:1, 3:2 or straight). Tap along. Then a Vivaldi recording of your choice, *Autumn*, movement 1: does the ensemble play the eighths equal or unequal? Claim: Type O about 2:1, Vivaldi depending on the recording (verify and note the ensemble).
checklist: Swing ratio in Type O estimated?
Eighth-note equality in Vivaldi noted with the ensemble named?

te5-2-2.title: Model · Swing and shuffle
te5-2-2.instructions: A shuffle riff notated straight with a swing indication; the preview plays 2:1. Play it three times: straight, 2:1, 3:1. Record and judge which ratio fits at 60 and which at 100 quarters. Write one bar out in triplets (quarter triplet + eighth triplet per beat) and compare readability with the swing notation.
checklist: Three ratios compared at two tempi?
One bar written out in triplets?

te5-2-3.title: Application · Swing and shuffle
te5-2-3.instructions: Write an eight-bar shuffle riff on E and A with one break (one bar of straight eighths as contrast). Fix the swing ratio and note it as a percentage for the drum machine. Record with shuffle accompaniment. Check whether the straight bar reads as contrast or as a mistake.
checklist: Riff notated with swing percentage?
Effect of the straight bar assessed?

tu5-3.title: Polyrhythm and hemiola
tu5-3.goal: Know two simultaneous subdivisions and the Baroque hemiola as a device against uniformity.
tu5-3.text:
Polyrhythm: two voices divide the same span differently, 3 against 2 or 4 against 3. The shared span is divided into the least common multiple: 3:2 into six (top 1,3,5; bottom 1,4), 4:3 into twelve. After learning, the helper count should disappear and only the shared beginning remain.

Hemiola: a change of grouping within the same eighths. In 6/8 six eighths are normally 3+3 (two pulses); the hemiola groups them 2+2+2 (three pulses) for one bar, usually before the cadence. The bar briefly feels like 3/4. Biber and Vivaldi place it in almost every triple meter before the close (verify): uniformity breaks, the cadence gains weight. In 3/4 across two bars: six quarters as 3+3 instead of 2+2+2, the same idea one level up.

In metal the hemiola is the accent shift 3+3+2 in 4/4 (phase 7 of the instrument course): eight eighths, but the accents come every three. Type O Negative use it in riffs with a straight hi-hat beneath so that the guitar runs "against" the drums (verify). My Dying Bride set 3 against 2 between violin (triplets) and riff (eighths) (verify).

The difference between polyrhythm and hemiola: polyrhythm is simultaneous (two layers), hemiola is successive (one layer changes grouping). Both depend on the base count staying audible; without a reference it is just another meter.

te5-3-1.title: Listen · Polyrhythm and hemiola
te5-3-1.instructions: Biber, a gigue or sarabande in triple meter: find the bar before a cadence in which the accent changes from two to three (or three to two). Tap the base count through it. Then Type O Negative, a riff of your choice with 3+3+2: does the hi-hat run straight beneath? Claim: hemiola in Biber before every cadence, 3+3+2 in Type O over a straight hi-hat (verify).
checklist: Hemiola bar in Biber located and base count held?
3+3+2 riff noted with hi-hat behaviour?

te5-3-2.title: Model · Polyrhythm and hemiola
te5-3-2.instructions: Three bars of 6/8 in 3+3, then bar 3 as hemiola: the same six eighths but accents and bass in 2+2+2. Bar 4 arrival. Clap the base pulse (two per bar) through all four bars, including the hemiola. Then play 3 against 2: right hand bar 3 as written, left hand bass as two dotted quarters instead of three quarters.
checklist: Base pulse held through the hemiola?
3 against 2 in bar 3 played with both hands?

te5-3-3.title: Application · Polyrhythm and hemiola
te5-3-3.instructions: Write eight bars in 6/8 with exactly two hemiolas, each before a form boundary. The bass makes the grouping audible. Record with 12/8 or 6/8 accompaniment (the drums stay 3+3). Check whether the hemiola reads as tension before the boundary or as stumbling.
checklist: Two hemiolas notated before form boundaries?
Effect against unchanged drums assessed?

tu5-4.title: Odd meters
tu5-4.goal: Understand 5/8, 7/8 and 5/4 as groupings and judge their place in this music.
tu5-4.text:
An odd meter is a chain of groups of two and three that does not split into equal halves. 5/8 = 2+3 or 3+2. 7/8 = 2+2+3, 3+2+2 or 2+3+2. 5/4 = 3+2 or 2+3 in quarters. The grouping is part of the composition, not just the notation; 2+3 and 3+2 are different rhythms. In eighth-note meters the tempo mark names the eighth.

Odd meters are rare in the references. My Dying Bride occasionally use them as riff extensions: a 4/4 riff gets a 7/8 or 5/4 bar that shifts the repetition (verify). Type O Negative stay almost entirely even. Vivaldi knows no odd meters, but his phrase lengths are often odd (5 or 7 bars), which works similarly: the expectation of the four-group is broken. Biber likewise in free movements (Praeludium).

Two uses: 1. As the basic meter of a section: the listener learns the grouping after two bars and then hears it as normal; that works well for 5/4 and 7/8, badly for 11 or 13. 2. As a single bar in an even context: a shortening (7/8 instead of 4/4, one eighth missing) or a lengthening (5/4, one quarter more). The second is more typical of doom: the riff "catches" once and moves on.

Rule: odd meters must come from the riff (the phrase really is seven eighths long), not from the wish to be odd. If you cannot sing the grouping, it is wrong.

te5-4-1.title: Listen · Odd meters
te5-4-1.instructions: My Dying Bride, "The Crown of Sympathy" and "Turn Loose the Swans": find spots where the riff seems one beat too short or too long. Count: 7/8? 5/4? Or only a syncopation? Claim: at least one bar in one of the two pieces is really odd (verify). Then Vivaldi, *Winter*, movement 1: count the length of the first solo phrase in bars.
checklist: Seemingly odd spots recounted and classified?
Phrase length in Vivaldi counted?

te5-4-2.title: Model · Odd meters
te5-4-2.instructions: Four bars of 7/8 in 2+2+3. The bass plays the group durations (quarter, quarter, dotted quarter). Say "1-2 1-2 1-2-3" and play. Rewrite the same riff as 2+3+2 (move the accents, adjust bass durations) and play both. Sing both groupings without an instrument; the one you can sing is the right one for you.
checklist: 2+2+3 spoken and played?
2+3+2 rewrite notated and both sung?

te5-4-3.title: Application · Odd meters
te5-4-3.instructions: Take an eight-bar 4/4 riff and change exactly one bar: once to 7/8 (shortening), once to 5/4 (lengthening). Notate both versions with meter changes. Play them and describe whether the riff "catches" (shortening) or "breathes" (lengthening). Decide which version you keep.
checklist: Both versions notated with meter changes?
Effect description and decision logged?

tu5-5.title: Tempo and decay: why slow works with gain
tu5-5.goal: Understand the relationship between tempo, sustain, distortion and reverb and derive tempo decisions from it.
tu5-5.text:
A clean guitar tone decays noticeably after about two to four seconds. Distortion compresses: the quiet phases of the decay are raised, the tone seems constant until it tips abruptly into noise. A distorted power chord carries six to ten seconds. At ♩ = 60 that is one and a half to two and a half bars. That is the physical basis of doom: whole notes are possible because the instrument holds them.

Conversely: at ♩ = 140 and eighths each tone lasts 0.2 seconds; distortion has no decay to compress, it only thickens the attack. Fast metal therefore sounds percussive, slow metal pad-like, with the same amp.

Reverb extends further. A room with two seconds of decay makes every tone half a beat longer at ♩ = 60. At fast tempo it smears the attacks. Doom can use reverb, thrash cannot. Type O Negative use long reverb and chorus because their tempi allow it (verify); Anathema use reverb on clean guitar where it fills the gaps between arpeggio tones (verify).

Vivaldi's strings have the problem reversed: the bow holds the tone as long as desired without distortion. In return there is no natural decay; note endings are bowing decisions. The churches where Baroque was played had three to five seconds of reverb, and the tempi of the slow movements are built on that.

Tempo decision: determine the longest note in your riff. Its duration in seconds must be shorter than the sustain of your rig. With whole notes at ♩ = 60 you need four seconds of sustain; check that at the amp, not in your imagination.

te5-5-1.title: Listen · Tempo and decay: why slow works with gain
te5-5-1.instructions: My Dying Bride, "Your River": measure the duration of the longest held guitar chord in seconds and convert it into bars at the measured tempo. Then Anathema, "Sentient": how long is the reverb on the clean guitar (time from attack to silence at a rest)? Claim: MDB hold across two bars, Anathema reverb over one second (verify).
checklist: Longest chord duration measured and converted to bars?
Reverb length in Anathema measured?

te5-5-2.title: Model · Tempo and decay: why slow works with gain
te5-5-2.instructions: Eight bars with ties across two and three bars. At ♩ = 60 the final chord lasts twelve seconds. Play the progression on guitar with your gain and measure how long each chord actually carries before it tips. Then set the tempo so that the longest chord just holds. Repeat clean: at what tempo does the clean version carry?
checklist: Sustain of your own rig measured in seconds?
Minimum tempo for gain and clean versions noted?

te5-5-3.title: Application · Tempo and decay: why slow works with gain
te5-5-3.instructions: Create a sustain table for your rig: clean, medium gain, high gain, each with and without reverb, each with seconds until audible tipping for E2, E3 and E4. From it derive for every setting the slowest sensible tempo for whole notes. This table belongs in the acoustics appendix of your log.
checklist: Table with 18 measurements?
Slowest tempo derived per setting?

tu5-6.title: Rubato, fermata, Baroque sense of time
tu5-6.goal: Know time stretching as an expressive device and where it is permitted in this music.
tu5-6.text:
Rubato means "stolen": time is stretched in one place and given back in another, so that the base pulse survives across the phrase. A fermata holds a tone or rest for an indefinite length; time stands still. Ritardando slows gradually, usually before a close. Accelerando speeds up.

The Baroque has less rubato than Romanticism, but not none: cadences are stretched, solo passages breathe, slow movements are dead without stretching. Vivaldi's Largo movements demand that the solo violin phrase freely over the steady bass (verify: compare two recordings). In the praeludia Biber writes free passages without a fixed meter that are meant to sound improvised.

Doom with drums has no rubato: the drum machine or the drummer holds. But doom has fermatas: the last chord of a section rings out, the drums drop out, then the next riff begins. My Dying Bride do this at almost every major boundary (verify). Type O Negative have intros and outros without meter in which the organ lies freely (verify). Anathema often begin pieces with a free guitar arpeggio before the pulse enters (verify).

For solo playing without drums rubato is the most important freedom: you can stretch a phrase because nobody holds against you. The danger is formlessness. Rule: rubato within the phrase, not between phrases; the start of every phrase lands on time. Fermata only at form boundaries and never twice in a row.

te5-6-1.title: Listen · Rubato, fermata, Baroque sense of time
te5-6-1.instructions: Vivaldi, *Winter*, movement 2, in two different recordings: measure the duration of the first eight bars in both. Where does the violin stretch? Then Anathema, "Eternity Part I", opening: how many seconds pass before a fixed pulse is audible? Claim: recordings differ by more than 10 %, Anathema intro free for over 20 seconds (verify).
checklist: Duration of the eight bars compared in two recordings?
Length of the free intro measured?

te5-6-2.title: Model · Rubato, fermata, Baroque sense of time
te5-6-2.instructions: A phrase with cadence and fermata: bars 1–4 in time, bars 5–6 final tone (hold it freely, longer than written), bar 7 silence (fermata on the rest), bar 8 new start, low. Play without click: stretch bar 4 (ritardando into the cadence), hold bars 5–6 by feel, begin bar 8 on a new pulse you set yourself. Record and measure how long your fermata was.
checklist: Ritardando, fermata and new start played without click?
Fermata length measured and assessed?

te5-6-3.title: Application · Rubato, fermata, Baroque sense of time
te5-6-3.instructions: Play your phase-1 piece from the instrument course twice without accompaniment: once strictly in time, once with rubato within phrases and one fermata at the form boundary. Compare the recordings: does each phrase start land on time? Does the fermata read as articulation or as interruption?
checklist: Both versions recorded?
Phrase starts and fermata effect assessed?

tu5-7.title: Agogics in doom: delay as a device
tu5-7.goal: Understand microtiming: laid-back, on the beat, ahead of the beat, and what doom uses of it.
tu5-7.text:
Agogics is the small deviation from the grid: a tone arriving ten to forty milliseconds after the beat sounds heavy ("laid-back"); one before it sounds pushing. Both at constant tempo. It is not rubato (the tempo stays) but placement.

Doom lives on laid-back. The snare on 3 minimally late, the guitar attack minimally behind the kick, the vocal behind everything. This creates weight because the ear hears the delay as inertia, as mass. My Dying Bride have it in the drums (verify); Type O Negative achieve it with programmed drums through deliberately late snares or through bass playing behind the machine (verify). Anathema play more on the beat; their weight comes from register and reverb, not timing (verify).

Vivaldi has agogics in the accent: the first beat is longer, not just louder. Baroque performance practice speaks of "good" and "bad" notes; the good ones may be longer. That is the same micro-delay applied to note lengths instead of attacks.

Device-neutral: on drum machines this is called "nudge", "micro-timing" or "offset": shifting single steps by milliseconds. The SR-18 barely can, Digitakt and SP-404 can per step. Without a device: programming the snare a sixteenth-triplet late is too much; real agogics lies below the grid. With your own hand: deliberately play behind the click, record, measure the gap.

Rule: one element behind the beat (usually snare or guitar), never all. If everything is late, only the tempo is slower.

te5-7-1.title: Listen · Agogics in doom: delay as a device
te5-7-1.instructions: My Dying Bride, "The Songless Bird", a half-time passage: listen to the snare on 3. Is it on the beat or behind it? Compare with Type O Negative, "Green Man": snare on 2 and 4, where? If you have a DAW: look at the waveform, measure kick-to-snare distance. Claim: MDB snare 10–30 ms late, Type O on the grid (verify).
checklist: Snare placement of both pieces assessed?
If DAW: distance measured in milliseconds?

te5-7-2.title: Model · Agogics in doom: delay as a device
te5-7-2.instructions: Four times the same bar: fifths on 1 and 3. Play bars 1–2 exactly on the click, bars 3–4 deliberately 20–30 ms behind, at unchanged tempo. Record. If you have a DAW, measure the gap; otherwise judge by comparison whether the second half feels heavier. Then exaggerate (an eighth late) and hear when weight turns into error.
checklist: Both halves recorded, gap measured or estimated?
Boundary between weight and error named?

te5-7-3.title: Application · Agogics in doom: delay as a device
te5-7-3.instructions: Program or tap a half-time pattern in two versions: snare on the grid, snare delayed by a small amount (nudge, or by hand). Play the same riff over both and record. Describe the difference and decide which version becomes your standard. Note the setting device-neutrally (milliseconds or percent of a sixteenth).
checklist: Two pattern versions recorded with the same riff?
Standard chosen and noted device-neutrally?

t6.title: Sound
t6.goal: Subtractive, wavetable and FM synthesis; pads, organ, strings; delay physics, tape and BBD, approximation on 2290, G-Major, Nova System; reverb, chorus, gain staging and frequency spaces in the arrangement.

tu6-1.title: Subtractive synthesis: oscillator, filter, envelope
tu6-1.goal: Master the signal chain of a subtractive synthesizer from waveform to output.
tu6-1.text:
Subtractive means: a harmonically rich signal is reduced by filters. The chain: oscillator → filter → amplifier, each with envelope and LFO as modulation.

Oscillator: sawtooth has all partials (1/n), sounds bright and cutting, the basis for strings and brass. Square has only odd partials, sounds hollow, clarinet-like; pulse width changes the spectrum (narrow = nasal). Triangle has odd partials at 1/n², soft, flute-like. Sine has only the fundamental. Two oscillators slightly detuned (5–15 cents) produce beating and width; that is the basis of every pad.

Filter: low-pass lets everything below the cutoff frequency through. Resonance emphasises the cutoff. 24 dB/octave (Moog type) cuts steeply and warm, 12 dB (Oberheim type) gently and open. High-pass removes lows (indispensable for pads over a guitar). Band-pass lets a band through, nasal.

Envelope ADSR: attack (time to maximum), decay (time to the sustain level), sustain (level while the key is held), release (time to silence after release). An envelope on the amplifier shapes loudness; one on the filter shapes the timbral course (cutoff opens on attack and closes). Pad: attack 0.5–2 s, release 1–3 s. Organ: attack 0, sustain full, release 0.1 s. Bass: attack 0, decay short, sustain medium.

LFO: slow oscillation modulating pitch (vibrato), filter (wah) or loudness (tremolo). Rate in Hz, amount in percent. An LFO on pulse width (PWM) is the classic string sound.

Nord Lead A1 and Blofeld are both subtractive (Blofeld also wavetable, unit 2). The terms are identical; only the front panel differs. All patch recipes in this course are formulated as parameters and translated to the devices in appendix D.

te6-1-1.title: Listen · Subtractive synthesis: oscillator, filter, envelope
te6-1-1.instructions: Type O Negative, "Love You to Death", keyboard pads under the chorus: determine by ear the waveform (bright/sawtooth-like or hollow/square), attack (immediate or swelling) and release (abrupt or lingering). Then Anathema, "Eternity Part I", string pad: the same. Claim: Type O organ with attack 0, Anathema pad with attack over 0.5 s (verify).
checklist: Waveform, attack, release of both pads estimated?
Estimate rebuilt on your own synth and compared?

te6-1-2.title: Model · Subtractive synthesis: oscillator, filter, envelope
te6-1-2.instructions: The same Em chord with four sounds; the piano preview shows only the tones. Build four patches on the synth: 1. one sawtooth, filter open, attack 0. 2. one square, otherwise identical. 3. one triangle. 4. two sawtooths, detune 10 cents, attack 1 s, release 2 s, cutoff half, high-pass 200 Hz. Play the chord with each and write the parameters as a table. Describe the overtones you hear in 1 compared with 2.
checklist: Four patches built and parameters tabulated?
Overtone difference saw/square described?

te6-1-3.title: Application · Subtractive synthesis: oscillator, filter, envelope
te6-1-3.instructions: Build three base patches for the course and save them: "Pad" (two oscillators, slow), "Organ" (square or sine stack, attack 0, short release), "Bass" (sawtooth, filter envelope, short decay). Write each as a device-neutral parameter list. Play Em–C–D–Em with each and check whether the patch matches its role.
checklist: Three patches saved and documented device-neutrally?
Role suitability checked with the progression?

tu6-2.title: Wavetable, FM and modulation
tu6-2.goal: Know the two other synthesis forms of the Blofeld and use modulation routing as a tool.
tu6-2.text:
Wavetable: instead of a fixed waveform the oscillator has a table of many waveforms (in the Blofeld 64 per table). One parameter (wave position) selects the current one; modulated by envelope or LFO, the sound travels through the table. This gives spectral motion a filter alone cannot supply: metallic, glassy, vowel-like. For pads that change slowly (wave position over 8 seconds with an envelope) this is the Blofeld sound par excellence.

FM (frequency modulation): one oscillator (modulator) modulates the pitch of another (carrier) so fast that new overtones arise. The frequency ratio determines whether the result sounds harmonic (integer: 1:1, 2:1, 3:1) or inharmonic (1:1.41). The modulation depth determines brightness. Bells, electric piano, metallic basses. The Blofeld has FM between its oscillators; the Nord Lead A1 only in reduced form. Type O Negative's bell and choir sounds are partly FM (verify: compare with a DX7 bell patch).

Modulation matrix: source → destination → amount. Sources: envelopes, LFOs, velocity, mod wheel, aftertouch, keytrack. Destinations: cutoff, pitch, wave position, pulse width, loudness, FM amount. Sound design is 80 % the choice of these connections. Examples: velocity → cutoff (hit harder = brighter), LFO → pitch at 5 Hz and 10 cents (vibrato), envelope → wave position (sound travels on attack), keytrack → cutoff (high notes brighter).

For you: wavetable for pads with inner motion, FM for bells and accents, subtractive for everything else. The Nord Lead A1 covers subtractive broadly; the Blofeld adds wavetable and FM.

te6-2-1.title: Listen · Wavetable, FM and modulation
te6-2-1.instructions: Type O Negative, "Red Water (Christmas Mourning)": the bells. Harmonic or inharmonic (does the tone have a clear fundamental or sound like metal)? Then Anathema, "Far Away", keyboard pad: does the sound change while a chord is held (spectral motion)? Claim: bells slightly inharmonic (FM-like), Anathema pad static (verify).
checklist: Harmonicity of the bells assessed?
Spectral motion of the pad assessed?

te6-2-2.title: Model · Wavetable, FM and modulation
te6-2-2.instructions: Bars 1–2 a held chord for a wavetable pad: sweep wave position with an envelope over 8 s. Bars 3–4 a bell line for FM: carrier 1:1, modulator 3.5:1, modulation depth from an envelope with short decay. Bars 5–6 both together. Build both patches (Blofeld or an FM-capable device) and note the parameters. If only the Nord Lead is available: use its FM amount and waveform morph.
checklist: Wavetable pad with audible motion over 8 s?
FM bell built with an inharmonic ratio?

te6-2-3.title: Application · Wavetable, FM and modulation
te6-2-3.instructions: Create a modulation table for your pad patch: five connections (source, destination, amount) with one sentence each on what they do musically. At least one connection on velocity, one on mod wheel. Play eight bars of Em–C with the patch and use both performance controls deliberately. Record.
checklist: Five modulation connections documented?
Velocity and mod wheel audible in the recording?

tu6-3.title: Pads, organ, strings: the keyboard roles of the references
tu6-3.goal: Program the three keyboard sounds that carry doom and gothic and assign them their role in the arrangement.
tu6-3.text:
Three sounds cover almost everything Josh Silver (Type O Negative), Martin Powell (My Dying Bride) and Anathema's keyboards do.

Organ: square or stacked sines (fundamental, octave, fifth, second octave: the drawbar idea), attack 0, sustain full, release short, little filtering, optional Leslie-like modulation (LFO on amplitude and slight pitch, 0.7 Hz slow / 6 Hz fast). Role: pad with the third, immobile, church sound. Type O Negative almost throughout (verify). Voicing: close position right hand from C4, omit the bass (the guitar has it).

Strings/pad: two or three sawtooths, detune 8–15 cents, PWM LFO 0.3 Hz, 24 dB low-pass with cutoff around 2 kHz, high-pass 150 Hz, attack 0.8 s, release 1.5 s, chorus or ensemble effect, reverb. Role: pad without attack, fills between guitar chords. My Dying Bride and Anathema (verify). Voicing: open position, top voice leads, slow voice leading from phase 2.

Choir: like pad, but band-pass around 800 Hz with slight resonance and a formant filter or wavetable with vowel waves; attack 1 s. Role: "voice" without text, in the register C4–C6. Type O Negative (verify).

Piano stays piano: no programming, but a role choice. In My Dying Bride the piano is often alone or with violin, never under the riff (verify). In Type O Negative it opens pieces and then disappears.

Rule: one keyboard sound per section. Two at once only if they occupy different registers (organ C4–C5, choir C5–C6).

te6-3-1.title: Listen · Pads, organ, strings: the keyboard roles of the references
te6-3-1.instructions: Type O Negative, "Haunted" and "Die with Me": assign each keyboard sound you hear to one of the three types (organ, pad, choir) and note its register. Then My Dying Bride, "Sear Me MCMXCIII": piano and what else? Claim: Type O organ plus choir in different registers, MDB piano without pad (verify).
checklist: Every keyboard sound heard typed and noted with register?
Simultaneous sounds checked for register separation?

te6-3-2.title: Model · Pads, organ, strings: the keyboard roles of the references
te6-3-2.instructions: Three roles over Em–C: bars 1–2 organ in close position from G4, bars 3–4 pad in open position with a held chord, bars 5–6 organ plus choir voice above (B5–C6). Program organ, pad and choir from the recipes in the text and play the six bars with sound changes. Note attack and release in seconds for each sound.
checklist: Three sounds programmed and played in alternation?
Attack/release documented per sound?

te6-3-3.title: Application · Pads, organ, strings: the keyboard roles of the references
te6-3-3.instructions: Record an eight-bar guitar riff. Lay three keyboard tracks over it, one each with organ, pad, choir, each in its register. Listen to every combination (riff + one sound) and decide which sound complements the riff best without masking it. Justify with register and attack.
checklist: Three combinations recorded?
Choice justified with register and attack in the log?

tu6-4.title: Delay physics: time, feedback, filter, modulation
tu6-4.goal: Understand the four parameters of every delay and calculate delay times from tempo.
tu6-4.text:
A delay stores the signal and plays it back later. Four parameters determine everything.

Time: the gap between original and repeat. Below 30 ms you hear no repeat but doubling or comb filtering. 30–100 ms: slapback, a single echo, rockabilly and vocals. 100–500 ms: rhythmic delay, audible as a repeat in time. Above 500 ms: spatial effect, ambient. Tempo sync: 60000 / BPM = quarter note in milliseconds. At ♩ = 60: quarter 1000 ms, eighth 500, dotted eighth 750, triplet 333. At 72: quarter 833, eighth 417, dotted eighth 625.

Feedback: the share of the output fed back into the input. 0 % = one echo. 30–50 % = three to five audible repeats. Above 70 % = long tail, from 100 % self-oscillation. Doom uses low feedback with long time rather than high feedback with short time.

Filter: every repeat is filtered. Low-pass makes the echoes darker (tape character), high-pass prevents mud in the bass. Without filtering the repeats stay as bright as the original and mask the next note.

Modulation: an LFO on the delay time creates pitch wobble in the repeats. Slight (0.3 Hz, little depth) = tape wow and flutter, warmth. Strong = chorus-like, seasick.

Musically: a dotted-eighth delay over eighth notes creates sixteenth patterns (the U2 effect). A quarter-note delay over whole notes thickens the pad. A delay on the clean arpeggio guitar fills gaps between notes (Anathema, verify). On distorted riffs delay is rarely useful because the signal is already dense; exceptions: solo and decays.

te6-4-1.title: Listen · Delay physics: time, feedback, filter, modulation
te6-4-1.instructions: Anathema, "Sentient" and "Angelica", clean guitar: do you hear repeats? Measure or estimate the delay time relative to the tempo (eighth? dotted eighth? quarter?). How many repeats? Do they get darker? Claim: dotted eighth or quarter, two to three repeats, filtered (verify).
checklist: Delay time determined as a note value?
Number and filtering of repeats described?

te6-4-2.title: Model · Delay physics: time, feedback, filter, modulation
te6-4-2.instructions: Bar 1 an arpeggio in eighths with rests. Bar 2 the same, but the repeats of a dotted-eighth delay are written out as sixteenths (only the first repeat, imagined quieter). Bars 3–4 a held chord, then with quarter-note delay as four attacks. Compute the delay times for ♩ = 60, 72 and 90. Set the dotted-eighth delay on one of your units and play bar 1: the result must sound like bar 2.
checklist: Delay times calculated for three tempi (eighth, dotted eighth, quarter)?
Dotted delay set on the unit, bar 1 produces bar 2?

te6-4-3.title: Application · Delay physics: time, feedback, filter, modulation
te6-4-3.instructions: Create a delay table for tempi from 50 to 100 in steps of five: quarter, eighth, dotted eighth, eighth triplet, half in milliseconds. Then build three delay settings for your rig: "Arpeggio" (dotted eighth, 35 % feedback, low-pass), "Pad" (quarter, 50 %, dark), "Solo" (eighth, 25 %, bright). Note each with all four parameters.
checklist: Table with 11 tempi × 5 values?
Three settings documented with four parameters?

tu6-5.title: Tape, BBD, digital: what is audible
tu6-5.goal: Recognise the three delay technologies by their artefacts and know which parameters emulate them.
tu6-5.text:
Tape delay (Echoplex, Space Echo, Binson): the signal is recorded to tape and read back delayed by a playback head. Artefacts: high-frequency loss per pass (each repeat darker, about 3–6 dB at 5 kHz), wow and flutter (slow pitch modulation, 0.3–1 Hz, a few cents), tape saturation (slight compression and distortion at high level; repeats become "softer" and louder than expected), noise. Time range typically 80–600 ms. Sound: warm, blurred, the repeats merge into a tail.

BBD (bucket brigade device, analog delay such as Memory Man, DM-2): a chain of capacitors passes the signal along, clocked by an oscillator. Artefacts: strong high-frequency loss (low-pass often at 3 kHz, each repeat darker), clock noise, slight distortion, short maximum time (300–600 ms on old units). Modulation is built in (chorus circuit): the clock is modulated by an LFO. Sound: dark, dense, "behind" the original.

Digital: exact copy, any time, no high-frequency loss unless deliberate. Sound: clear, present, can seem clinical; repeats compete with the original.

The same four parameters from unit 4 cover everything: tape = medium time, moderate low-pass, slight modulation, saturation (if available). BBD = strong low-pass, built-in modulation, short time. Digital = filter off, modulation off. The references: Type O Negative on guitar and bass more chorus (BBD family) than delay (verify); Anathema digital or tape-like delay on clean guitar (verify); My Dying Bride reverb instead of delay (verify).

Discrimination test: listen to the third repeat. Tape: darker and slightly wobbling. BBD: much darker, almost only mids. Digital: identical to the original.

te6-5-1.title: Listen · Tape, BBD, digital: what is audible
te6-5-1.instructions: Take two reference passages with audible delay: Anathema, "Sentient" (clean guitar) and a passage of your choice from any album with a clearly recognisable echo. Apply the discrimination test: third repeat, darker? wobbling? identical? Assign tape, BBD or digital. Claim: Anathema digital or tape, not BBD (verify).
checklist: Third repeat assessed at two passages?
Technology assigned with reasoning?

te6-5-2.title: Model · Tape, BBD, digital: what is audible
te6-5-2.instructions: A single tone per bar so the repeats stand free. On one unit set three delays with the same time (quarter) and the same feedback (50 %): 1. tape model: low-pass 5 kHz, modulation 0.5 Hz slight, saturation if available. 2. BBD model: low-pass 2.5 kHz, modulation 0.8 Hz slightly deeper. 3. digital: everything off. Play the tone and listen to the third repeat. Note the differences in words.
checklist: Three models set with the same time and feedback?
Differences of the third repeat described?

te6-5-3.title: Application · Tape, BBD, digital: what is audible
te6-5-3.instructions: Play the same four-bar arpeggio with the three delay models and record. Listen to each recording with the guitar riff underneath (from an earlier recording). Decide which model sits best under the riff without masking it, and which sounds best alone. The two answers may differ.
checklist: Three recordings compared with and without the riff?
Two decisions with reasoning logged?

tu6-6.title: Approximation on 2290, G-Major, Nova System
tu6-6.goal: Emulate tape and BBD character with the parameters of the three TC units and document the results as presets.
tu6-6.text:
All three units are digital delays; tape and BBD have to be built from time, feedback, filter and modulation. Parameter names differ; the following mapping is compiled from manuals and must be checked at the unit (verify).

TC 2290: delay time in ms up to 32 s (depending on memory), feedback in percent, "feedback high-cut"/filter in the feedback path, modulation via the internal LFO on delay time (pitch mod) with speed and depth, "dynamic delay" (ducking: the delay gets quieter while you play). Tape approximation: time from the table, feedback 40 %, high-cut as low as the unit allows (around 5 kHz), pitch mod speed 0.4 Hz, depth minimal. BBD approximation: high-cut lower (2–3 kHz if reachable; otherwise EQ before the delay), mod speed 0.8 Hz, depth a little higher, time under 400 ms. The 2290 colours very little by itself; its character is the modulation.

TC G-Major: delay block with types (single, ping-pong, dual, "tape" or similar depending on firmware), feedback, hi-cut and lo-cut in the feedback, modulation (speed, depth), tempo sync with note value. Tape approximation: type tape if available, otherwise single with hi-cut 4–5 kHz, feedback 40 %, mod depth small. BBD: hi-cut 2.5 kHz, lo-cut 150 Hz, mod slightly higher. The G-Major also has chorus, pitch and reverb in the same chain; mind the block order.

TC Nova System: delay block with types (clean, analog, tape, ping-pong, dynamic, depending on firmware), feedback, hi-cut, lo-cut, tempo sync. The types "analog" and "tape" are already approximations; check how strongly they filter and modulate and correct with hi-cut and modulation. Nova has drive and compressor before the delay; for BBD character use slight drive before the delay.
