Procedure: 1. Determine the reference sound (tape or BBD, time as a note value). 2. Choose the unit. 3. Build the preset from the table. 4. Apply the discrimination test (third repeat). 5. Save as a preset and log the parameters. Appendix D holds the translation table of parameter names.

te6-6-1.title: Listen · Approximation on 2290, G-Major, Nova System
te6-6-1.instructions: Listen to Anathema, "Sentient", clean guitar, and define the target: note value, approximate feedback (number of audible repeats), brightness of the repeats. Write a target description in five parameters before touching a unit. Claim: dotted eighth, three repeats, medium filtering (verify).
checklist: Target description with five parameters written before building?
Feedback estimated from the repeat count?

te6-6-2.title: Model · Approximation on 2290, G-Major, Nova System
te6-6-2.instructions: Test material: an arpeggio at ♩ = 72. Build the tape preset in turn on the 2290, G-Major and Nova System from the recipes in the text: time 625 ms (dotted eighth at 72), feedback 40 %, high-cut around 5 kHz, modulation slight. Play the arpeggio with each unit and record. Note the actual parameter names and values per unit. Where a unit lacks a parameter, note the substitute.
checklist: Tape preset built and recorded on all three units?
Parameter names and substitutes documented per unit?

te6-6-3.title: Application · Approximation on 2290, G-Major, Nova System
te6-6-3.instructions: Repeat the procedure for the BBD preset on all three units. Compare the six recordings (2 models × 3 units) blind: shuffle the order and assign by ear. Note the hit rate and which unit comes closest to which model. Save the two best as named presets.
checklist: Six recordings assigned blind, hit rate noted?
Two presets saved and documented?

tu6-7.title: Reverb: room, plate, spring, and when none
tu6-7.goal: Recognise reverb types by their parameters and understand reverb as a register decision.
tu6-7.text:
Reverb is the sum of thousands of reflections. Parameters: pre-delay (time to the first reflection, 0–100 ms; larger = larger room and more separation from the original), decay/reverb time (time to −60 dB, 0.5–10 s), damping/high-damp (highs die earlier than lows, as in real rooms), diffusion (density of reflections), mix. A high-pass on the reverb signal (150–300 Hz) keeps the bass range clean; that is the most important setting for this music.

Types: room (short, 0.5–1.5 s, natural), hall (long, 2–5 s, concert hall, church), plate (dense, bright, without room feel, classic for vocals and snare), spring (metallic, guitar amplifier, short "boing"), ambient/shimmer (with pitch shift, no model in the references).

The references: My Dying Bride use long reverb on violin and vocals, short or none on the riff (verify). Type O Negative have reverb on everything but with a high-pass so the bass stays dry (verify). Anathema put plate or hall on the clean guitar and little on the distorted one (verify). Vivaldi and Biber were played in churches and halls; historical recordings have 2–4 s of natural reverb that is part of the sound.

Rule: reverb lengthens tones (phase 5) and fills registers. On the foundation (bass, low guitar) no or minimal reverb with a high-pass, otherwise mud. On line and pad (violin, pad, lead guitar) long reverb. On the riff: room or nothing. In solo playing without a band, reverb is the only "second instrument" you have; use it, but only on top.

The three TC units each have a reverb block; G-Major and Nova with types (room, hall, plate, spring), the 2290 without (only via delay networks). Appendix D maps the parameters.

te6-7-1.title: Listen · Reverb: room, plate, spring, and when none
te6-7-1.instructions: My Dying Bride, "Sear Me MCMXCIII": estimate the reverb time on the violin (seconds from note end to silence) and on the piano. Then Type O Negative, "Haunted": does the bass have reverb? The organ? Claim: MDB violin over 3 s, Type O bass dry, organ long (verify).
checklist: Reverb times estimated?
Reverb per instrument in Type O determined?

te6-7-2.title: Model · Reverb: room, plate, spring, and when none
te6-7-2.instructions: Bars 1–2 a riff with rests, bars 3–4 a high line with rests. Play bars 1–2 with room (0.8 s, high-pass 200 Hz, mix 15 %) and with hall (3 s, mix 40 %): the rests must stay audible in the first case and are filled in the second. Play bars 3–4 with the same two settings. Decide for each half which setting fits and note the parameters.
checklist: Both halves played with both reverb types?
Assignment with parameters logged?

te6-7-3.title: Application · Reverb: room, plate, spring, and when none
te6-7-3.instructions: Build two reverb presets on the G-Major or Nova System: "Riff" (room, short, high-pass high, little mix) and "Line" (hall or plate, long, pre-delay 40 ms, more mix). Play an eight-bar solo piece alternating between riff and high line and switch presets at the boundaries. Record and judge whether the change disturbs as a room change or helps as a register change.
checklist: Two presets built and documented?
Switching effect assessed in the log?

tu6-8.title: Chorus, flanger, phaser: the Type O sound
tu6-8.goal: Distinguish the three modulation effects and use chorus as a width tool for bass and guitar.
tu6-8.text:
All three are short delays with modulated time mixed with the original. The difference is the time and whether there is feedback.

Chorus: 15–35 ms, LFO 0.3–2 Hz, no or little feedback. Result: pitch beating like two slightly detuned instruments, width, "ensemble". Stereo chorus sends original and effect to different sides. This is the BBD technology from unit 5 in short form; old chorus pedals are BBD.

Flanger: 1–10 ms, slow LFO, with feedback. Result: a comb filter sweeping through the spectrum, "jet plane". Conspicuous; rare in the references.

Phaser: no delay but all-pass filters shifting phase; notches in the spectrum sweep. Softer than a flanger, without pitch beating. Classic on electric piano and organ.

Type O Negative: chorus on bass and guitar almost throughout (verify). The bass with chorus and octaver (phase 2) becomes wide and deep at once; the guitar in B with chorus loses edge and gains pad. That is why the album sounds full despite few instruments. Anathema: chorus on clean guitar, occasionally (verify). My Dying Bride: almost no chorus (verify).

Setting for bass: chorus rate 0.5 Hz, depth 30 %, mix 40 %, high-pass on the effect signal so the fundamental stays dry (otherwise the foundation blurs). For clean guitar: rate 0.8 Hz, depth 40 %, mix 50 %. For distorted guitar: after the distortion, rate 0.3 Hz, depth 20 %, mix 30 %; more gets seasick.

Unit mapping: G-Major and Nova have chorus, flanger, phaser as blocks. The 2290 has chorus via modulated short delays. Nord Lead A1 and Blofeld have chorus as an effect section, the Blofeld also phaser and flanger. Appendix D.

te6-8-1.title: Listen · Chorus, flanger, phaser: the Type O sound
te6-8-1.instructions: Type O Negative, "Love You to Death", bass under the first verse and guitar in the chorus: do you hear beating (chorus)? Estimate the rate (slow below 1 Hz or faster). Then Anathema, "Angelica", clean guitar: chorus? Claim: Type O bass and guitar with slow chorus, Anathema little (verify).
checklist: Chorus on bass and guitar in Type O confirmed and rate estimated?
Anathema guitar assessed?

te6-8-2.title: Model · Chorus, flanger, phaser: the Type O sound
te6-8-2.instructions: The same power chord four times. Play it dry, with chorus (25 ms, 0.5 Hz, 30 %), with flanger (3 ms, 0.2 Hz, feedback 50 %), with phaser (4 stages, 0.3 Hz). Record all four. For each effect describe whether the pitch beats (chorus), the spectrum sweeps (flanger/phaser), and whether the foundation blurs. Repeat with a high-pass on the effect signal.
checklist: Four versions recorded and artefacts described?
High-pass effect on the foundation assessed?

te6-8-3.title: Application · Chorus, flanger, phaser: the Type O sound
te6-8-3.instructions: Rebuild the Type O bass sound: octaver (if available, otherwise add keyboard bass an octave lower), slow chorus, high-pass on the chorus signal, slight distortion. Play a four-bar riff and record. Compare with a dry version under your guitar riff: which carries better? Note the chain with all values.
checklist: Chain with octave, chorus, high-pass built and documented?
Comparison under the guitar riff logged?

tu6-9.title: Gain staging and distortion types
tu6-9.goal: Understand the guitar signal chain as a series of levels and match distortion types to the sound goal.
tu6-9.text:
Gain staging means: at every stage of the chain the level is such that the next stage neither hisses (too quiet) nor distorts unintentionally (too loud). The chain: pickup → (pedals) → preamp → effects loop (where 2290, G-Major, Nova sit) → power amp → speaker. Distortion belongs before the effects loop; delay, reverb, chorus after. Otherwise the repeats get distorted too and smear.

Distortion types: overdrive (soft clipping, tube preamp, dynamic: play softly = nearly clean), distortion (hard clipping, more compression, even), fuzz (extreme clipping, near-square waveform, doom classic since Sabbath, muddy on chords), high gain (multi-stage preamp distortion, very compressed, metal standard). More gain = more combination tones (phase 0) = fewer tolerable intervals. Rule: as little gain as the sustain goal allows (phase 5).

The references: My Dying Bride distortion medium to high, guitars in thirds therefore in the high register (verify). Type O Negative distortion with chorus, rather medium, few highs, lots of low mids (verify). Anathema two guitars: one clean with compressor, one medium distortion (verify).

Level control in the loop: G-Major and Nova have input and output levels; so does the 2290. Target: input LED just below clip on the loudest chord. Too quiet → hiss with reverb and delay. Too loud → digital clipping, hard and ugly. Nova also has its own drive blocks that belong before the modulation effects.

Compressor: before distortion it increases sustain and smooths the attack (clean arpeggio, Anathema). After distortion it is mostly redundant because distortion already compresses.

te6-9-1.title: Listen · Gain staging and distortion types
te6-9-1.instructions: Compare the distortion of three riffs: My Dying Bride, "The Crown of Sympathy"; Type O Negative, "Wolf Moon"; Anathema, "Sentient" (distorted part). Assign each a type (overdrive, distortion, fuzz, high gain) and estimate the gain (low, medium, high). Claim: all three medium, none fuzz or high gain (verify).
checklist: Three riffs with type and gain estimate?
Low-mid and high content described per riff?

te6-9-2.title: Model · Gain staging and distortion types
te6-9-2.instructions: Per bar an Em triad with the third, then a power chord without it. Play the four bars with four gain levels: clean, overdrive, distortion, fuzz (or the four stages of your amp). In each bar hear whether the third still appears as a tone or already as noise. Note for each level: third usable yes/no, sustain in seconds, attack hard/soft.
checklist: Four gain levels noted with third and sustain verdicts?
Gain level for thirds and gain level for power chords fixed?

te6-9-3.title: Application · Gain staging and distortion types
te6-9-3.instructions: Draw your entire signal chain with level at each stage: pickup, pedals, preamp, loop (which unit in which order), power amp. Set the input levels of the effects units by the rule (just below clip on the loudest chord) and note the values. Play a riff with delay and reverb and check whether the repeats are clean (undistorted).
checklist: Signal chain drawn with order and levels?
Repeats confirmed undistorted?

tu6-10.title: Frequency spaces in the arrangement
tu6-10.goal: Distribute all sound sources of a piece so that each has its range; EQ as space-making, not as beautification.
tu6-10.text:
An arrangement is a frequency plan. Every source has a fundamental range and an overtone range; neither may overlap unplanned with other sources. Phase 3 named the ranges: sub 20–60, bass 60–250, low mids 250–500, mids 500–2k, highs 2k–20k Hz.

Typical distribution for your setup: kick 50–80 Hz plus attack 3–5 kHz. Bass 60–200 Hz plus overtones up to 1 kHz. Distorted guitar 100 Hz–4 kHz, centred 200–800 Hz. Clean guitar 150 Hz–6 kHz. Pad 300 Hz–8 kHz with high-pass at 300. Organ 250 Hz–5 kHz. Choir/line 500 Hz–8 kHz. Hi-hat from 5 kHz.

Tools: high-pass on everything that is not foundation (the most important rule). Low-pass on distortion above 6–8 kHz (fizz gone). Narrow cut where two sources collide: cut the guitar at 300 Hz if the bass sits there; the pad at 800 Hz if the vocal or line sits there. Never two sources equally loud in the same range.

The references as frequency plans: Type O Negative: bass alone at the bottom, guitar in the low mids, organ and choir in the mids and highs, vocals in two octaves between; a perfect stack (verify). My Dying Bride: guitars double each other, bass doubles the guitars; violin and vocals above everything; the stack is dense below and thin above (verify). Anathema: clean and distorted guitar share the mids via stereo position, not frequency (verify).

In solo playing (guitar alone or keyboard alone) the frequency plan is the register of the voices: bass low, melody high, inner voice between. The instrument course taught this musically; here is the acoustic reasoning.

te6-10-1.title: Listen · Frequency spaces in the arrangement
te6-10-1.instructions: Draw a frequency plan for three passages (source, estimated range from–to Hz): Type O Negative, "Be My Druidess", chorus; My Dying Bride, "Your River", riff with violin; Anathema, "Eternity Part I", full section. Mark overlaps. Claim: Type O without overlap, MDB overlap at the bottom, Anathema overlap in the mids (verify).
checklist: Three frequency plans drawn?
Overlaps marked and compared with the claim?

te6-10-2.title: Model · Frequency spaces in the arrangement
te6-10-2.instructions: The stack grows by one layer per bar: bass E2, guitar fifth E3–B3, pad from G4, line from G5. Rebuild it with your sources: keyboard bass, guitar, pad patch, line on guitar or synth. Put a high-pass at 300 Hz on pad and line. Listen to the stack with and without the high-passes. Note which layer masks the foundation without the high-pass.
checklist: Four layers built with your own sources?
High-pass effect assessed per layer?

te6-10-3.title: Application · Frequency spaces in the arrangement
te6-10-3.instructions: Create the frequency plan for your final piece from the instrument course, extended with drums, bass and one keyboard layer. For each source enter range, high-pass frequency and one cut where it collides with another. Record a four-bar passage with all layers, once without and once with the EQ plan, and compare.
checklist: Frequency plan with high-pass and cut per source?
Comparison without/with EQ logged?

t7.title: Form
t7.goal: Riff form and verse/chorus, suite and dance movements, ritornello and programme music, long forms, contrast and density arc, intro/outro/transition, the voice as a register gap.

tu7-1.title: Riff form versus verse and chorus
tu7-1.goal: Distinguish the two basic constructions of rock form and know which the references choose.
tu7-1.text:
Verse/chorus (song form): sections with different functions, usually A (verse, lyrics narrate, harmonically open) and B (chorus, lyrics repeat, harmonically closed, denser), often with C (bridge, contrast, once only). Typical order: intro – A – B – A – B – C – B – outro. The form lives on recognising the chorus. Type O Negative are at home here: *October Rust* is a song album with extended intros and outros (verify).

Riff form: sections are riffs, not functions. Riff 1 (8 bars, four times), riff 2 (8 bars, four times), riff 1 shortened, riff 3 (new tempo or meter), riff 2 as the ending. No chorus in the song sense, but return. The form lives on contrast between riffs and on the length of repetitions. My Dying Bride build this way: pieces of 8–12 minutes from five to seven riffs, each long enough to become a state (verify).

Anathema mix: song form with riff lengths. Verses are four to eight bars on one riff, choruses likewise, but the sections last twice as long as in a pop song (verify).

Baroque: Biber's dance movements are binary (A A B B, each part repeated), Vivaldi's ritornello movements alternate tutti and solo (phase 3). Both are closer to riff form than to verse/chorus: sections are musical states, not lyric functions.

Decision for your piece: song form if one idea (the chorus) should outshine everything else. Riff form if several ideas are equal and time carries. Without vocals riff form is the natural route; an instrumental "chorus" needs a motif as strong as a lyric.

te7-1-1.title: Listen · Riff form versus verse and chorus
te7-1-1.instructions: Sketch the form of Type O Negative, "Love You to Death", and My Dying Bride, "The Songless Bird", as a letter chain with bar counts (A8 B8 A8 …). Count the distinct sections. Claim: Type O three to four section types with chorus return, MDB five to seven riffs without a chorus (verify).
checklist: Both forms as letter chains with bar counts?
Number of section types compared?

te7-1-2.title: Model · Riff form versus verse and chorus
te7-1-2.instructions: A miniature song form: A (two bars, open on an E pedal), B (two bars, harmonically moving, higher). Twice, with a different ending. Play it and describe what makes B the "chorus" (register, bass change, final note). Then rebuild the same eight bars as riff form: A four times, then B four times, without alternation. Which version carries longer?
checklist: Chorus features of B named?
Riff version played and endurance compared?

te7-1-3.title: Application · Riff form versus verse and chorus
te7-1-3.instructions: Decide for your final piece: song form or riff form. Write the form plan as a letter chain with bar counts and tempo per section before writing a single note. Justify the choice in two sentences referring to one reference. The plan must cover at least 48 bars.
checklist: Form plan with bar counts and tempi, at least 48 bars?
Choice justified with a reference?

tu7-2.title: Suite and dance movements: Biber
tu7-2.goal: Understand the suite as a sequence of contrasting short forms and use it as a model for an album or a long piece.
tu7-2.text:
Biber's *Harmonia artificioso-ariosa* (1696) consists of seven partitas, each a suite: praeludium, then dance movements (allemande, courante, sarabande, gigue, plus aria, gavotte, passacaglia, ciacona depending on the partita). Each movement has a fixed character through meter, tempo and rhythm: allemande 4/4 moderate with upbeat; courante 3/2 or 3/4 flowing; sarabande 3/4 slow with emphasis on 2; gigue 6/8 or 12/8 fast, dotted; ciacona/passacaglia 3/4 over a bass model.

The principle: contrast through type, not through material. All movements are in the same key; what changes is the shape of time. A fifteen-minute suite has six different feels of time in one key. That is the reverse of the doom principle, where one feel of time (slow, half-time) runs over different harmonies.

Scordatura: Biber writes for retuned violins. The tuning is part of the composition; it enables chords and resonances impossible in normal tuning. That is the exact parallel to P4 and to Type O Negative's B tuning: the tuning chooses the music. Biber's Partita VII calls for two violas d'amore, instruments with sympathetic strings, i.e. built-in reverb.

Transfer: an album or a long piece as a suite: praeludium (free, rubato, phase 5), slow movement (sarabande feel: 3/4, emphasis on 2), ostinato movement (ciacona: bass model, phase 3), fast movement (gigue: 12/8, phase 5), ending. All in E, A or D. My Dying Bride come close to this in their multi-part pieces (verify); Type O Negative have in "Haunted" a kind of suite within one piece (verify).

te7-2-1.title: Listen · Suite and dance movements: Biber
te7-2-1.instructions: Biber, one partita complete (I or III): note per movement meter, tempo (estimated), character in one word and key. Then Type O Negative, "Haunted": count the sections with a different feel of time. Claim: Biber six movements in one key, "Haunted" three to four feels of time in one key (verify).
checklist: Movement table of the partita filled in?
Feels of time in "Haunted" counted?

te7-2-2.title: Model · Suite and dance movements: Biber
te7-2-2.instructions: A sarabande: 3/4, slow, the second beat is long (quarter–half). Eight bars in E minor with leading tone. Play it and emphasise the half note on 2, not the 1. Then rewrite the same eight bars as a gigue: 12/8 (each 3/4 bar becomes one 12/8 bar: quarter → dotted quarter), double tempo. The character change comes from the shape of time alone.
checklist: Sarabande played with emphasis on 2?
Gigue rewrite of the same tones notated and played?

te7-2-3.title: Application · Suite and dance movements: Biber
te7-2-3.instructions: Plan a suite in E of four movements: praeludium (free, 16 bars without fixed pulse), sarabande (3/4, 16 bars), ciacona (4-bar bass model, at least 6 passes), gigue (12/8, 16 bars). For each movement write meter, tempo, bass model and one motif. Compose the first movement completely.
checklist: Four movements planned with meter, tempo, bass, motif?
Praeludium fully notated and played?

tu7-3.title: Ritornello and programme music: Vivaldi
tu7-3.goal: Master the ritornello form as an alternation of return and episode and understand programme as a formal aid.
tu7-3.text:
*Le quattro stagioni* (1725) are four violin concertos with three movements each (fast, slow, fast). The fast movements are ritornello forms: the tutti presents a theme (ritornello), the soloist plays episodes, the ritornello returns in various keys and lengths, at the end complete in the home key. Typical: R (tonic) – ep – R (dominant or relative) – ep – R (other key) – ep – R (tonic). Four to five ritornelli, three to four episodes between.

The programme: Vivaldi attached a sonnet to each concerto and wrote the lines into the score (birdsong, thunderstorm, sleeping shepherd, hunt, icy wind). The music depicts images: trills = birds, tremolo in the bass = thunder, dotted rhythms = chattering teeth. The programme helps the form: the listener knows why a section arrives, and the composer has a reason for contrast.

Transfer to doom: the reference albums are programme music with lyrics instead of a sonnet. An instrumental piece can have a silent programme: a scene, a sequence only you know. That is not mysticism but a formal aid: if you know section B is "the thunderstorm", you know how dense, how loud, how long.

Ritornello as riff form: one riff (R) returns between free sections (ep), each time slightly different (shortened, another key, another texture). That is exactly the solo-segno-coda model of the instrument course (phase 7), only with more return. My Dying Bride do this without naming it (verify).

Rule: the ritornello must be complete the first time so that the shortened returns stay recognisable. The last return is complete again.

te7-3-1.title: Listen · Ritornello and programme music: Vivaldi
te7-3-1.instructions: Vivaldi, *Summer*, movement 3 (Presto): mark every ritornello entry with length and key (tonic, dominant, other). Count the episodes. Then *Spring*, movement 1: which programme images do you recognise (birds, brook, thunderstorm)? Claim: Presto with five ritornelli, Spring with three recognisable images (verify).
checklist: Ritornello entries noted with length and key?
Programme images named with their musical device?

te7-3-2.title: Model · Ritornello and programme music: Vivaldi
te7-3-2.instructions: Ritornello form in eight bars: R (two bars, motif with leading tone), episode (sequence in eighths over E and D), R′ shortened to one bar, episode over A and B (dominant-pedal feel), R complete as the ending. Play it and mark every R entry. Then replace R′ with another episode and hear whether the piece loses its anchor.
checklist: R entries marked and shortening recognised?
Version without R′ played and effect assessed?

te7-3-3.title: Application · Ritornello and programme music: Vivaldi
te7-3-3.instructions: Write a silent programme for your final piece: three images or states in one sentence each. Assign each a section and derive tempo, density, register from it. Then build one riff as a ritornello returning between the three sections, complete the first and last time, shortened between. Form plan with bar counts.
checklist: Three programme images with derived parameters?
Ritornello plan with complete and shortened entries?

tu7-4.title: Long forms: carrying eight to twelve minutes
tu7-4.goal: Know how My Dying Bride build long pieces and name the tools for it.
tu7-4.text:
*Turn Loose the Swans* has pieces of seven to twelve minutes. What holds them together is not a chorus but a web of return, contrast and build.

Tools: 1. Riff lengths: each riff runs long enough to become a state (at least four times eight bars at ♩ = 60, i.e. over two minutes). 2. Few riffs: five to seven per piece, not fifteen. 3. Return: at least one riff comes back after a long absence, often in another texture (piano instead of guitar, or vice versa). 4. One break: a section that refuses everything else (silence, piano only, spoken voice only, another tempo). 5. Build at the end: the densest point sits in the last quarter. 6. No ending by cadence but by thinning or breaking off (phase 4).

The form of time is epic: the listener should lose the clock. Hence no constant four-group expectation; phrases of six, ten or twelve bars occur and section lengths vary (verify). The vocals are lyrics, but the music carries without them; an instrumental version of an MDB piece would still be a piece.

The danger of long forms: arbitrariness. The test: can every riff justify why it stands where it stands? If two sections are interchangeable, one is superfluous. And: what returns? Without return it is a sequence of events, not a piece.

Baroque parallel: Vivaldi's concertos are short (3–4 minutes per movement), but the ritornello form is a model for length: with seven ritornelli and six episodes it carries twelve minutes. Biber extends through variation over ostinato. Both are return; MDB have it intuitively.

te7-4-1.title: Listen · Long forms: carrying eight to twelve minutes
te7-4-1.instructions: My Dying Bride, "The Crown of Sympathy" (over twelve minutes): draw a timeline in minutes. Enter: every riff (letter), its length, returns, the break, the densest point. Check the six tools from the text individually. Claim: five to seven riffs, one break, densest point after minute 9 (verify).
checklist: Timeline with riffs, lengths, returns, break, density?
Six tools individually confirmed or refuted?

te7-4-2.title: Model · Long forms: carrying eight to twelve minutes
te7-4-2.instructions: A long form in miniature: riff A (power chords), riff B (melody), break (silence, then one tone), A returning in another texture (single voices like piano instead of fifths). Play the eight bars. Then extend mentally: A four times, B four times, break two bars, A′ four times. That is 34 bars, over two minutes at ♩ = 60. Play this version through and time it.
checklist: Eight bars played and the four building blocks named?
34-bar version played through and timed?

te7-4-3.title: Application · Long forms: carrying eight to twelve minutes
te7-4-3.instructions: Plan a piece of at least eight minutes at ♩ = 60 (i.e. at least 120 bars). At most six riffs. Enter into a timeline: riff, length in bars, texture, returns, the break, the densest point. Apply the interchangeability test to every pair of riffs. Compose the first 32 bars.
checklist: Timeline over at least 120 bars with at most six riffs?
Interchangeability test documented, first 32 bars notated?

tu7-5.title: Contrast, density arc, dynamics
tu7-5.goal: Understand density as a plannable curve across a piece and create dynamics without a volume knob.
tu7-5.text:
Density has four dimensions: number of voices, number of attacks per bar, register width (distance from lowest to highest tone), sonic density (gain, reverb, chorus). Each can be controlled individually. A section with one voice, many attacks, narrow register and heavy gain is dense in a different way from one with four voices, few attacks, wide register and clean.

The density arc of a piece: draw the four dimensions over the timeline. Typical for doom: voices and register grow until the last quarter, attacks stay low, gain is constantly high, with a drop in the middle (the break from unit 4). Typical for Type O Negative: density jumps at section boundaries (verse thin, chorus full) without an arc within sections (verify). Typical for Vivaldi: ritornello dense, episode thin, alternating; the arc is a zigzag with rising peaks.

Dynamics without a knob: loud is relative. A passage becomes loud when something before it was quiet. Four bars of silence or a single voice before the full riff make the riff louder than any knob could. That is the terraced dynamics of the Baroque (Vivaldi's tutti/solo) and the half-time drop in doom. Crescendo (gradual) hardly exists in the Baroque and in doom only as density growth: one voice after another added, not everything louder together.

Contrast needs reference: something is only dark if something before was bright. Hence the C Lydian section in the instrument course (phase 6): it exists so that the return to E sounds dark.

Rule: per piece one maximum of all four dimensions, and it is not at the beginning. Per piece one minimum, and it is not at the end.

te7-5-1.title: Listen · Contrast, density arc, dynamics
te7-5-1.instructions: Anathema, "Eternity Part I" and Vivaldi, *Winter*, movement 1: draw the density arc for both in four lines (voices, attacks, register, sound) over time. Where is the maximum? Where the minimum? Claim: Anathema arc with one maximum at the end, Vivaldi zigzag with maximum in the last ritornello (verify).
checklist: Two density arcs drawn with four lines?
Maximum and minimum of both pieces located?

te7-5-2.title: Model · Contrast, density arc, dynamics
te7-5-2.instructions: A density arc in eight bars: bar 1 one voice, bar 2 bass added, bar 3 middle voice added, bar 4 all with more attacks (maximum). Bar 5 silence (minimum), bar 6 one high tone, bars 7–8 wind-down. Play it and count voices and attacks for every bar. Hear how loud bar 6 feels after bar 5 although it is a single tone.
checklist: Voices and attacks per bar counted?
Perceived loudness of bar 6 described?

te7-5-3.title: Application · Contrast, density arc, dynamics
te7-5-3.instructions: Draw the density arc for your planned long piece in four lines over the form plan. Fix maximum and minimum (not at the start, not at the end). Place at least two bars of minimum before the maximum. Compose the four bars around the maximum and record them: two bars minimum, two bars maximum.
checklist: Four density lines drawn over the form plan?
Minimum-to-maximum passage composed and recorded?

tu7-6.title: Intro, outro, transition
tu7-6.goal: Treat the three seams of a piece as form sections of their own, not leftover space.
tu7-6.text:
Intro: it sets key, tempo, sound and expectation. Four kinds: 1. Riff without drums (the listener learns the riff, then the pulse arrives; MDB, verify). 2. A foreign instrument alone (piano, organ, strings; Type O Negative, verify). 3. Free sound without pulse (arpeggio, reverb; Anathema, verify). 4. The full riff at once (no intro; rare in these references). Length: 8 to 32 bars in doom; the intro may be a section of its own.

Outro: it ends. Four kinds: 1. Thinning (voices disappear one after another until one remains). 2. Return of the intro (frame; Type O Negative often, verify). 3. Fade-out (a recording technique, not a formal device; avoid except as quotation). 4. Break-off on a chord with long decay (MDB, verify). Baroque: Vivaldi ends with the complete ritornello, Biber with the cadence of the last dance movement; no outro in the rock sense.

Transition: the spot between two sections. Tools: fill (phase 3), dropout (one bar of bass only or drums only), overlap (the pad of the old section still lies when the new one begins), common tone (one voice holds across the boundary), tempo modulation (new section at half or double tempo without breaking the pulse: ♩ = 60 becomes ♩ = 120 with snare on 2 and 4 instead of 3; feels like acceleration but is the same grid). Type O Negative often change sections abruptly with one bar of silence (verify); My Dying Bride overlap with violin or decay (verify).

Rule: a transition succeeds when the listener notices the boundary but does not stumble. If they do not notice, it is not a new section; if they stumble, a tool is missing.

te7-6-1.title: Listen · Intro, outro, transition
te7-6-1.instructions: Compare the intros of "Love You to Death" (Type O), "Your River" (MDB), "Sentient" (Anathema): kind (1–4), length in bars, what arrives first (key, tempo, sound). Then one outro each: kind (1–4). Claim: three different intro kinds, two different outro kinds (verify).
checklist: Three intros with kind, length and order of elements?
Three outros with kind?

te7-6-2.title: Model · Intro, outro, transition
te7-6-2.instructions: Intro (one voice, then bass added), riff, transition by dropout (one bass hit, then silence), new section B on A, outro as frame (the intro voice returns, bass disappears). Play the eight bars. Replace the transition (bar 5) once with overlap (bass holds E through) and once with a fill from the preview accompaniment; hear which transition makes B clearer.
checklist: Intro, transition and outro played as sections of their own?
Two alternative transitions compared?

te7-6-3.title: Application · Intro, outro, transition
te7-6-3.instructions: For your final piece write intro and outro as sections of their own (at least 8 bars each) and assign one tool to every transition in the form plan. Compose intro, the first transition and the outro. Record intro and outro back to back and hear whether they fit as a frame.
checklist: Intro and outro 8+ bars each, transition tool per boundary?
Intro/outro frame recorded and assessed?

tu7-7.title: The voice as a register gap
tu7-7.goal: Understand the place vocals occupy in the references and fill that place instrumentally or leave it deliberately empty.
tu7-7.text:
This course does not cover vocals. But four of the five references have them, and their absence leaves a hole you need to know.

Register: Steele (Type O Negative) sings bass-baritone, about E2–E4, often doubled in octaves (verify). Stainthorpe (My Dying Bride) growls in the riff register (around E2–E3) and speaks/sings above it (E3–E4) (verify). Cavanagh (Anathema) sings tenor, E3–A4 (verify). Vivaldi has no voice, but the solo violin occupies exactly the soprano register (G4–E6). Biber likewise.

Function: in Type O and Anathema the voice carries the melody; in MDB it carries lyrics and timbre, the melody often lies in the violin. Without a voice what is missing is: the line in the mids (E3–E4 for Steele/Stainthorpe, E3–A4 for Cavanagh). In Vivaldi nothing is missing; his model is instrumental.

Three answers for instrumental playing: 1. Put the line on an instrument that sits in the vocal register: guitar on the D/G/C strings, keyboard right hand around C4, synth lead. That is Vivaldi's solution (violin instead of soprano). 2. Leave the register empty and make the gap a sonic feature: bass below, pad above, air between. That is a sound of its own, not a mistake. 3. Occupy the line in turns: section A guitar, section B keyboard, like two singers.

What does not work: filling the vocal register with chords. Chords in E3–E4 are the riff register; they make density, not melody. A line needs a voice, not a block.

Rule: before writing a piece, decide who sings. If nobody, decide whether the gap is intentional.

te7-7-1.title: Listen · The voice as a register gap
te7-7-1.instructions: Listen to one minute each of Type O Negative, "Love You to Death", and Anathema, "Angelica", and imagine the voice removed. What remains in the register E3–A4? Is it empty? Then Vivaldi, *Winter*, movement 2: the violin as voice; which instrument in your setup could take this line? Claim: in Type O the organ stays in that register, in Anathema nothing (verify).
checklist: Register content without the voice described for both pieces?
Instrument for the Vivaldi line chosen and justified?

te7-7-2.title: Model · The voice as a register gap
te7-7-2.instructions: Bass below, pad above, and the vocal register (B3–A4) in the middle voice: bars 1–2 empty (gap as sound), bars 3–4 a line for guitar, bars 5–6 a line for keyboard (different character), bars 7–8 empty again. Play the eight bars with your instruments. Describe the gap in bars 1–2 and 7–8: does it feel empty or wide? Test-fill it with a chord in E3–E4 and hear the difference.
checklist: Gap, guitar line, keyboard line played?
Effect of the gap and the chord filler compared?

te7-7-3.title: Application · The voice as a register gap
te7-7-3.instructions: Decide for every section of your final piece: who occupies the vocal register (guitar, keyboard, nobody)? Enter it in the form plan. At least one section leaves the gap open, at least one fills it with a line. Compose one of each and record both.
checklist: Register occupation per section in the form plan?
One empty and one occupied section recorded?

t8.title: Own language
t8.goal: What the references share, your own style rules, a composition workflow, distributing roles from one pair of hands, recording and reproducibility, repertoire, and a career without money.

tu8-1.title: What the five references share and what they do not
tu8-1.goal: Name the shared grammar of the references in ten sentences and see the differences as options.
tu8-1.text:
Shared: 1. A foundation that changes less often than the line. 2. Minor as base colour with b6 as the character tone. 3. Fourth/fifth motion in the bass (E–A–D, circle of fifths, lamento). 4. Repetition as form: riff, ostinato, ritornello. 5. Contrast through register and density, not through tempo. 6. Long tones: whole and half notes are normal values. 7. Two-part writing (thirds, sixths, contrary motion) over the foundation. 8. One clear climax per piece, late. 9. The instrument's tuning as a compositional device (scordatura, B tuning, P4). 10. A sonic space in which every role has its register.

Not shared, hence a choice: cadence (Vivaldi always, MDB almost never). Tempo (Vivaldi 100–140, doom 50–80). Gain (metal yes, Baroque no; but the sustain goal is the same). Form (suite, ritornello, riff, song). Voice (four have it, one does not). Programme (Vivaldi explicit, Type O via lyrics, MDB via lyrics, Biber none). Swing (Type O occasionally, otherwise straight). Odd meters (MDB rarely, otherwise never).

The common denominator is not a style but an attitude to time: it may be long because the foundation carries. Vivaldi and doom share the pedal point, the sequence, the descending bass; they differ in repetition rate and resolution. Type O Negative are the bridge: Beatles cadences at Sabbath tempo with church organ. Anathema are the way out of metal with the same harmony.

For your language: the ten shared points are the grammar. The options are the vocabulary. A piece that breaks the grammar sounds foreign; one that varies only in vocabulary sounds like you and still like this field.

te8-1-1.title: Listen · What the five references share and what they do not
te8-1-1.instructions: Choose one piece from each reference (five in total) and check the ten shared points as a table: point × piece, yes/no/partly. Then the eight options: which option does each piece take? Claim: at least eight of the ten points hold for all five (verify).
checklist: Table 10 × 5 filled in?
Options per piece noted and claim checked?

te8-1-2.title: Model · What the five references share and what they do not
te8-1-2.instructions: Eight bars containing all ten points: slowly changing bass in fourths/thirds, minor with b6 (C), repetition of the motif, two-part writing with a held inner voice, long values, climax late (bars 7–8 with the only cadence). Play the bars and find for each of the ten points the spot where it is fulfilled. Then remove one point (e.g. replace the cadence with D–Em) and hear whether the piece still belongs to the field.
checklist: Ten points located in the example?
One point removed and belonging assessed?

te8-1-3.title: Application · What the five references share and what they do not
te8-1-3.instructions: Write eight bars that deliberately break three of the ten points (e.g. fast bass changes, major, no repetition). Play them next to the model. Describe which break carries the piece furthest out of the field. That is the border of your language; note it.
checklist: Three breaks notated and played?
Strongest break named as the border in the log?

tu8-2.title: Writing your own style rules
tu8-2.goal: Derive a personal rulebook of ten to fifteen sentences from grammar and vocabulary.
tu8-2.text:
A style is a set of decisions you do not make anew every time. The references have such rules, mostly unwritten: Type O Negative tune to B, use chorus on everything, employ organ and let the bass lead the melody. My Dying Bride play half-time, lead two guitars in thirds, use violin as a third voice and end without a cadence. These rules are recognisable because they are consistent.

Your rules arise from four sources: 1. Instrument: P4 guitar, 49 keys, three synths, three effects units. What the setup does well becomes a rule; what it cannot do becomes an exclusion. 2. References: which options from unit 1 do you take? Cadence yes or no, tempo, form. 3. Ear: what you wrote as "fits" in the log in phases 0–7. 4. Borders: what you recognised as a break in unit 1.

Form of a rule: short, testable, with an exception. "Bass changes at most every two bars; exception: cadence." "Thirds never below C4; exception: clean." "One leading tone per piece." "Tempo 55–75 in quarters; 12/8 at 40–50 in dotted quarters." "Keyboard never in the guitar register unless the guitar is silent." "Delay only on clean guitar." "Every piece has a break." "No fade-out."

Rules are not shackles but time savers: if you know the bass stays calm, you need not think about the bass and can think about the line. They are revisable; a piece that breaks a rule and is better changes the rule.

Ten to fifteen rules suffice. More is a manual, fewer is not a style.

te8-2-1.title: Listen · Writing your own style rules
te8-2-1.instructions: Derive the unwritten rules from one album each: *October Rust* and *Turn Loose the Swans*, five rules each in the form "short, testable, with exception". Check every rule against a second piece from the same album. Claim: at least four of five rules hold album-wide (verify).
checklist: Ten rules in testable form?
Every rule checked against a second piece?

te8-2-2.title: Model · Writing your own style rules
te8-2-2.instructions: Five example rules as bars: 1. Bass at most every two bars (bars 1–4). 2. Thirds only above C5 (bar 2). 3. Every phrase has a rest (bar 3). 4. Held tone across a bass change (bars 4–5). 5. Break before the ending (bar 7). Play the eight bars and name each rule at its spot. Then write your own first rule and change the eight bars so that they fulfil it.
checklist: Five rules located in the example?
Own rule formulated and implemented in the example?

te8-2-3.title: Application · Writing your own style rules
te8-2-3.instructions: Write your rulebook: ten to fifteen rules from the four sources, each short, testable, with exception. Check your longest piece so far against every rule and mark violations. Decide per violation: change the piece or change the rule. The rulebook is a living document; date it.
checklist: 10–15 rules in testable form, dated?
Own piece checked, violations decided?

tu8-3.title: Composition workflow: from motif to arrangement
tu8-3.goal: Have a fixed order that leads from an idea to a finished piece without getting lost in details.
tu8-3.text:
Seven steps, in this order, each with a testable result.

1. Motif (one day): three to five tones with rhythm, singable, notated. Test: can you sing it without the sheet after an hour's break? 2. Foundation (one day): bass path for 8–16 bars under the motif, mode fixed. Test: the bass alone forms a shape. 3. Form plan (one day): letter chain with bar counts, tempo, density arc, break, climax, cadence yes/no. After phase 7. Test: the plan is readable without notes. 4. Sketch (two to three days): every section in bass and line, no inner voices, no sound. Test: the sketch can be played through in one pass, with mistakes. 5. Inner voices and textures (two to three days): where three layers, where arpeggio, where chord, where gap. After phases 2 and 3. Test: every voice singable alone. 6. Sound (one to two days): patches, effects, frequency plan, drums. After phase 6. Test: a four-bar passage sounds like the target. 7. Score and recording (two days): cleanly notated, recorded on two days. After instrument course phase 8.

The order matters: sound before form leads to presets without a piece; inner voices before foundation to chords without bass. If at step 5 you notice step 3 was wrong, go back. Backwards is allowed, skipping is not.

The references presumably worked differently (band in the rehearsal room), but the result can be read this way: in MDB the riff (steps 1+2 at once) is the core; in Type O Negative the song (step 3 early); in Anathema the texture (steps 5 and 6 early). Vivaldi had step 3 as a convention (ritornello form) and did not need to plan it.

Schedule: at four hours a week an eight-minute piece takes six to ten weeks. That is normal. One piece per quarter is a good rate.

te8-3-1.title: Listen · Composition workflow: from motif to arrangement
te8-3-1.instructions: Take a reference piece (Type O Negative, "Green Man") and reconstruct the seven steps backwards: what is the motif? The bass path? The form plan? Where are inner voices, where gaps? Which sounds? Write every step in two lines. Claim: motif and bass path are fully audible in the first 30 seconds (verify).
checklist: Seven steps reconstructed backwards?
Motif and bass path from the first 30 seconds written?

te8-3-2.title: Model · Composition workflow: from motif to arrangement
te8-3-2.instructions: The workflow in eight bars: the same motif four times, each time one layer more: alone, with bass (step 2), with inner voice (step 5), with texture (inner voice in eighths, steps 5+6). Play each stage and apply the respective test from the text: motif singable? Bass alone a shape? Inner voice singable alone? Texture without losing the line?
checklist: Four stages played?
Four tests applied and results noted?

te8-3-3.title: Application · Composition workflow: from motif to arrangement
te8-3-3.instructions: Run the workflow completely for a new piece of at least 32 bars. Keep one log entry per step with date and test result. If you go back, note why. Result: score, two recordings, seven log entries.
checklist: Seven log entries with date and test result?
Score and two recordings present?

tu8-4.title: Distributing roles: guitar, bass, drums, synth from one pair of hands
tu8-4.goal: Lay out a piece so that one person can record all roles in turn and the result sounds like an ensemble.
tu8-4.text:
Without a band there are two routes: solo playing (the instrument course) or layered recording (overdub). The second needs planning because every role is recorded alone and cannot adapt.

Recording order: 1. Drums or click (the grid; phases 3 and 5, programmed device-neutrally). 2. Bass (the foundation; decides harmony). 3. Rhythm guitar (riff; listens to the bass). 4. Keyboard pad (listens to the guitar, fills register). 5. Line (lead guitar or synth; listens to everything). 6. Ears off, wait a day, then frequency plan (phase 6) and corrections.

Rules for layers: every role has its register (phase 6, unit 10). Every role has its rhythm: drums hold, bass holds or walks, guitar strikes, pad lies, line breathes. Two roles with the same rhythm are one role (doubling, phase 3); that is allowed but a decision. Every role has rests; a layer that never falls silent is a carpet, not an instrument.

What overdub cannot do: react. A bassist who listens to the guitarist plays differently from a bass track against a guitar track. Substitute: record in two passes, adjusting the earlier layer in the second. And: set agogics (phase 5) deliberately per layer because it does not arise by itself.

The references: Type O Negative is a studio album with many layers; that is the proof that layering can replace a band (verify). Anathema sound like a band in a room. MDB in between. For you: solo playing remains the test (does the piece carry alone?), layering is the release.

te8-4-1.title: Listen · Distributing roles: guitar, bass, drums, synth from one pair of hands
te8-4-1.instructions: Type O Negative, "Be My Druidess": count the layers (drums, bass, guitars, keyboards, voices) and determine each one's rhythm role (holds, walks, strikes, lies, breathes). Find two layers with the same rhythm (doubling). Claim: at least six layers, two of them doubled (verify).
checklist: Layers counted and rhythm role noted per layer?
Doubling found?

te8-4-2.title: Model · Distributing roles: guitar, bass, drums, synth from one pair of hands
te8-4-2.instructions: Four roles, four rhythms: bass holds (whole notes), guitar strikes (quarters with rests), pad lies (whole notes, other register), line breathes (rest, then two tones). Record the four bars as four layers in turn, in the order from the text, each against the previous recording. Listen to the result: does it sound like four instruments or like one person four times?
checklist: Four layers recorded in the given order?
Ensemble impression assessed and reason named?

te8-4-3.title: Application · Distributing roles: guitar, bass, drums, synth from one pair of hands
te8-4-3.instructions: Record 16 bars of your final piece as a layered recording: drums (programmed), bass, guitar, keyboard, line. Note per layer register, rhythm role and agogic decision. Compare with your solo version of the same 16 bars: what does layering gain, what does it lose?
checklist: Five layers documented with register, role, agogics?
Layered/solo comparison logged?

tu8-5.title: Recording and reproducibility
tu8-5.goal: Treat a recording as a document: what is captured so that a piece is playable again in a year.
tu8-5.text:
A recording is not the piece; it is a performance. The piece is the score plus the sound documentation. Reproducible means: you can play it the same way in a year with the same means, and someone else could approximate it with theirs.

What must be documented: 1. Score (instrument course phase 8): clef, key signature, meter, tempo unit, all voices, form signs, position marks. 2. Sound sheet: per role instrument, patch (parameter list, device-neutral plus device preset), effects (unit, preset, the four delay parameters, reverb type), gain level, frequency plan. 3. Drum grid (16 steps, velocities, swing percent, nudge). 4. Recording protocol: date, order of layers, tempo, which recording is the reference. 5. Deviations: where the recording departs from the score and why (rubato, mistake, spontaneous change).

Three recordings per piece, as in the instrument course: with drums, alone, with an improvised variant. The solo version is the test; if it does not carry, the piece depends on production. That is not wrong, but it must be conscious.

The references as documents: Vivaldi and Biber exist as scores; every recording is a reading, and comparing two recordings (phase 5) shows what the score leaves open. Type O Negative exists only as a recording; the band played it differently live. For you: score and recording together so that both are possible.

Format question: score as sheet music (paper or PDF), sound sheet as text, drums as grid. Not buried in a DAW project that will no longer open in five years.

te8-5-1.title: Listen · Recording and reproducibility
te8-5-1.instructions: Compare two recordings of Vivaldi, *Summer*, movement 3, by different ensembles: tempo, equality of eighths, ornaments, density of the continuo. List five differences. Then: which of these are in the score, which are reading? Claim: tempo and ornaments are reading, pitches and form are score (verify).
checklist: Five differences between two recordings listed?
Each difference classified as score or reading?

te8-5-2.title: Model · Recording and reproducibility
te8-5-2.instructions: Four bars as a complete document. For this example write the sound sheet (guitar: gain level, reverb; bass: sound; drums: half-time grid with velocities) and a recording protocol with today's date. Record the four bars. Then read only from your document and play them again without hearing the recording. Compare: what is missing from the document?
checklist: Sound sheet and protocol written, recording made?
Reproduced from the document and gaps named?

te8-5-3.title: Application · Recording and reproducibility
te8-5-3.instructions: Create the complete document for your final piece: score, sound sheet, drum grid, recording protocol, deviation list. Three recordings on three days. File the document so that it is readable without software (PDF, text, paper). Check after a week: can you rebuild the piece from the document alone?
checklist: Five document parts present, three recordings?
Rebuild checked after a week?

tu8-6.title: Repertoire: pieces, versions, set
tu8-6.goal: Turn individual pieces into a stock that stays playable and fits into an order.
tu8-6.text:
A repertoire is a set of pieces you can play at any time. Not those you could once play. The references have repertoires of 30–60 pieces over decades; a set is 8–12 of them in an order.

Maintenance: every piece has a state: new (in progress), active (playable any time, played in the last four weeks), resting (playable after a day's practice), archived (documented, no longer played). Reactivate one resting piece each week so that the active stock rotates. Four hours a week carry about six to eight active pieces alongside new work.

Versions: a piece exists in several versions: solo (guitar alone), solo (keyboard alone), layered recording, short version (4 minutes instead of 9), variant in another key (instrument course phase 8: E → A). Versions are not copies; each is its own decision about what the piece is at its core. Vivaldi reworked his own concertos several times; Type O Negative have pieces in radio and album versions (verify).

Set: an order of pieces is a form on a higher level with the same rules: contrast, density arc, climax late, frame (first and last piece related). Keys: neighbours in the circle of fifths (E, A, D) flow; a third leap (E → C) is a break, for the middle. Tempi: not two slow doom pieces in a row unless intended. A 40-minute set is five to six pieces of this length.

The suite (phase 7) is the Baroque model for a set: movements in one key with different feels of time. An album is a recorded set.

te8-6-1.title: Listen · Repertoire: pieces, versions, set
te8-6-1.instructions: Analyse *October Rust* as a set: key, tempo, length and density of every piece in a table. Draw the density arc of the album. Where is the break, where the climax? Then the same for one Vivaldi season (three movements). Claim: *October Rust* has its climax in the second half and a frame of intro and outro (verify).
checklist: Album table with four columns per piece?
Density arc of the album and the season drawn?

te8-6-2.title: Model · Repertoire: pieces, versions, set
te8-6-2.instructions: A set in four bars: each bar stands for one piece. E calm, A denser (fifth-related, flows), C as break (third leap), E as climax and frame. Play the four bars and hear the transitions: E → A soft, A → C hard, C → E return. Then assign your own pieces so far to these four positions.
checklist: Three transition qualities heard and named?
Own pieces assigned to the four positions?

te8-6-3.title: Application · Repertoire: pieces, versions, set
te8-6-3.instructions: Create a repertoire list: every own piece with state (new, active, resting, archived), versions, key, tempo, length, date of last performance. From the active and resting pieces assemble a set of 30–40 minutes with reasons for the order by key, tempo, density. Play the set through once and time it.
checklist: Repertoire list with state and versions?
Set with justified order played through once?

tu8-7.title: A career without money: publish, repeat, develop
tu8-7.goal: Set up a musical career as a practice over years, with publishing as discipline, not as goal.
tu8-7.text:
A career without income is a practice with a public. Three components: work (the pieces and their documents), rhythm (when something gets finished), public (who hears it).

Work: the repertoire from unit 6, growing by about four pieces per year at four hours a week. In five years twenty pieces, ten of them active. That is an album and a set.

Rhythm: publishing as a deadline, not as a feeling. One piece per quarter, documented and recorded, regardless of whether it is the best. One set per year, played through and recorded. Vivaldi wrote on commission with deadlines; Biber for the court; the bands for label contracts. The deadline is what amateurs mostly lack, and it is free.

Public: hearing is enough. A recording that someone hears is published. Forms: one page with the recordings and scores (no account, no comments, no numbers), a performance for two people, one piece per year sent to a person who understands it. No platform that measures reach; reach is the currency you do not need. What you need is feedback from the few who listen.

Development: the rulebook (unit 2) is revised yearly. One piece per year breaks a rule deliberately. Every two years a new tool (an instrument, a technique, a form); after this course: write your own unit. Every five years check the references: are they still the same? What has been added?

The measure: not whether someone buys it, but whether you still want to play it in ten years. Vivaldi was forgotten for 200 years; *Turn Loose the Swans* is over thirty years old and still heard. That is no guarantee, but the only reference that counts.

te8-7-1.title: Listen · A career without money: publish, repeat, develop
te8-7-1.instructions: Listen to *Turn Loose the Swans* complete, in one pass, without notes. Afterwards write from memory: which three passages stayed? Why? Repeat with one Vivaldi season. Claim: the remembered passages are returns or breaks, never openings (verify).
checklist: Three remembered passages each with reason?
Claim about return/break checked?

te8-7-2.title: Model · A career without money: publish, repeat, develop
te8-7-2.instructions: Five years as eight bars: the line rises from E4 through the triad to the climax E5 (year 5, album) and returns to the starting tone, changed by the journey. The bass stays E, changes once to A and C (new tool, break) and returns. Play the bars and set a date for each: what is finished at the end of that year?
checklist: Eight bars played and read as a schedule?
One date and one result per year fixed?

te8-7-3.title: Application · A career without money: publish, repeat, develop
te8-7-3.instructions: Write your career plan on one page: work (pieces per year), rhythm (quarterly deadlines for the next two years with dates), public (the form you choose and the two people who hear first), development (the next tool, the next rule revision). Publish the first finished piece of this course in the chosen form by the first deadline.
checklist: One-page plan with dated deadlines for two years?
First piece published in the chosen form?

ta.title: Appendices
ta.goal: Reference: acoustics and tuning, distortion and intermodulation, delay arithmetic, device translation tables, chord symbols. No tasks.

ta-1.title: A · Acoustics and tuning
ta-1.goal: Frequencies, cents, fret calculation, string tension, tunings.
ta-1.text:
**Frequency from MIDI number.** f = 440 · 2^((n − 69) / 12). A4 = MIDI 69 = 440 Hz. C4 = 60. Every octave doubles; every semitone multiplies by 2^(1/12) ≈ 1.05946.

**Frequency table (equal temperament, A4 = 440 Hz), rounded.**

- E1 41.2 · A1 55.0 · D2 73.4 · G2 98.0 · C3 130.8 · F3 174.6
- E2 82.4 · A2 110.0 · D3 146.8 · G3 196.0 · C4 261.6 · F4 349.2
- E3 164.8 · A3 220.0 · D4 293.7 · G4 392.0 · C5 523.3 · F5 698.5
- E4 329.6 · A4 440.0 · D5 587.3 · G5 784.0 · C6 1046.5 · F6 1396.9
- E5 659.3 · A5 880.0 · D6 1174.7 · B0 30.9 · B1 61.7 · B2 123.5
- B3 246.9 · B4 493.9 · B5 987.8 · F#2 92.5 · F#3 185.0 · F#4 370.0
- G#2 103.8 · G#3 207.7 · G#4 415.3 · C#3 138.6 · C#4 277.2 · C#5 554.4
- D#3 155.6 · D#4 311.1 · D#5 622.3 · Eb2 77.8 · Db3 138.6 · Bb2 116.5

**Cents.** 1 cent = 1/100 semitone. Distance between two frequencies in cents: c = 1200 · log2(f2 / f1). Pure fifth 3:2 = 701.96 cents, tempered 700 (2 cents too small). Pure major third 5:4 = 386.3, tempered 400 (14 cents too wide). Pure minor third 6:5 = 315.6, tempered 300 (16 cents too narrow). Seventh partial 7:4 = 968.8, tempered minor seventh 1000 (31 cents difference). Pitch discrimination threshold about 5 cents; beating audible from about 1 Hz difference.

**Overtone series.** Partial n has frequency n · f. Over E2 (82.4 Hz): 1 E2 · 2 E3 · 3 B3 · 4 E4 · 5 G#4 (−14 cents) · 6 B4 · 7 D5 (−31 cents) · 8 E5 · 9 F#5 · 10 G#5 · 11 between A5 and A#5 · 12 B5. Harmonic over fret 12 = partial 2, fret 7 (and 19) = partial 3, fret 5 (and 24) = partial 4, fret 4 (and 9, 16) = partial 5, fret 3.2 = partial 6.

**Fret calculation.** With scale length L (nut to bridge) fret n sits at d = L · (1 − 2^(−n/12)) from the nut. For L = 648 mm (25.5 in): fret 1 36.4 · fret 2 70.7 · fret 3 103.1 · fret 4 133.7 · fret 5 162.5 · fret 7 215.7 · fret 9 263.4 · fret 12 324.0 · fret 24 486.0 mm. Fret 12 halves the string. The distance between frets shrinks by a factor of 0.9439 per fret.

**Intonation.** Pressing down stretches the string and raises the pitch; therefore the saddle is set slightly longer than the calculated scale (compensation, 1–4 mm, more for thicker strings). Check: harmonic at fret 12 against fretted tone at fret 12; fretted too sharp → lengthen the string.

**String tension.** T = 4 · L² · f² · μ (μ = mass per length). A fourth lower (E → B) lowers f to 0.749; T falls to 0.561. To keep the same tension μ must rise by a factor of 1.78, the diameter by √1.78 ≈ 1.33. A .046 becomes about .061. P4 (C4 F4 instead of B3 E4): the two high strings one semitone higher; tension rises by a factor of 1.12; unproblematic at .009/.011, with heavier sets choose one step thinner.

**Tunings.** Standard E2 A2 D3 G3 B3 E4 (intervals 5-5-5-4-5 semitones). P4 E2 A2 D3 G3 C4 F4 (5-5-5-5-5). Type O Negative B1 E2 A2 D3 F#3 B3, standard a fourth lower (verify). Bass E1 A1 D2 G2. Violin G3 D4 A4 E5 (fifths). Biber scordaturas: a different tuning per partita, written in the score; the tablature-like notation shows fingerings, not sounding pitches.

**Sustain measurement.** Strike the tone, stopwatch, time until audible tipping into noise or until −40 dB on a level meter. One table per rig and register (phase 5, unit 5).

ta-2.title: B · Distortion and intermodulation
ta-2.goal: Calculate combination tones, interval table over E, rules for register and gain.
ta-2.text:
**Clipping.** An overdriven amplifier cuts off the peaks. Soft clipping (tube, overdrive) rounds, producing mainly odd and quiet even overtones. Hard clipping (diode, distortion) produces stronger and higher overtones up to a square wave (fuzz). Every single tone gets overtones at 2f, 3f, 4f …; that is the "brightness" of distortion.

**Intermodulation.** Two tones f1 < f2 produce combination tones: difference f2 − f1, sum f1 + f2, and higher orders 2f1 − f2, 2f2 − f1, 3f1 − 2f2 … The stronger the clipping, the louder the higher orders. All combination tones are real frequencies in the output signal; they are not an auditory illusion.

**Table over E3 (164.8 Hz).** Interval · upper tone · difference · nearest tone · 2f1 − f2 · nearest tone:

- Octave E4 329.6 · diff 164.8 = E3 · 2f1−f2 0 (none)
- Fifth B3 246.9 · diff 82.1 ≈ E2 · 2f1−f2 82.7 ≈ E2
- Fourth A3 220.0 · diff 55.2 ≈ A1 · 2f1−f2 109.6 ≈ A2
- Major third G#3 207.7 · diff 42.9 ≈ E1 · 2f1−f2 122.0 ≈ B2
- Minor third G3 196.0 · diff 31.2 ≈ B0 · 2f1−f2 133.6 ≈ C3 (foreign in Em)
- Major second F#3 185.0 · diff 20.2 (below hearing, roughness) · 2f1−f2 144.6 ≈ D3
- Minor second F3 174.6 · diff 9.8 (beating) · 2f1−f2 155.0 ≈ D#3
- Tritone A#3 233.1 · diff 68.3 ≈ C#2 · 2f1−f2 96.5 ≈ G2
- Minor sixth C4 261.6 · diff 96.8 ≈ G2 · 2f1−f2 68.0 ≈ C#2
- Major sixth C#4 277.2 · diff 112.4 ≈ A2 · 2f1−f2 52.4 ≈ G#1

**Reading.** Octave, fifth, fourth: all combination tones are chord tones or their octaves. Major third: difference is the root, second order is B (fifth), hence viable. Minor third: difference below the bass, second order C: a foreign tone that makes the minor third muddy. Seconds: roughness instead of tone. Sixths: foreign tones, but quiet and high enough to count as colour.

**Over E2 (82.4 Hz)** all difference tones halve: fifth → 41 Hz (E1, pressure), minor third → 15.6 Hz (below hearing, modulation only), second order 66.8 Hz ≈ C2. Hence avoid low thirds and keep fifths low.

**Rules.** 1. Below E3 only root, octave, fifth. 2. Thirds from E3 at medium gain, from E4 at high gain. 3. The major third tolerates more gain than the minor. 4. Under gain sixths are the better thirds (inversion upward). 5. Less gain or a low-pass before the distortion reduces intermodulation more than any EQ after it. 6. Two guitars in thirds: both with less gain than the riff, both above E3.

ta-3.title: C · Delay arithmetic and time values
ta-3.goal: Milliseconds from tempo and note value, swing percentages, pre-delay and room size.
ta-3.text:
**Basic formula.** Quarter in ms = 60000 / BPM (BPM in quarters). Eighth = quarter / 2. Sixteenth = quarter / 4. Dotted eighth = quarter · 0.75. Eighth triplet = quarter / 3. Quarter triplet = quarter · 2/3. Half = quarter · 2. Whole = quarter · 4. In 12/8 with tempo ♩. = BPM: dotted quarter = 60000 / BPM, eighth = one third of it.

**Table (quarter · eighth · dotted eighth · eighth triplet · half), ms:**

- 50: 1200 · 600 · 900 · 400 · 2400
- 55: 1091 · 545 · 818 · 364 · 2182
- 60: 1000 · 500 · 750 · 333 · 2000
- 65: 923 · 462 · 692 · 308 · 1846
- 70: 857 · 429 · 643 · 286 · 1714
- 72: 833 · 417 · 625 · 278 · 1667
- 75: 800 · 400 · 600 · 267 · 1600
- 80: 750 · 375 · 563 · 250 · 1500
- 85: 706 · 353 · 529 · 235 · 1412
- 90: 667 · 333 · 500 · 222 · 1333
- 95: 632 · 316 · 474 · 211 · 1263
- 100: 600 · 300 · 450 · 200 · 1200
- 120: 500 · 250 · 375 · 167 · 1000
- 140: 429 · 214 · 321 · 143 · 857

**Rhythmic delays.** Dotted eighth over eighth notes yields a sixteenth grid (each repeat lands a sixteenth before the next attack). Quarter delay over half notes doubles the attacks. Eighth-triplet delay over straight eighths creates a shuffle feel. Two delays (quarter and dotted eighth) together give the dense U2 pattern. At doom tempi delays are long: a quarter at 60 = one second; that is already spatial.

**Feedback and number of repeats.** Number of audible repeats ≈ log(0.01) / log(feedback), for a −40 dB audibility limit: feedback 30 % → 4, 50 % → 7, 70 % → 13, 90 % → 44. In practice (with filtering) about half.

**Swing percentage.** Share of the first eighth in the quarter: 50 % straight, 58 % light, 62 % medium, 67 % triplet (2:1), 75 % dotted (3:1). For sixteenth swing the same at eighth level. Digitakt scale 50–80 %, SP-404 "shuffle" 50–100 % depending on model (verify), SR-18 fixed steps (verify).

**Pre-delay and room.** Sound 343 m/s → 1 ms ≈ 34 cm. Pre-delay 10 ms ≈ first reflection after a 3.4 m detour (small room), 30 ms ≈ 10 m (hall), 60 ms ≈ 20 m (church). Reverb time RT60: time to −60 dB. Living room 0.4 s, studio 0.3 s, hall 1.5–2.5 s, church 3–8 s.

**Haas effect.** Two signals less than 30–40 ms apart are heard as one, localised toward the earlier. A doubling delay of 15–25 ms without feedback widens without sounding like an echo.

**Microtiming.** At ♩ = 60 a sixteenth lasts 250 ms; laid-back sits at 10–40 ms, i.e. 4–16 % of a sixteenth. On devices with stepped nudge: Digitakt ±23 steps per sixteenth (verify), i.e. about 11 ms per step at 60 BPM.

ta-4.title: D · Device tables
ta-4.goal: Generic terms from phases 3, 5 and 6 mapped to Nord Lead A1, Blofeld, TC 2290, G-Major, Nova System, SR-18, Digitakt, SP-404. All device names from manuals, to be checked at the unit.
ta-4.text:
All names in this appendix are compiled from manuals and memory and must be checked at the unit (verify). Where a unit lacks a parameter, the substitute is listed.

**Synthesis: generic → Nord Lead A1 → Blofeld.**

- Waveform → Osc Waveform (saw, pulse, tri, sine, limited wavetables) → Osc 1–3 Shape (pulse, saw, tri, sine, Alt 1/2 = wavetables)
- Second oscillator, detune → Osc Config (mix, detune, sync, FM, noise …) → Osc 2 + Osc 3, detune per osc
- Pulse width / PWM → Osc Config pulse width; LFO → Shape → pulsewidth per osc; mod matrix → PW
- FM → Osc Config FM mode (limited) → FM source/amount per osc
- Wavetable position → not available (waveform morph as substitute) → Wave per osc (Alt waves), modulatable
- Low-pass 24 dB → Filter Type LP24 / Ladder M → Filter 1/2 type LP 24 dB
- Low-pass 12 dB → LP12 → LP 12 dB
- High-pass → HP → HP 12/24 dB
- Band-pass → BP → BP 12/24 dB
- Cutoff / resonance → Freq / Res → Cutoff / Resonance
- Filter envelope → Mod Env to filter (amount) → Filter Env (amount per filter)
- Amplifier envelope ADSR → Amp Env A D S R → Amp Env (A D S R, plus Env 3/4)
- Keytrack → Filter KB Track → Keytrack per filter
- LFO rate / amount / destination → LFO 1/2 Rate, Amount, Dest → LFO 1–3 Speed, Shape; destination via mod matrix
- Modulation matrix → limited (Mod Env, LFO dest, velocity/mod wheel dest) → Modifier + Mod Matrix (16 slots: source, amount, dest)
- Velocity → cutoff → Velocity Dest → mod matrix Velocity → Cutoff
- Chorus → FX: Chorus / Ensemble → Effect 1/2: Chorus
- Phaser / flanger → FX: Phaser / Flanger → Effect: Phaser / Flanger
- Delay → Delay (tempo sync) → Effect 2: Delay / Clocked Delay
- Reverb → Reverb (Room, Stage, Hall) → Effect 2: Reverb
- Distortion → FX: Drive → Effect: Overdrive
- Unison / width → Unison → Unisono (dual/triple …) + detune

**Effects: generic → TC 2290 → G-Major → Nova System.**

- Delay time → Delay (ms, up to memory limit) → Delay Time / tempo sync with note value → Delay Time / Tempo with note value
- Feedback → Feedback (%) → Feedback → Feedback
- Filter in feedback (low-pass) → feedback filter / hi-cut, otherwise EQ before (verify) → Hi-Cut → Hi-Cut
- High-pass in feedback → not available, EQ before → Lo-Cut → Lo-Cut
- Modulation of delay time → Mod: Speed, Depth (pitch/delay mod) → Mod Speed, Depth → Mod Speed, Depth (depending on type)
- Delay type tape → build from filter + mod → type "Tape" if firmware, otherwise Single + Hi-Cut → type Tape
- Delay type BBD/analog → build from filter + mod, time under 400 ms → Single + Hi-Cut 2.5 kHz + mod → type Analog
- Ducking → Dynamic Delay → Dynamic Delay → Dynamic Delay
- Ping-pong → Pan Mod (verify) → Ping-Pong → Ping-Pong
- Reverb type → not available (delay network) → Reverb: Hall, Room, Plate, Spring → Reverb: Spring, Hall, Room, Plate
- Reverb time → — → Decay → Decay
- Pre-delay → delay without feedback before reverb (external) → Pre-Delay → Pre-Delay
- Reverb high-pass → — → Lo-Color / Lo-Cut (verify) → Lo-Color / Lo-Cut (verify)
- Chorus → short delay 15–35 ms + mod → Chorus (Speed, Depth, Width) → Chorus
- Flanger → delay 1–10 ms + feedback + mod → Flanger → Flanger
- Phaser → — → Phaser → Phaser
- Compressor → — → Compressor → Compressor
- Distortion → — → — → Drive (several types)
- Input level → Input Level → Input Level → Input Gain
- Tempo sync → tempo entry / tap (verify) → Tap Tempo, MIDI Clock → Tap Tempo, MIDI Clock

**Drums: generic → SR-18 → Digitakt → SP-404.**

- Pattern grid (16 steps) → Step Edit in pattern mode → Trigs, 16 per page, pattern up to 64 → pattern sequencer with quantize (check grid)
- Instrument per step → drum pad assignment (kit) → Track 1–8, sample per track → pad per bank
- Velocity → pad hit / velocity curve (verify) → velocity per trig (1–127) → pad velocity, fixed steps depending on model (verify)
- Swing → swing steps (verify) → Swing 50–80 % per pattern → shuffle value (verify)
- Nudge / microtiming → not available → microtiming per trig (±23/384) → limited depending on model (verify)
- Fill → fill pattern (A/B fill) → conditional trigs / separate pattern → separate pattern
- Pattern change → pattern chain / song mode → chain / song mode → pattern chain
- Tempo → BPM on the unit or MIDI clock → BPM or MIDI clock → BPM or MIDI clock
- Level per instrument → kit mix → track level → pad level
- Hi-hat open/closed → separate pads → separate samples, choke group → separate pads, mute group (verify)

**Course convention.** Patch and preset recipes in the course always name the generic column. To transfer: find the row, read the device column, enter the value, note the actual result in the log. Deviations between table and unit belong in this appendix.

ta-5.title: E · Chord symbol reference
ta-5.goal: Every common symbol with tones over E, A and D.
ta-5.text:
**Reading order.** Root · type (nothing = major, m, dim/°, aug/+) · seventh (7 minor, maj7/Δ major) · extension (9, 11, 13) · alteration (b5, #5, b9, #9, #11, b13) · addition (add) · omission (no3, no5) · bass (/X). The symbol fixes tones, not spacing, doubling or duration.

**Table: symbol · over E · over A · over D.**

- 5 (power chord) · E B · A E · D A
- major · E G# B · A C# E · D F# A
- m · E G B · A C E · D F A
- dim / ° · E G Bb · A C Eb · D F Ab
- aug / + · E G# B# · A C# E# · D F# A#
- sus2 · E F# B · A B E · D E A
- sus4 · E A B · A D E · D G A
- 6 · E G# B C# · A C# E F# · D F# A B
- m6 · E G B C# · A C E F# · D F A B
- 7 · E G# B D · A C# E G · D F# A C
- maj7 / Δ · E G# B D# · A C# E G# · D F# A C#
- m7 · E G B D · A C E G · D F A C
- m(maj7) · E G B D# · A C E G# · D F A C#
- dim7 / °7 · E G Bb Db · A C Eb Gb · D F Ab Cb
- m7b5 / ø · E G Bb D · A C Eb G · D F Ab C
- 7sus4 · E A B D · A D E G · D G A C
- add9 · E G# B F# · A C# E B · D F# A E
- madd9 · E G B F# · A C E B · D F A E
- 9 · E G# B D F# · A C# E G B · D F# A C E
- maj9 · E G# B D# F# · A C# E G# B · D F# A C# E
- m9 · E G B D F# · A C E G B · D F A C E
- 11 (third usually omitted) · E B D F# A · A E G B D · D A C E G
- m11 · E G B D F# A · A C E G B D · D F A C E G
- 13 · E G# B D F# C# · A C# E G B F# · D F# A C E B
- 7b9 · E G# B D F · A C# E G Bb · D F# A C Eb
- 7#9 · E G# B D G (F##) · A C# E G C (B#) · D F# A C F (E#)
- 7#11 · E G# B D A# · A C# E G D# · D F# A C G#
- 7b5 · E G# Bb D · A C# Eb G · D F# Ab C
- maj7#11 · E G# B D# A# · A C# E G# D# · D F# A C# G#
- m6/9 · E G B C# F# · A C E F# B · D F A B E

**Slash chords.** X/Y: chord X with bass tone Y. Em/G first inversion, Em/B second. Em/C is not an Em chord over C but sounds as Cmaj7 without a doubled root; if C is the bass, the chord is called Cmaj7. Rule: if the bass tone is a chord tone, it is an inversion; if not, it is usually a different chord with a different name. Em/D is Em7 in third inversion. D/E is an Esus sound (E D F# A), often written E9sus4.

**Degrees in E Aeolian (triads · seventh chords).** i Em · Em7; ii° F#dim · F#m7b5; III G · Gmaj7; iv Am · Am7; v Bm · Bm7; VI C · Cmaj7; VII D · D7. Harmonic minor changes: V B · B7; vii° D#dim · D#dim7; III+ G+ · Gmaj7#5. Melodic minor additionally changes: ii F#m · F#m7; IV A · A7; vi° C#dim · C#m7b5.

**Degrees in A Aeolian.** Am, Bdim, C, Dm, Em, F, G; harmonic: E, G#dim. **In D Aeolian.** Dm, Edim, F, Gm, Am, Bb, C; harmonic: A, C#dim.

**Common symbols in the references (per course analysis, verify).** Power chords (all metal references). Plain triads Em, C, D, Am, G, B (Type O Negative, MDB). madd9 and maj7 as pads (Anathema). Dominant sevenths and dim7 (Vivaldi, Biber, Type O at closes). sus4 → 3 as suspension (Baroque).

**Your notation.** Symbols above the notes are commentary; the notes are binding. For power chords write the symbol with 5, not the triad name, so that the missing third is documented.

ui.lead: From imagined sound to instrument. P4 guitar with bass and melody; keyboard for synth and piano. Doom, Gothic and Baroque as musical directions.

ui.logLead: Local practice journal. Mark an exercise as reliable after two practice days without aids. A backup includes completion marks, notes and deletion records. Restoring merges entries, so contributions from several devices can be combined manually. No automatic network sync. Recheck older completion marks for revised exercises.

ui.schedule:
A, B, C: 45 minutes guitar + 15 minutes keyboard each. D: 15 minutes guitar + 45 minutes keyboard. This gives 3 × 45 + 15 = 150 guitar minutes and 3 × 15 + 45 = 90 keyboard minutes.

**45 minutes:** 5 recall · 10 one difficulty · 20 listening, playing and varying · 5 recording · 5 break/log. **15 minutes:** 3 recall · 8 application · 4 recording/log.

Work on one unit per instrument. First task already secure → move to application. Resolve unfamiliar movements without time pressure, then stabilise with a click. Increase tempo only while pulse and tone remain controlled.

**Move on:** meet the criteria on two practice days, including one attempt without aids. Isolate a difficult passage, then return to a whole phrase. Notation is the main view, position is above it, and aids can be enabled.
ui.hardware:
**MX49:** Drum kit on Part 10. Choose the appropriate USB MIDI output or MIDI interface.

**SR-18:** MIDI CH = 10, DRUM IN = ON: V1, NOTE MAP = NORMAL. Under NOTE, assign pads accordingly: kick 36, snare 38, closed hi-hat 42, click/rim 37. Stop its own pattern. The SR-18 needs a MIDI interface with a DIN output.

The website sends individual notes, not MIDI clock or transport commands to the internal sequencer. Set sounds and volume on the device. Click/drums have no internal fallback. Score preview separately uses browser sound.
ui.remoteUpdate: Journal updated from another browser tab.
ui.swingFeel: Swing reading: preview uses a 2:1 study ratio; tempo counts quarters.
ui.pianoLoadError: Could not load the piano. Check your connection and press Listen to retry.
ui.previewInterrupted: Preview stopped after a playback interruption. Press Listen to restart.
ui.guitarAttack: Attack: pick in the right hand, legato/tapping in the left. Initially spread shared entries briefly from low to high; do not reattack sustained notes. Piano preview plays the rhythmic voice framework, not this distribution of physical attacks.
ui.verify: Verify the claim against the album; log the timestamp after the first listen.
